items.title: LFX Term 3: Per-instrumentation configuration: let users control how individual instrumentations behave
items.body:
## Problem

Users can only turn instrumentations on or off (`OTEL_GO_ENABLED/DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS`); there is no way to configure how one behaves: capture specific HTTP headers or gRPC metadata, redact URL query parameters, opt into a semconv migration gradually, or set any library-specific option. Configuration granularity was the top post-v1 community ask, and upcoming work (messaging span-links migration, GenAI content capture) needs an opt-in mechanism; ad-hoc env vars per feature do not scale.

## Proposed solution

Adopt the OTel [declarative configuration](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-configuration) model instead of inventing our own format. Its `instrumentation/development` node defines exactly this surface:

```yaml
instrumentation/development:
  general:                        # cross-language, semconv-domain keyed
    http:
      server:
        request_captured_headers: [X-Tenant-Id]
    messaging:
      semconv:
        dual_emit: true           # migration gate
  go:                             # language-specific, owned by us
    kafka-go:
      enabled: ${OTEL_GO_KAFKA:-true}
```

otelc reads the file at build time and exposes the values to hooks at runtime; existing env vars keep working and take precedence. Mechanics go in a follow-up ADR.

Similar approach to what Java agent does.

Context: the SDK half of that model is stable (Go has `otelconf`); the instrumentation node is experimental, consumed by the Java agent, and implemented by nothing in Go yet. The closed `general` node gives us cross-language semantics (captured headers, URL sanitization, per-domain semconv migration); the open `go:` node is a free-form `<instrumentation-name>: <options>` map we fully own, so upstream coverage never limits us. Gaps we hit get proposed upstream.

## Goals

1. otelc accepts the config file; hooks read their configuration at runtime with documented precedence (env vars > file > defaults).
2. First consumers on existing instrumentations: HTTP captured headers (net/http, gin), URL sanitization, gRPC metadata capture (under `go:`), enable/disable expressed as `go: <name>: enabled`.
3. A maintainable process, not just options: each instrumentation declares its configurable options in a manifest (as the Java agent does with `metadata.yaml`); the `go:` validation schema, a generated catalog of every configurable option, and defaults all derive from it, and CI forbids hooks from reading undeclared configuration. This makes "what can I configure?" a build artifact that cannot drift from the code.
4. ADR settling the model: the split with `otel.instrumentation.go` (tool files decide what gets woven, this file decides how it behaves), the decision tree for which parameters become configurable and where they live (semconv opt-in must use upstream `general` keys; cross-library gaps ship under `go:` with an upstream proposal; library-specific stays under `go:`), and a development-to-stable lifecycle for options.

## Concerns to discuss

- `instrumentation/development` is experimental upstream; Java ships it anyway. Comfortable building on it now (pinning a schema version)?
- otelc is a build tool: file must exist at build time; deploy-time changes go through `${ENV}` substitution or env vars, unlike the Java agent.
- Configurable options are permanent API surface: `general`/shared additions need maintainer sign-off; library-local options ride normal review. Is that the right review gate?
- `go:` key naming/ownership, incl. third-party instrumentation packages.
- Keep `OTEL_GO_*` env vars indefinitely or deprecate once config lands?

items.title: Record compile-time otelc (probe) version on telemetry resource
items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

After `otelc go build`, there is no reliable way to tell **which version of `otelc` produced a given application binary**.

Today:

- `otelc version` only reports the version of the **currently installed CLI**, not the tool that historically built a binary.
- Injected instrumentation uses `ModuleVersion()` (from `debug.ReadBuildInfo().Main.Version`) as the instrumentation scope version. For local/`(devel)` builds this typically falls back to `"dev"`, which is the **application module** version semantics, not the compile-time probe/`otelc` version.
- Resource setup uses detectors such as `resource.WithFromEnv()`, so users can set `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` at **runtime**, but that is easy to misconfigure and can drift from the version that actually performed the instrumentation.

This makes multi-version rollouts, regressions, and “which probe built this binary?” debugging harder.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Discuss whether `otelc` should **bake the compile-time probe version into the instrumented binary** and expose it on the OpenTelemetry Resource using the [Telemetry distro](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/resource/#telemetry-distro) semantic conventions:

- `telemetry.distro.name` — e.g. `opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation` (official distros SHOULD prefer an `opentelemetry-` prefix)
- `telemetry.distro.version` — the exact `otelc` version used for that build (tag + commit / the same string `otelc version` reports)

Ideal properties:

1. The value is fixed at **compile time** and travels with the binary (not only via launch-time env).
2. It appears on exported traces/metrics/logs Resource so backends can filter/group by probe version.
3. It merges correctly with `resource.Default()` / `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` (user-provided attributes should keep their documented precedence).

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

1. **Runtime-only**: CI captures `otelc version` and sets `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=telemetry.distro.name=...,telemetry.distro.version=...` at process start. Works today, but is operationally fragile and not self-describing from the binary alone.
2. **Instrumentation scope version only**: Continue using / extending scope `Version`. Less ideal for “which agent/distro built this”, since scope version is per-instrumentation-library and currently tied to app `ModuleVersion()`.
3. **Out-of-band metadata**: Image labels / SBOM / CI artifacts. Useful for ops, but not visible in OTLP Resource.

**Additional context**

- Spec: [Resource semantic conventions — Telemetry distro](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/resource/#telemetry-distro)
- Other language auto-instrumentation agents (e.g. Java) already populate `telemetry.distro.*` for this reason.
- Open questions for maintainers / the community:
  - Is baking distro attributes at compile time in scope for `otelc`?
  - Preferred `telemetry.distro.name` string?
  - Preferred injection mechanism (generated runtime constant during preprocess / embed tool version into `pkg/runtime` / rewrite at instrumentation time)?
  - Should this also align instrumentation scope versions, or keep distro version strictly on Resource?

Happy to help iterate on design or a prototype if this direction looks desirable.

items.title: LFX Mentorship 2026 Term 3 — Zero-code AI Agent observability for otelc
items.body:
## Summary

This is the upstream project-idea issue for a **CNCF LFX Mentorship 2026 Term 3** program under OpenTelemetry, targeting `opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation` (`otelc`) — OpenTelemetry's compile-time, zero-code instrumentation for Go.

The goal is to design and build an **AI provider adapter interface** in `otelc` that emits the `gen_ai.*` semantic conventions (spans, metrics, events) through a single shared abstraction, so AI providers and libraries plug into a common contract instead of being instrumented ad hoc. The already-merged OpenAI instrumentation (#604) is migrated onto this interface as the reference, then extended to `anthropic-sdk-go`, **Gemini, MCP, and LangChain**. MCP/LangChain require non-HTTP hooks (following the Kafka/Redis instrumentation patterns) rather than the HTTP-based path. This design-first framing gives the mentee real architecture and problem-solving work rather than repetitive per-library instrumentation.

## Motivation

Community demand is concrete and vendor-neutral: the OpenAI instrumentation (#604) closed community issue #327, and the request pipeline is active (#706 for aws-sdk-go-v2, #553 MongoDB shipped). AI Agent frameworks are a fast-growing gap for zero-code Go observability.

## Deliverables (week-by-week)

A per-week plan where each milestone ships a **runnable demo + green CI** so progress is visible at a glance: adapter interface + OpenAI migration → `anthropic-sdk-go` → Gemini → MCP → LangChain, each with instrumentation rules, tests under the paired `test/` directory, and an example app emitting `gen_ai.*` spans.

## Privacy posture

Message bodies are **off by default** and strictly opt-in via `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT` — nothing is captured unless the operator turns it on.

items.title: fix(runtime): instrumented apps ignore SIGTERM, breaking graceful telemetry shutdown
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Instrumented applications only register a shutdown handler for `SIGINT` (`os.Interrupt`) in `pkg/runtime/setup.go`. They do **not** handle `SIGTERM`, which is the standard shutdown signal used by Kubernetes, Docker, and systemd.

As a result, when an instrumented app receives SIGTERM, it exits immediately without flushing OpenTelemetry telemetry. The `otelc` CLI itself handles both `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM`, and the gRPC demo README documents that both signals trigger graceful shutdown - but the injected runtime only implements `SIGINT`.

### Environment

- OS: Linux (also affects other Unix-like systems; Windows behavior may differ)
- Go Version: 1.25.0
- Version: `otelc` built from `main` at commit `6ca7a2020abd` (2026-07-19)

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Build the instrumented gRPC demo server:
   ```bash
   cd demo/app/grpc/server
   otelc go build -o /tmp/grpc-server-instr .
   ```

2. Run the server with console trace export:
   ```bash
   OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=console OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none \
     OTEL_GO_SIMPLE_SPAN_PROCESSOR=false \
     /tmp/grpc-server-instr -port=50123
   ```

3. In another terminal, send **SIGTERM** to the server process:
   ```bash
   kill -TERM <pid>
   ```

4. Observe the process exits with code **143** and there are **no** graceful shutdown log messages.

5. For comparison, repeat steps 1–2, then send **SIGINT** instead:
   ```bash
   kill -INT <pid>
   ```

6. Observe the process exits with code **0** and logs:
   ```
   received signal, initiating graceful shutdown
   OpenTelemetry SDK shutdown completed successfully
   ```

**Relevant code:**

- Runtime handler only registers `os.Interrupt`: `pkg/runtime/setup.go` (line ~310)
- `otelc` CLI handles both signals: `tool/cmd/otelc/main.go` (line ~111)
- Docs claim both work: `demo/app/grpc/README.md` (line ~107)
- Integration test only covers SIGINT: `test/integration/grpc_server_test.go` (line ~88)

### Expected behavior

When an instrumented application receives **SIGTERM**, it should behave the same as on **SIGINT**:

- Log `received signal, initiating graceful shutdown`
- Call `Shutdown()` to flush pending traces/metrics/logs
- Exit cleanly (exit code 0)

This matches the documented behavior in `demo/app/grpc/README.md` and is required for correct shutdown in container/orchestrator environments.

### Additional context

| Signal  | Exit code | Graceful shutdown? |
|---------|-----------|-------------------|
| SIGTERM | 143       | No                |
| SIGINT  | 0         | Yes               |

items.title: fix(runtime): handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown
items.body:
## Description

Instrumented applications now handle **SIGTERM** in addition to **SIGINT** for graceful OpenTelemetry SDK shutdown.

Changes:
- Register `syscall.SIGTERM` alongside `os.Interrupt` in `pkg/runtime/setup.go`
- Extract `shutdownSignals()` so the registered signals are explicit and testable
- Add `TestShutdownSignals` unit test in `pkg/runtime/setup_test.go`
- Extend gRPC integration tests to cover SIGTERM shutdown (previously only SIGINT was tested)

When an instrumented app receives SIGTERM (the standard shutdown signal from Kubernetes, Docker, and systemd), it now flushes pending telemetry before exiting - matching the behavior already documented in `demo/app/grpc/README.md` and implemented in the `otelc` CLI itself.

## Motivation

The injected runtime only registered a handler for `os.Interrupt` (SIGINT). Production environments typically send **SIGTERM** on shutdown, not SIGINT.

**Before this fix:**
- SIGINT → graceful shutdown, exit 0, telemetry flushed
- SIGTERM → immediate kill, exit 143, telemetry lost

**After this fix:**
- Both SIGINT and SIGTERM trigger graceful shutdown and telemetry flush

This aligns runtime behavior with:
- `tool/cmd/otelc/main.go` (CLI handles both signals)

items.title: fix(tool): reject malformed version ranges in instrumentation rules
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Malformed `version` ranges in instrumentation rules are **accepted at load time** but produce **incorrect matching behavior** with no error or warning.

The docs specify the format as `start_inclusive,end_exclusive` (e.g. `v0.11.0,v0.12.0`), and empty/invalid `target` values are rejected loudly at parse time - but **`version` is never validated**. Typos cause instrumentation to silently not apply, or to apply far too broadly.

**Verified behavior** (`tool/util/shared.go` → `VersionInRange`):

| Rule `version` | Test version | Result | Problem |
|----------------|--------------|--------|---------|
| `v1.0.0,v2.0.0` | `v1.5.0` | ✅ match | Correct |
| `v1.0.0,` (trailing comma) | `v1.5.0` | ❌ no match | Silent miss - instrumentation never applies |
| `,v2.0.0` (missing lower bound) | `v0.5.0` | ✅ match | Overly broad -matches versions that should be excluded |
| `v1.0.0,v2.0.0,v3.0.0` (extra comma) | `v1.5.0` | ❌ no match | Silent miss - user likely meant a valid range |

Rules with these malformed values load without error because `tool/internal/setup/match.go` validates `target` but passes `version` straight to `VersionInRange()`.

### Environment

- OS: Linux
- Go Version: 1.25.0
- Version: `otelc` v1.0.1 / main branch

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Run this small program using `VersionInRange` from `tool/util`:

   ```go
   package main

   import (
       "fmt"
       "go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/tool/util"
   )

   func main() {
       cases := []struct{ version, versionRange string }{
           {"v1.5.0", "v1.0.0,v2.0.0"},
           {"v1.5.0", "v1.0.0,"},
           {"v0.5.0", ",v2.0.0"},
           {"v1.5.0", "v1.0.0,v2.0.0,v3.0.0"},
       }
       for _, c := range cases {
           fmt.Printf("VersionInRange(%q, %q) = %v\n", c.version, c.versionRange, util.VersionInRange(c.version, c.versionRange))
       }
   }
   ```

2. Observe output:
   ```
   VersionInRange("v1.5.0", "v1.0.0,v2.0.0") = true
   VersionInRange("v1.5.0", "v1.0.0,") = false
   VersionInRange("v0.5.0", ",v2.0.0") = true
   VersionInRange("v1.5.0", "v1.0.0,v2.0.0,v3.0.0") = false
   ```

3. Create a rule YAML with `version: "v1.0.0,"` or `version: ",v2.0.0"` - it loads without error.

4. Compare with empty `target`, which **is** rejected at load time in `tool/internal/setup/match.go` (lines 84–86).

### Expected behavior

Invalid `version` ranges should be **rejected at rule load time** with a clear error (consistent with how invalid `target` values are handled), for example:

- Trailing comma: `v1.0.0,`
- Missing lower bound: `,v2.0.0`
- More than one comma: `v1.0.0,v2.0.0,v3.0.0`
- Empty version components

At minimum, malformed ranges should not silently cause instrumentation to never match or to match all versions.

### Additional context

- **Docs:** `docs/rules.md` line 74 defines format as `start_inclusive,end_exclusive`
- **Code:** `tool/util/shared.go` lines 127–146 (`VersionInRange`)
- **Load path:** `tool/internal/setup/match.go` line 109 (`matchVersion`) - no validation before use
- **Existing tests:** `tool/util/shared_test.go` covers valid ranges only; no malformed-range cases
- **Suggested fix:** Add `ValidateVersionRange()` at rule load time (alongside existing `ValidateTarget()`), plus unit tests for malformed inputs

**Impact:** Version gating is a safety mechanism for instrumentation rules. Silent failures make typos very hard to debug - especially in CI/CD where rules are applied automatically.

items.title: OpenAI middleware does not reassemble request/response bodies on preview read errors
items.body:
### Problem

While checking the current `upstream/main`, I found that the OpenAI middleware still returns early on preview read errors before reassembling the request/response body.

This affects all three OpenAI versions:

- `instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go/middleware.go`
- `instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go/v2/middleware.go`
- `instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go/v3/middleware.go`

### Current behavior

In the request path, the middleware reads a bounded preview of `req.Body` for attribute parsing. If that read fails, it returns before rebuilding the original body stream for the SDK.

In the response path, the middleware reads a bounded preview of `resp.Body` for attribute parsing. If that read fails, it returns before rebuilding the original body stream for the caller.

So on read-error paths, the body may already be partially consumed when control returns.

### Expected behavior

The body should be reassembled before checking the preview read error, so the SDK/caller still sees the original stream behavior and error path.

### Evidence

OpenAI request path:
- `instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go/middleware.go`
- `instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go/v2/middleware.go`
- `instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go/v3/middleware.go`

OpenAI response path:
- same files as above

Anthropic already uses the safer pattern and has regression coverage for it:
- `instrumentation/github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-go/middleware.go`
- `instrumentation/github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-go/middleware_test.go`

items.title: fix(tool): reject malformed version ranges
items.body:
## Description

Adds `ValidateVersionRange()` and rejects malformed `version` fields at rule load time, consistent with how invalid `target` values are already handled.

Changes:
- Add `ValidateVersionRange()` in `tool/util/shared.go`
- Call it from `tool/internal/setup/match.go` when rules are loaded
- Add unit tests in `tool/util/shared_test.go`
- Add `TestMatchDeps_InvalidVersionRangeRejected` in `tool/internal/setup/match_test.go`

Valid formats (per `docs/rules.md`):
- `""` - match all versions
- `"v1.0.0"` - minimum version
- `"v1.0.0,v2.0.0"` - `start_inclusive,end_exclusive`

Invalid formats now fail loudly at load time instead of being accepted silently.

## Motivation

Malformed `version` ranges were accepted without error but produced incorrect matching behavior:

| Malformed `version` | Before (bug) |
|---------------------|--------------|
| `v1.0.0,` (trailing comma) | Rule loaded; instrumentation never matched |
| `,v2.0.0` (missing lower bound) | Rule loaded; matched too broadly |
| `v1.0.0,v2.0.0,v3.0.0` (extra comma) | Rule loaded; instrumentation never matched |
| `v2.0.0,v1.0.0` (inverted range) | Rule loaded; nonsensical matching |

This is inconsistent with `target` validation, which already fails loudly at load time. Version gating is a safety mechanism - silent failures from typos are hard to debug.

Fixes #717 

---

items.title: [DRAFT] Generate Go semconv instrument registration from the Weaver registry
items.body:
> [!NOTE]
> This issue is a proposal still in draft

## Problem

schemas/otelc/ declares the telemetry each instrumentation emits, but nothing verifies the declaration matches the Go code. The three CI guarantees today are:

1. .semconv-version, registry_manifest.yaml, and Go import paths agree on the version string.
2. weaver registry check proves the YAML resolves against upstream.
3. Manual co-maintenance, via source-of-truth comments in the YAML.

None of these read the Go code.

The same contract is written out by hand in three places:

1. **Emission.** `instrumentation/net/http/semconv/client.go` registers six instruments with hardcoded names, units, descriptions, and bucket boundaries.
2. **Declaration.** `schemas/otelc/groups/http.yaml` restates them.
3. **Verification.** `test/testutil/semconv.go` hardcodes attribute names as bare strings: `"gen_ai.usage.total_tokens"`, `"k8s.object.kind"`, `"k8s.object.api_version"`.

The three are joined only by a comment. Concretely: remove `http.client.connection.duration` from the YAML, or add a new metric in Go without declaring it, and CI stays green. With 8 instrumentation files in the registry, drift is a matter of time.

## Proposal

Make the registry the thing the code is derived from or checked against, never a parallel description of it. Three tiers, because the three signal types are at different stages of upstream support.

### Tier 1: Metrics. Delete ours, adopt upstream's generated types.

Upstream already generates typed Go metric packages from this same registry, and `httpconv` contains exactly the 10 types `http.yaml` declares. The generated API makes drift structural rather than a matter of care: required attributes are positional and typed, so omitting one does not compile, and optional attributes exist only as `Attr*` methods on that specific metric type, so `AttrClientAddress` is not reachable from `ClientRequestDuration` at all. Names, units, descriptions and attribute sets all regenerate on every semconv release, which means a semconv upgrade surfaces as a compile failure at the exact call sites that need attention.

gRPC already works this way. `net/http` is the only instrumentation that hand-writes registration, and it is the one that drifted.

**Action:** move HTTP metric registration into `net/http/client` and `net/http/server` on `httpconv`, mirroring gRPC's `initInstrumentation`, wire the hooks to actually record, and delete the hand-rolled registration plus the unused `RecordMetrics` (~100 lines). Types cannot catch a metric that is declared but never registered, so one contract test closes that direction: every conv type exposes `Name()`, so compare that set against the YAML.

Net effect: we delete code rather than add a generator.

### Tier 2: Attributes upstream has not defined. Generate them.

Nine attributes are declared locally with `id:`: `k8s.object.uid` / `.name` / `.api_version` / `.kind`, `k8s.objects.count` / `.is_in_initial_list`, and three `gen_ai.*`. Three things are wrong with how they exist in Go. They are inconsistently typed, with `K8SObjectUID` a bare string and `GenAIUsageTotalTokensKey` an `attribute.Key`. The `gen_ai.*` block is duplicated verbatim across four packages and grows with every library and every major version. And the tests bypass the constants entirely, hardcoding raw strings in `streaming_test.go`, `middleware_integration_test.go` and `genai_test.go` in all four packages plus `testutil/semconv.go:158`, so the declaration exists and nothing is obliged to use it.

Generating them collapses all three: one definition in the registry, one generated file in the shared `pkg/` module (all four packages already depend on it via `replace`), imported everywhere including tests.

Worth naming plainly: none of the nine are genuinely library-specific. There is nothing openai-shaped about time-to-first-token. All nine sit in namespaces the SIG owns, so we are squatting, and they should be proposed upstream in parallel. That is not a reason to defer the codegen. Semconv moves in months, a rejected proposal still leaves us needing the constant, and when one graduates the change is a one-line `id:` to `ref:` swap that the compiler traces to every call site.

**Action:** generate with `weaver registry generate` from `id:` declarations **only, never `ref:`**, since anything with `ref:` already ships upstream and regenerating it would create a competing symbol for the same attribute.

### Tier 3: Spans. Generate the declared set, assert the superset.

Spans are the bulk of what we emit, 10 groups against 2 metric groups, and upstream generates nothing for them: every `*conv` package contains one file, `metric.go`. We should not invent a span API ahead of upstream, and largely cannot, since [weaver#819](https://github.com/open-telemetry/weaver/issues/819) is open and the registry cannot express a span name yet.

But the `semconv_grouped_spans` filter does let us generate the declared attribute set per group, which turns this from "hand-write an assertion per span group" into "generate a table, write one helper":

```go
RequireSpanMatchesRegistry(t, span, "span.otelc.k8s.informer.object")
// fails if the span emits an attribute the registry does not declare
```

This complements the existing `testutil` helpers rather than replacing them. They assert required attributes are present (subset); this asserts nothing undeclared is emitted (superset). A superset check also fits spans better than types would: `k8s.yaml` already notes its list is "the union of all possible attributes", and attribute sets conditional on object kind are something a test can express but a signature cannot.

**Limit worth stating:** `testutil/collector.go` exposes only `GetTraces()`, so this is traces-only and cannot catch metric drift. Acceptable because Tier 1 puts metrics under the compiler, but nobody should expect otherwise.

## Config-driven attributes

#705 makes emission configuration-dependent, so it is fair to ask what a build-time contract can say about `request_captured_headers: [X-Tenant-Id]`. Mostly this is already solved upstream and we should not invent anything.

**Header capture is a template attribute, not a new mechanism.** semconv models `http.request.header` as `template[string[]]`, and weaver generates a key *builder* rather than a constant:

```go
func HTTPRequestHeader(key string, val ...string) attribute.KeyValue {
	return attribute.StringSlice("http.request.header."+key, val)
}
```

So the split is clean: **the registry declares the family, the config picks the members.** #705 should declare `ref: http.request.header` in `http.yaml` and call the upstream builder, not define per-header attributes. Each tier then has a defined answer:

- **Tier 2** must generate a builder function, not a constant, for any locally-declared `template[...]` attribute. This is a template requirement, worth writing down before we have one.
- **Tier 3's matcher must be prefix-aware.** An emitted `http.request.header.x-tenant-id` has to match declared template `http.request.header`. Exact set membership would false-fail the moment #705 lands, so the helper must resolve templates rather than compare strings.
- **Tier 1 cannot check these, and we should say so.** `Record(ctx, val, method, addr, port, attrs ...attribute.KeyValue)` ends in a variadic, which is the escape hatch config-driven attributes go through. The compiler verifies the required set and nothing about the variadic. Metric attributes added by config are outside the guarantee.

**`dual_emit` is a different axis and genuinely unresolved.** Emitting two semconv versions at once conflicts with a registry that pins exactly one, via `.semconv-version` and the `registry_manifest.yaml` dependency, with a CI guard asserting they match. Either the registry gains a second dependency and the tiers become version-aware, or dual-emit is scoped as a migration-window feature that the contract deliberately does not describe. That is an ADR, not a checkbox.

## Guidelines: adding a metric

The part that has to outlive this issue. Proposed contribution rule:

**1. Check for an upstream `*conv` type first.** semconv is organised by domain, not by library, so a new instrumentation nearly always lands in an existing package:

| Domain | Package | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP | `httpconv` | net/http, gin |
| RPC | `rpcconv` | grpc |
| Database | `dbconv` | database/sql, redis, mongo |
| Messaging | `messagingconv` | kafka |
| GenAI | `genaiconv` | openai, anthropic |
| Kubernetes | `k8sconv` | client-go |

**2. If a type exists, use it. Do not hand-roll `meter.Int64Histogram(...)`.** Hand-rolling restates the name, unit, description and buckets that upstream already generates. That is how `http.yaml` drifted.

**3. Register in the hook package, not in `semconv/`.** gRPC is the reference: instruments are package-level vars in `grpc/client` and `grpc/server`, initialised in `initInstrumentation` next to the tracer and propagator, recorded by the hook. `net/http` put them in `semconv/`, which is how they ended up orphaned with a nil meter and no caller.

**4. Store the concrete conv type, not a narrowing interface.** gRPC is not a clean exemplar here: `client_hook.go:37` defines `type int64Hist interface { RecordSet(ctx, int64, attribute.Set) }` and stores request/response size behind it. Those are still constructed by `rpcconv`, so name and unit stay upstream, but `RecordSet` takes an arbitrary attribute set, so the typed-attribute guarantee is gone for 4 of gRPC's 10 metrics. Narrow only where a test fake genuinely requires it.

**5. Declare it in `schemas/otelc/groups/<lib>.yaml`.** The contract test then fails if the two sets diverge in either direction.

**6. If no upstream type exists, that is a signal, not a blocker.** Prefer proposing to the semconv SIG. Hand-roll only as a last resort, declare with `id:`, and open the upstream issue in the same PR.

For attributes the same shape applies: `ref:` when upstream defines it, `id:` when it does not, `template[...]` when the set is open-ended or config-driven, and `id:` in an upstream-owned namespace means we are squatting and should upstream it.

## Enforcement

| Tier | Enforced by |
|---|---|
| 1 | the Go compiler, plus a contract test for the metric name set |
| 2 | `make generate` and a CI `git diff --exit-code` |
| 3 | the existing e2e suite, which already collects pdata |

Generated files carry `// Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT.` and live in `zz_generated_*.go`. Hand-written logic stays in the existing files, same package.

## Open decisions (ADR material)

1. **Manifest location.** `otelc.yaml` is colocated, `schemas/otelc/groups/*.yaml` is centralised, #705 proposes a third. Pick one home before adding a third file per instrumentation.
2. **File naming.** Registry files are per-library but attribute groups are per-domain, which is why `anthropic-sdk-go` has no group. Resolve alongside the above.
3. **`dual_emit` and version pinning.** See [Config-driven attributes](#config-driven-attributes).

## Acceptance criteria

**Tier 1**
- [ ] HTTP metric registration moved to the hook packages on `httpconv`, matching gRPC
- [ ] Hooks actually record the 10 metrics `http.yaml` declares (currently zero)
- [ ] Hand-rolled registration and unused `RecordMetrics` deleted
- [ ] Contract test asserting declared metric names match registered instruments

**Tier 2**
- [ ] Weaver template generating constants from `id:` only, never `ref:`
- [ ] Template attributes generate a key builder, not a constant
- [ ] `gen_ai.*` generated once into `pkg/`, imported by all four packages
- [ ] `testutil/semconv.go` and per-package tests use the constants, not raw strings
- [ ] `make generate` plus CI clean-tree check
- [ ] `gen_ai.usage.total_tokens` history checked upstream: propose, or drop it (derivable from input + output, so the omission may be deliberate)
- [ ] Upstream proposals opened for `gen_ai.response.time_to_first_token` and `gen_ai.request.is_stream`

**Tier 3**
- [ ] Generated `Declared` span table plus `RequireSpanMatchesRegistry`, wired end to end for one span group
- [ ] Superset matcher resolves `template[...]` attributes by prefix
- [ ] Upstream issue opened for span codegen, linked here

**Guidelines and decisions**
- [ ] The six rules documented in the contribution guide
- [ ] gRPC's `int64Hist` narrowing revisited or justified in a comment
- [ ] #705 declares `ref: http.request.header` rather than per-header attributes
- [ ] Manifest location, file naming, and `dual_emit` decided with #705

items.title: wrap_call rules fatal on multi-file packages when only some files contain matching calls
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`wrap_call` instrumentation rules crash the build when the target package has **multiple `.go` files** and only some of those files contain the matching function call.

During setup, call rules are attached to **every** source file in the package. During instrumentation, `applyCallRule` fatals if a file has no matching call - even though `match.go` documents that files without matches should be a no-op.

**Error:**
```
Assertion failed: call rule did not match any call
```

This breaks real-world packages where call sites live in one file (e.g. `handler.go`) and helper code lives in another (e.g. `utils.go`).

---

### Environment

- **OS:** Linux (also affects any OS; not platform-specific)
- **Go Version:** 1.25.0
- **Version:** `main` (latest as of Jul 2026)

---

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Create a Go package with two files:

   **`calls.go`**
   ```go
   package main

   import "unsafe"

   func CallSizeof() {
       _ = unsafe.Sizeof(42)
   }
   ```

   **`other.go`**
   ```go
   package main

   func Helper() {
       println("no matching calls here")
   }
   ```

2. Add an instrumentation rule targeting `unsafe.Sizeof`:

   **`rules.yml`**
   ```yaml
   wrap_sizeof:
     target: main
     where:
       function_call: unsafe.Sizeof
     do:
       - wrap_call:
           replace: "Wrapper({{ . }})"
   ```

3. Build with `otelc`:
   ```bash
   otelc go build .
   ```

4. See error  build fatals with:
   ```
   Assertion failed: call rule did not match any call
   ```

**Minimal unit-level reproduction** (same root cause):

```go
// File with fmt.Println — no unsafe.Sizeof
err := applyCallRule(ctx, callRule, file)
// → Fatal: "call rule did not match any call"
```

**Why existing tests miss this:** all `call-rule-*` golden fixtures use a single `source.go` file. Setup adds call rules to all files in a package, but the test harness only models one file.

---

### Expected behavior

- Build should **succeed**
- Files containing matching calls (e.g. `calls.go`) should be instrumented
- Files with no matching calls (e.g. `other.go`) should be **skipped silently** (no-op), as documented in `match.go`:

  > *"Files without matching calls are a no-op in applyCallRule."*

---

### Additional context

**Contradiction in the codebase:**

| Location | Behavior |
|----------|----------|
| `tool/internal/setup/match.go:370–376` | Adds call rules to **all** source files in the package |
| `tool/internal/instrument/apply_call.go:33` | `util.Assert(...)` fatals if **no** call matched in a file |

**Verified locally:**
- `preciseMatching` with 2 files → call rule added to **both** files
- `applyCallRule` on a file without matching calls → **fatal** (not no-op)

items.title: fix(instrument): no-op call rules on files without matching calls
items.body:
## Description

When a package has multiple `.go` files, the setup phase attaches `wrap_call` rules to every source file in the package. The instrument phase previously fatalled on files that contained no matching call sites:

```
Assertion failed: call rule did not match any call
```

This change makes `applyCallRule` return early (no-op) when neither `append_args` nor `replace` modified the file, matching the behavior documented in `match.go`.

Tests added:
- `TestApplyCallRule_NoMatchIsNoOp` - unit test for the no-op path
- `TestPreciseMatching_CallRuleAddedToAllFiles` - setup attaches call rules to all files
- `TestInstrument_CallRuleMultiFilePackage` - end-to-end multi-file package build

## Motivation

Real-world packages often split call sites across files (e.g. `handler.go` has the instrumented call, `utils.go` does not). Call rules must not crash the build on files without matching calls; those files should be skipped silently while files with matches are still instrumented.

Fixes #732

items.title: Integration/e2e tests stuck and panic instead of skipping when Docker is unavailable in macOS and Linux
items.body:
### Describe the bug

The Kafka and k8s tests use `testcontainers-go`, which needs a running Docker. They only skip when the OS is Windows. On macOS or Linux, if Docker is not running, they don't skip. The test hangs for about 80 seconds and then panics with a Docker error and a full stack trace.

The three tests that start containers and only guard against Windows:

- `test/integration/kafka_client_test.go`
- `test/integration/k8s_client_test.go`
- `test/e2e/kafka_test.go`

### Environment

- OS: macOS (arm64)
- Go Version: 1.25.4
- Version: v1.0.1+8dec5d9

### To Reproduce

1. Make sure Docker is not running.
2. Run `make build`.
3. Run the Kafka integration test: `go -C test test -v -tags integration -run '^TestKafkaClient$' ./integration/...`
4. Wait around 80 seconds and see the panic:

```
--- FAIL: TestKafkaClient (82.68s)
panic: rootless Docker not found [recovered, repanicked]
...
go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/test/integration.startKafkaContainer(...)
	test/integration/kafka_client_test.go:80
```

### Expected behavior

Skip with a clear message when Docker is not available, the same way it already skips on Windows, instead of hanging and then panicking.

### Additional context

`testcontainers-go` ships a helper for this case: `testcontainers.SkipIfProviderIsNotHealthy(t)`. Adding it after the existing Windows check turns the 80s panic into `--- SKIP (0.00s)`. CI is unaffected since it has Docker available.

This was also the intent in #661, which describes the Kafka test as "skipping on Windows/macOS if Docker isn't available". Only the Windows case ended up in the code.

I'd like to fix this with a PR (add the helper to the three files). Happy to open it if that works.

items.title: Instrumenting a func with a blank named return + unnamed param/receiver produces uncompilable code
items.body:
## Description

If the tool instruments a function that has **both**:

- an unnamed or blank (`_`) parameter, or an unnamed receiver, **and**
- a blank (`_`) *named* return value

…the generated signature ends up with `_ignoredParam0` in two binding
positions, and the instrumented package won't compile:

```
_ignoredParam0 redeclared in this block
```

Worse, the error points at generated code the rule author never wrote.

### Reason:

In `tool/internal/instrument/apply_func.go`, `insertTJump` runs both collectors
on the same `funcDecl`:

```go
retVals := collectReturnValues(funcDecl) // blank named return -> _ignoredParam0
args    := collectArguments(funcDecl)    // unnamed param/recv  -> _ignoredParam0
```

Both rename blank/unnamed bindings using the same `ignoredParam` ("_ignoredParam")
prefix, and each keeps its **own** `idx` that starts at 0. Since the receiver,
params, and named results all share one scope in Go, the two `_ignoredParam0`
bindings collide. With multiple blanks on each side you get `_ignoredParam1`,
`_ignoredParam2`, … colliding too.

Unnamed *returns* dodge this because they use a separate prefix
(`_unnamedRetVal`) — so only a blank `_` **named** return trips it.

## Reproduce

All three of these turn a green `go build` into a compile error once instrumented:

```go
func F(_ int) (_ error)          { return nil }
func F(int) (_ error)            { return nil }
func (T) M() (_ error)           { return nil }
```

Rendering the rewritten AST and feeding it to `go/types` (or plain `go build`)
confirms it:

```
func F(_ignoredParam0 int) (_ignoredParam0 error)   // _ignoredParam0 redeclared
func (_ignoredParam0 T) M() (_ignoredParam0 error)  // _ignoredParam0 redeclared
```

Control: `func F(int) (int)` renders as
`func F(_ignoredParam0 int) (_unnamedRetVal0 int)` and compiles fine. That's the
boundary that shows the two prefixes are what save the common case.
items.author: Anshumancanrock

items.title: chore: add auto-regenerate bundle workflow and improve conflict guidance
items.body:
## Summary

Add a GitHub Action workflow that allows maintainers to automatically regenerate `tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz` on PR branches by commenting `/regenerate-bundle`. This resolves the recurring binary merge conflict issue when multiple PRs modify `pkg/` or `instrumentation/` directories.

## Problem

Every PR that modifies `pkg/` or `instrumentation/` must regenerate the embedded bundle file. Since Git cannot auto-merge binary files, once one PR merges, all other open PRs immediately have a merge conflict on `tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz`.

## Solution

1. **New workflow** (`.github/workflows/regenerate-bundle.yaml`): Triggered by maintainer comment `/regenerate-bundle` on a PR. It checks out the PR branch, runs `make package`, and pushes the updated bundle.
   - Security: Only OWNER/MEMBER/COLLABORATOR can trigger
   - Fork PRs: Workflow posts a comment with manual resolution instructions (GITHUB_TOKEN cannot push to forks)

2. **Updated `.gitattributes`**: Mark `tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz` as binary to prevent line-ending conversion.

3. **Improved error message** in `verify-bundle.sh`: Provides clear instructions for contributors on how to resolve bundle conflicts.

## Usage

For same-repo branch PRs with bundle conflicts:
1. Maintainer comments `/regenerate-bundle` on the PR
2. Bot regenerates and pushes the updated bundle

For fork PRs:
```bash
git fetch upstream main
git rebase upstream/main
make package
git add tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz
git commit --amend --no-edit
git push --force-with-lease
```

items.title: fix(instrument): avoid _ignoredParam name collision in generated sign…
items.body:
## Description

Instrumenting a function with both a blank/unnamed param (or unnamed receiver)
and a blank (`_`) named return generated uncompilable code:

```
_ignoredParam0 redeclared in this block
```

`collectArguments` and `collectReturnValues` both renamed blank bindings with the
same `_ignoredParam` prefix, each counting from 0. Since a receiver, params, and
named results share one Go scope, the two `_ignoredParam0` bindings collided.

### Fix

Fixes #736

Blank named returns now use their own `_ignoredRetVal` prefix, mirroring the
existing `_unnamedRetVal` handling for unnamed returns. Params and returns can no
longer produce the same name.

## Tests

- Unit regression that type-checks the rewritten signature via `go/types`.
- New golden fixture that compiles a blank-param + blank-named-return function
  through the real toolchain (fails without the fix).

items.title: `Implement where.file.has_directive filter (documented but unsupported)`
items.body:
### Describe the bug

The `where.file.has_directive` predicate is **documented** in the rules schema and [docs/rules.md](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/blob/main/docs/rules.md), but **not implemented** at build time. Any rule using it fails with:

```
where.file.has_directive is not yet supported
```

This blocks rule authors from targeting source files that carry specific `//go:` directives (for example `//otelc:span`), even though the underlying AST helper already exists and is used elsewhere in the tool.

**Gap between docs and code:**

| Location | Behavior |
|----------|----------|
| `docs/rules.md` | Lists `has_directive` as a valid `where.file` predicate |
| `tool/internal/rule/base.go` | Field defined: `HasDirective string` with comment "validated, not yet executed" |
| `tool/internal/setup/filter.go:308-309` | Returns error: `where.file.has_directive is not yet supported` |
| `tool/internal/ast/directive.go` | `FileHasDirective()` already implemented and tested |
| `tool/internal/setup/match.go` | Uses `FileHasDirective()` for **directive rules**, but not for **file filters** |

Rule authors expect to write rules like "only instrument files that contain `//otelc:external-log`" using `where.file.has_directive`, but the build rejects them.

---

### Environment

- **OS:** Linux (any OS; not platform-specific)
- **Go Version:** 1.25.0
- **Version:** `main` / latest `otelc`

---

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Create an instrumentation rule using `where.file.has_directive`:

   **`otelc.yaml`**
   ```yaml
   trace_directive_files:
     target: example.com/app
     where:
       file:
         has_directive: otelc:span
       func: Handler
     do:
       - inject_hooks:
           before: BeforeHandler
           path: example.com/instrumentation/app
   ```

2. Build with `otelc`:
   ```bash
   otelc go build .
   ```

3. See error at rule load time:
   ```
   where.file.has_directive is not yet supported
   ```

4. Compare with existing test fixture that expects this rejection:

   **`tool/internal/setup/testdata/where/err_has_directive.yml`**
   ```yaml
   has_directive: otelc:span
   ```

   **`tool/internal/setup/filter_test.go`** confirms `Build()` returns an error for this predicate today.

**Existing infrastructure (ready to wire up):**

```go
// tool/internal/ast/directive.go
func FileHasDirective(file *dst.File, directive string) bool { ... }
```

Directive rules in `match.go` already use this for matching; only the `where.file` filter path is missing.

---

### Expected behavior

- Rules with `where.file.has_directive` should load and apply successfully
- Files containing the specified directive comment should match the filter
- Files without the directive should be skipped (same semantics as `has_func`, `has_struct`, etc.)
- Behavior should match what is documented in `docs/rules.md`

**Example that should work after the fix:**

```yaml
trace_directive_files:
  target: example.com/app
  where:
    file:
      has_directive: otelc:span
    func: Handler
  do:
    - inject_hooks:
        before: BeforeHandler
        path: example.com/instrumentation/app
```

---

### Additional context

**Root cause:** `buildFile()` in `tool/internal/setup/filter.go` explicitly rejects `has_directive` instead of compiling a filter:

```go
case def.HasDirective != "":
    return nil, ex.Newf("where.file.has_directive is not yet supported")
```


**Impact:** Rule authors cannot use a documented predicate to scope instrumentation to files marked with otelc directives. This limits fine-grained control that the schema already promises.

## Proposed changes

This PR implements opt-in message content capture natively within the `openai-go` instrumentation. 

Following @NameHaibinZhang's recent guidance that content capture is a cross-cutting capability requiring tight scoping and zero-overhead defaults, this implementation:
- Strictly gates capture logic behind the `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT` environment variable (evaluated at `init`).
- Safely handles truncation bounds (`maxRequestBodySize`) to prevent OOM panics on massive payloads (e.g., multimodal base64 image strings).
- Unifies the `gen_ai.content.completion` event format across both standard responses and SSE chunked streaming (`processChatChunk` accumulation).
- Preserves zero-overhead telemetry execution when the flag is disabled.

This serves as a functional benchmark for designing the cross-cutting adapter abstraction needed in #709.

- [x] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality)

### gRPC-Go: xDS RBAC and HTTP/2 Vulnerabilities
[GHSA-hrxh-6v49-42gf](https://redirect.github.com/advisories/GHSA-hrxh-6v49-42gf)

<details>
<summary>More information</summary>

#### Details
Multiple security vulnerabilities have been identified and addressed in grpc-go affecting the xDS RBAC authorization engine (internal/xds/rbac) and the HTTP/2 transport server implementation (internal/transport). These vulnerabilities could result in:

- Authorization Bypass (Fail-Open) when translating xDS RBAC policies containing `Metadata` or `RequestedServerName` fields.
- Denial of Service (High CPU Consumption) due to an HTTP/2 Rapid Reset mitigation bypass during client-initiated stream resets.
- Denial of Service (Server Panic) when parsing crafted xDS RBAC policies containing `NOT` rules around unsupported fields.

##### Impact
_What kind of vulnerability is it? Who is impacted?_

##### xDS RBAC Authorization Bypass via `Metadata` & `RequestedServerName` matchers

- Affected Component: xDS RBAC 
- Impact: When building policy matchers for gRPC RBAC from xDS configurations, unsupported `permission` and `principal` rules (specifically `Metadata` and `RequestedServerName`) were silently ignored and treated as no-ops.
  - If an authorization policy relied purely on these matchers for access control, treating those rules as no-ops effectively removed the restrictions.
- If these unsupported rules were nested inside logical `NOT` rules (`Permission_NotRule` / `Principal_NotId`) or multi-condition `OR/AND` rules, silently dropping them changed the boolean logic flow of the authorization engine.

As a result, policy evaluation decisions could fail open, allowing unauthorized clients to access protected gRPC services or resources.

##### HTTP/2 Rapid Reset Mitigation Bypass / Denial of Service via Stream Aborts

- Affected Component: HTTP/2 transport
- Impact: Earlier mitigations in grpc-go for HTTP/2 Rapid Reset only applied threshold checks to items that directly resulted in control frames being written back to the wire, such as `SETTINGS` ACKs or server-initiated `RST_STREAM`s.

When a client initiated a rapid flood of stream creation (`HEADERS`) immediately followed by stream termination `RST_STREAM`, items queued up in the control buffer without counting against the transport response frame threshold. An attacker can repeatedly trigger this flood sequence to bypass reader blocking, resulting in high CPU usage, and Denial of Service (DoS).

##### Denial of Service (Panic) in xDS RBAC Engine via Unsupported Fields inside NOT Rules

- Affected Component: xDS RBAC 
- Impact: The xDS RBAC policy translators recursively generate matchers for nested rules. When a `NOT` rule wrapped an unsupported or unhandled field (such as `SourcedMetadata`), the recursive step returned an empty matcher. This could result in a runtime panic when the RBAC engine attempts to authorize an incoming request.

An attacker or misconfigured/malicious xDS management server delivering an LDS/RDS update containing a `NOT` rule around an unhandled field causes the gRPC server process to crash immediately (CWE-248 / Denial of Service).

##### Patches
_Has the problem been patched? What versions should users upgrade to?_

All three issues have been fixed in `master` and will be released in 1.82.1 shortly.

##### Workarounds
_Is there a way for users to fix or remediate the vulnerability without upgrading?_

If upgrading grpc-go immediately is not possible, apply the following workarounds based on your deployment architecture:

* For xDS RBAC Vulnerabilities & Panics: Ensure that upstream xDS management servers do not push RBAC policies containing `Metadata`, `RequestedServerName`, or `NOT` rules wrapping unsupported fields (such as `SourcedMetadata`) to grpc-go servers.
* For HTTP/2 Rapid Reset DOS: Configure upstream reverse proxies or load balancers (such as Envoy) with strict HTTP/2 `max_concurrent_streams` limits and active rate limiting on `RST_STREAM` frequency per connection.

##### Severity

  | Vulnerability | Qualitative Severity | Approximate CVSS v3.1 Score | Primary Impact |
  | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
  | **xDS RBAC Authorization Bypass** | **High** | `8.2` | Unauthorized Access / Fail-Open |
  | **HTTP/2 Rapid Reset DOS Bypass** | **High** | `7.5` | High CPU Consumption / Denial of Service |
  | **xDS RBAC Engine Server Panic** | **Medium** | `5.9` | Process Crash / Denial of Service |

#### Severity
- CVSS Score: 8.8 / 10 (High)
- Vector String: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`

items.title: Migrate HTTP metrics to OpenTelemetry httpconv typed builders
items.body:
## Summary

Replace hard-coded HTTP metrics initialization in `instrumentation/net/http/semconv/` with upstream `httpconv` typed builders from `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/v1.37.0/httpconv`, aligning with the existing gRPC `rpcconv` pattern established in `instrumentation/google.golang.org/grpc/`.

This is the **Tier 1** action item from #728.

## Problem

Current HTTP metrics (10 total: 6 client + 4 server) are manually created with hard-coded names, units, descriptions, and histogram buckets in `semconv/client.go` and `semconv/server.go`. This approach:

1. Duplicates information already defined in `schemas/otelc/groups/http.yaml`
2. Is prone to drift — adding/removing metrics in Go code won't fail CI
3. Is inconsistent with gRPC, which already uses `rpcconv` typed builders

## Target State

- Use `httpconv.ClientRequestDuration`, `ClientRequestBodySize`, `ClientResponseBodySize`, `ClientActiveRequests`, `ClientOpenConnections`, `ClientConnectionDuration` builders
- Use `httpconv.ServerRequestDuration`, `ServerRequestBodySize`, `ServerResponseBodySize`, `ServerActiveRequests` builders
- Leverage `.RecordSet()` for cleaner metric recording
- Achieve parity with gRPC `rpcconv` implementation pattern

## Reference Implementation

gRPC client hook (`instrumentation/google.golang.org/grpc/client/client_hook.go`):

```go
import "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/v1.37.0/rpcconv"

var (
    clientDuration        rpcconv.ClientDuration
    clientRequestSize     rpcconv.ClientRequestSize
    // ...
)

func initInstrumentation() {
    clientDuration, err = rpcconv.NewClientDuration(meter)
    // ...
}
```

## Work Breakdown

### Phase 1: HTTP Client (can be done independently)
- [ ] Migrate `HTTPClient` struct fields to `httpconv` types
- [ ] Replace `NewHTTPClient()` with `httpconv.New*` builders  
- [ ] Update `RecordMetrics()` to use `RecordSet()`
- [ ] Update `client_hook.go` integration
- [ ] Update client unit tests and hook tests

### Phase 2: HTTP Server (after Phase 1 validates the pattern)
- [ ] Migrate `HTTPServer` struct fields to `httpconv` types
- [ ] Replace `NewHTTPServer()` with `httpconv.New*` builders
- [ ] Update `RecordMetrics()` to use `RecordSet()`
- [ ] Update `server_hook.go` integration
- [ ] Update server unit tests and hook tests

### Phase 3: Verification
- [ ] Integration tests pass (`test/integration/http_client_test.go`, `http_server_test.go`)
- [ ] No regression for OpenAI/Anthropic middleware (they suppress HTTP instrumentation via context)
- [ ] Contract test: registered metric names match `schemas/otelc/groups/http.yaml` declarations

## Files Affected

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `instrumentation/net/http/semconv/client.go` | Replace with httpconv builders |
| `instrumentation/net/http/semconv/server.go` | Replace with httpconv builders |
| `instrumentation/net/http/client/client_hook.go` | Integrate new metrics |
| `instrumentation/net/http/server/server_hook.go` | Integrate new metrics |
| `instrumentation/net/http/semconv/client_test.go` | Adapt to new API |
| `instrumentation/net/http/semconv/server_test.go` | Adapt to new API |

## Dependencies

- None — `httpconv` is already available in `go.opentelemetry.io/otel` v1.37.0+
- No new module dependencies required

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All 10 HTTP metrics created via `httpconv` typed builders
- [ ] No hard-coded metric names/units/descriptions remain in semconv/
- [ ] All existing tests pass
- [ ] `make all` passes cleanly
- [ ] Pattern consistent with gRPC `rpcconv` usage

## Related

- #728 (parent vision issue)
- PR #696 (established Weaver registry infrastructure)

items.title: ADR 0006: Semconv Telemetry Contract Organization
items.body:
## Summary

This ADR formalizes the file organization and version management strategy for the semconv telemetry contract registry established in PR #696.

## Core Decisions

1. **Centralized file organization**: All telemetry contract files reside under `schemas/otelc/groups/`, one YAML file per instrumentation family. Sub-directories are permitted for logical grouping as the set grows.

2. **Single global semconv version**: The project maintains one version in `.semconv-version`, with atomic upgrades across all instrumentations.

3. **Contributor requirement**: New instrumentations must include a corresponding group file declaring all emitted telemetry.

4. **Future path**: Code generation from the registry (Tier 2/3 of #728) is deferred to a subsequent ADR.

## Key Rationale

The Weaver tool chain imposes hard constraints:
- Single `registry_manifest.yaml` per registry
- Single directory tree for all group files (recursive scanning)
- No support for merging multiple independent registries
- No support for validating against multiple upstream semconv versions simultaneously

These constraints make the centralized approach the only viable option without introducing custom aggregation tooling.

## Alternatives Considered and Rejected

- **Colocated** (semconv.yaml alongside instrumentation code): Would require an aggregation build step to produce a single registry for Weaver; introduces new failure modes.
- **Codegen framework**: Appropriate for Tier 2/3 but should not be coupled with this file organization decision.
- **Dual-emit in registry**: Weaver cannot validate contracts against multiple semconv versions; handle at code layer instead.

## Draft ADR

The draft is available at `docs/adr/0006-semconv-telemetry-contract-organization.md` (status: Proposed).

A PR will follow for review and acceptance.

## Related

- #728 (parent vision issue - this ADR provides the design foundation for Tier 2/3)
- #744 (Tier 1: Migrate HTTP metrics to httpconv typed builders)
- PR #696 (established the Weaver registry infrastructure)

items.title: make lint-schema fails when the checkout path contains a space
items.body:
## Summary

`make lint-schema` aborts before weaver runs if the repository is checked out to a path containing a space.

## Reproduction

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation "my repo"
$ cd "my repo" && make lint-schema
Validating otelc semantic-convention registry (schemas/otelc)...
grep: /home/user/my: Is a directory
grep: repo/schemas/otelc/registry_manifest.yaml: No such file or directory
::error::Could not read the upstream version from /home/user/my repo/schemas/otelc/registry_manifest.yaml
make: *** [Makefile:763: lint-schema] Error 1
```

## Cause

The version guard in the `lint-schema` recipe interpolates `$(OTELC_REGISTRY_DIR)` (= `$(CURDIR)/schemas/otelc`) unquoted:

https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/blob/main/Makefile#L765

The shell word-splits it, so `grep` receives several arguments instead of one path, `MANIFEST_VERSION` comes back empty, and the guard exits 1 with a misleading "Could not read the upstream version" message — it reads as a corrupt or missing manifest rather than a quoting problem.

The `lint-schema.sh` invocation ten lines below already quotes the same variable, so this looks like an oversight rather than a deliberate choice.

## Fix

Quote it. One-line change; PR to follow.

## Out of scope

GNU make cannot handle spaces in *target* names, so `$(TOOLS) = $(CURDIR)/.bin` still emits `warning: overriding recipe for target ...` on such a checkout. That is a make limitation with no quoting fix, and it is only a warning — `lint-schema` is a hard failure, which is what this issue is about.

## Environment

- Docker 29.0.1, `otel/weaver:v0.19.0`, GNU Make 4.3, Linux
- Reproduced on `main` @ 3b20754

CI is unaffected: GitHub runners check out to a space-free path.

`make lint-schema` fails when the repository is checked out to a path containing a space: the unquoted `$(OTELC_REGISTRY_DIR)` word-splits, so `grep` gets several arguments instead of one path, the version guard reads an empty `MANIFEST_VERSION`, and the target exits before weaver runs.

Quote it, as the `lint-schema.sh` invocation ten lines below already does.

### Before

```console
$ make lint-schema
Validating otelc semantic-convention registry (schemas/otelc)...
grep: /home/pradhyum/go: Is a directory
grep: compler: No such file or directory
::error::Could not read the upstream version from /home/pradhyum/go compler intru/.../schemas/otelc/registry_manifest.yaml
make: *** [Makefile:763: lint-schema] Error 1
```

### After

```console
$ make lint-schema
Validating otelc semantic-convention registry (schemas/otelc)...
Upstream semconv dependency: v1.37.0 (matches .semconv-version)
weaver registry check passed: schemas/otelc is valid.
```

Verified on a checkout under a path with a space, with Docker 29.0.1 and `otel/weaver:v0.19.0`. No behaviour change on paths without spaces — the same string is passed to `grep`, just as a single argument.

items.title: docs(schemas): add telemetry contracts for the remaining instrumentations
items.body:
Closes #746.

Adds the ten missing contract files under `schemas/otelc/groups/`, taking coverage from 8/23 to **23/23** instrumentation modules.

Each file was written from the instrumentation's hooks rather than from the issue's summary, which changed three of the classifications:

| File | Modules | Emits |
|---|---|---|
| `anthropic.yaml` | `anthropics/anthropic-sdk-go` | GenAI client span, 18 attributes |
| `gin.yaml` | `gin-gonic/gin` | **no span of its own** — adds `http.route` to the enclosing `net/http` server span |
| `otel-sdk.yaml` | `otel/init`, `otel`, `otel/sdk/trace`, `otel/trace` | **eight upstream `go.*` runtime metrics** (from `init`); the other three emit nothing |
| `logs.yaml` | `log`, `log/slog`, `logrus` | nothing — trace-context injection into the application's own logs |
| `runtime.yaml` | `runtime` | nothing — goroutine-local context propagation |

### Three deviations from the issue's list, and why

1. **`go.opentelemetry.io/otel/init` is not infrastructure-only.** It calls `runtime.StartRuntimeMetrics()`, which starts `contrib/instrumentation/runtime` and emits eight upstream `go.*` metrics. This was the only genuinely undeclared user-visible telemetry in the repo.
2. **gin creates no span.** A gin app is served through `net/http`, so the server span already exists when gin's router runs; `BeforeNext` only renames it and sets `http.route`. Declaring a span group would have misrepresented that, so the file declares the attribute instead.
3. **The log instrumentations emit no OTel telemetry.** They add `trace_id`/`span_id` to the application's *own* log records. Those keys never reach an exporter and do not follow OTel attribute naming, so they are deliberately **not** declared as registry attributes — declaring them would claim otelc emits telemetry it does not.

The five instrumentations that emit nothing get files with `groups: []` and a comment explaining why, so a *missing* file — not an empty one — signals an undeclared instrumentation.

### One metric deliberately left undeclared

`go.schedule.duration` requires `runtime.NewProducer()` to be registered with the metric reader, and `pkg/runtime/setup.go` does not register it, so otelc does not emit it today. Declaring it would have been exactly the declaration/emission drift the registry exists to prevent. Happy to open a follow-up if registering the producer is wanted.

Also note the issue body says 15 missing but lists 10: 23 modules − 13 already covered by the 8 existing files = 10.

### Validation

`make lint-schema` (`otel/weaver:v0.19.0` via Docker), plus a negative control confirming the check is not vacuous — a deliberately broken `ref:` is rejected:

```console
$ ls schemas/otelc/groups/
anthropic.yaml  database-sql.yaml  gin.yaml  grpc.yaml  http.yaml  k8s.yaml  kafka.yaml
logs.yaml  mongo.yaml  openai.yaml  otel-sdk.yaml  redis.yaml  runtime.yaml

$ make lint-schema
Validating otelc semantic-convention registry (schemas/otelc)...
Upstream semconv dependency: v1.37.0 (matches .semconv-version)
weaver registry check passed: schemas/otelc is valid.

# negative control: break one ref on purpose
$ sed -i 's/- ref: gen_ai.usage.input_tokens/- ref: bogus.attr/' schemas/otelc/groups/anthropic.yaml
$ make lint-schema
weaver registry check produced diagnostics:
  "UnresolvedAttributeRef": { "attribute_ref": "bogus.attr", ... }
  Provenance: otelc:/otelc-registry/groups/anthropic.yaml
make: *** [Makefile:761: lint-schema] Error 1
```

28 raw weaver diagnostics, all the expected `DuplicateMetricName` mirrors of upstream metrics, 0 surviving `lint-schema-filter.jq`.

`markdownlint` clean on both edited docs.

> Running `make lint-schema` locally required #750 first, since my checkout path contains a space.

items.title: test: reproduce logrus AfterLogrusNew init-order panic
items.body:
## Description

Building and running an otelc-instrumented app that has `github.com/sirupsen/logrus` anywhere in its dependency graph -- even if the application never calls a single logrus function -- currently prints this before any application code runs:

```
failed to exec After hook AfterLogrusNew
assignment to entry in nil map
```

## Cause

`AfterLogrusNew` (the compile-time hook on `logrus.New()`, wired via `//go:linkname`) fires while logrus's own `var std = New()` package-level initializer runs. `go:linkname` doesn't create a normal Go import edge, so Go's init-order guarantees don't apply here: the hook implementation package's own state (`hookInitMap`) is not guaranteed to be initialized yet when the hook fires. The resulting nil-map write panics, and the panic is silently recovered by the generated hook trampoline (`tool/internal/instrument/impl.tmpl`), so the process keeps running.

## Minimal reproduction

This is not specific to any particular usage pattern -- it reproduces unconditionally, even when the application code never references `github.com/sirupsen/logrus` at all:

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	_ "github.com/sirupsen/logrus"
)

func main() {
	fmt.Println("app never touches logrus directly")
}
```

Built and run with `otelc go build -a`:

```
$ /tmp/logrusblankimport-repro
failed to exec After hook AfterLogrusNew
assignment to entry in nil map
{"time":"...","level":"INFO","msg":"trace provider initialized with auto-export"}
{"time":"...","level":"INFO","msg":"meter provider initialized with auto-export"}
{"time":"...","level":"INFO","msg":"logger provider initialized with auto-export"}
{"time":"...","level":"INFO","msg":"OpenTelemetry initialized","instrumentation_name":"go.opentelemetry.io/otelc","instrumentation_version":"dev"}
{"time":"...","level":"INFO","msg":"runtime metrics enabled"}
app never touches logrus directly
```

The panic fires before any application code runs, from logrus's own package-level `var std = New()` initializer -- confirming the trigger is logrus being present in the build graph at all, not anything the application itself does with it.

## User impact

Every user who builds with `otelc` and has logrus anywhere in their dependency graph sees this panic-looking message on every startup, unconditionally, regardless of how (or whether) their own code uses logrus. There is nothing an application can do about it -- the trigger is logrus's own package init, which runs before `main`.

This PR adds a regression test documenting the panic, skipped for now so it doesn't block CI on an existing, unfixed issue.

items.title: injected SIGTERM/SIGINT handler forces os.Exit(0) instead of re-raising the signal
items.body:
### Describe the bug

The auto-injected runtime installs a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that flushes telemetry and
then calls `os.Exit(0)` (`pkg/runtime/setup.go`, `setupSignalHandler`). Flushing on
shutdown is the intended behavior; taking over the process exit is not. This handler is
injected into **every** instrumented binary (`otelc.yaml` → `target: main` →
`init_otelsdk.go` → `SetupOTelSDK` → `Initialize` → `setupSignalHandler`), with no opt-out.

```go
go func() {
    sig := <-sigCh
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    _ = Shutdown(ctx)       // flush telemetry — fine
    signal.Reset(signals...)
    os.Exit(0)              // this is the problem
}()
```

Two consequences:

1. **It races the application's own signal handler.** `signal.Notify` is additive, so if
   the app already handles SIGTERM (any server doing a graceful drain), both handlers run
   concurrently. The injected one calls `os.Exit(0)` the moment `Shutdown()` returns,
   often within milliseconds when there's little to flush. `os.Exit` runs no deferred
   cleanup, so the app is cut off mid-drain: in-flight requests dropped, buffers unflushed,
   partial writes.

2. **It rewrites the exit code to 0.** Without instrumentation, SIGTERM to a handler-less
   app exits 143. With instrumentation, the same signal exits 0. Anything that branches on
   exit status (`systemd Restart=on-failure`, supervisord `exitcodes`, etc.) now reads an
   external kill as a clean stop.

Both effects contradict the "transparent, no behavior change" goal of compile-time
instrumentation. Note the project's own CLI does this correctly:
`tool/cmd/otelc/main.go` uses `signal.NotifyContext` and never calls `os.Exit`.

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Instrument any Go server that installs its own SIGTERM handler for graceful shutdown
   (e.g. `http.Server.Shutdown` on a drain that takes longer than the telemetry flush).
2. Run the instrumented binary and send it SIGTERM (`kill -TERM <pid>`, or a Kubernetes /
   Docker / systemd stop).
3. Observe the process exit before the app's own shutdown completes. Deferred cleanup
   does not run, and in-flight work is dropped.
4. Check the exit code: it is `0`, not `143`, even though the process was terminated by an
   external signal.

### Expected behavior

Instrumentation flushes telemetry on shutdown without taking over the process lifecycle:
the application's own signal handling still runs to completion, and the process exit code
reflects the signal (e.g. 143 for SIGTERM) rather than being rewritten to 0.

items.title: Signature filters fatal on functions with slice/chan/map params instead of no-match
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Signature sub-filters (`signature_contains`, `param`, `result`, `last_result`, and exact `signature`) **fatal during `otelc setup`** when they scan a function whose parameters or return types use composite Go types (`[]T`, `chan T`, `map[K]V`, `func(...)`, etc.).

The tool calls `util.Unimplemented` → `ex.Fatalf` instead of returning “no match” or recursing into element types. This aborts the entire build.

**Docs vs behavior mismatch:** `docs/rules.md` states that if a parameter or return uses a composite type, “the filter will never match it.” The actual behavior is a **hard crash**, not a non-match.

**Affected code path:**

- `tool/internal/ast/typename.go` - `parsedTypeName.matches()` hits the `default` branch for `*dst.ChanType`, `*dst.ArrayType`, `*dst.MapType`, `*dst.FuncType`, etc. and calls `util.Unimplemented(...)`.
- Triggered via `fieldListContainsType()` → `matchesSignatureContains()` / `funcDeclMatchesFilters()` in `tool/internal/ast/shared.go`.

**Example crash (verified locally):**

Target function: `func(ch chan int) error`  
Rule filter: `signature_contains: {args: [int]}`  

```
Unimplemented: signature filter: unsupported type node *dst.ChanType
```

Same crash occurs for common stdlib-style signatures such as `func Read(p []byte) (n int, err error)` when using `signature_contains: {args: [byte]}` - the filter looks for `byte` but hits `[]byte` and fatals.

---

### Environment

- **OS:** Linux (any OS; not platform-specific)
- **Go Version:** 1.25.0
- **Version:** `main` / latest `otelc`

---

### To Reproduce

**Option A - unit-level (fastest):**

1. In `tool/internal/ast/funcmatch_test.go`, add a test for a function with a composite param:

   ```go
   // func(ch chan int) error
   decl := makeFuncDecl(
       []*dst.Field{field(&dst.ChanType{Value: ident("int")})},
       []*dst.Field{field(ident("error"))},
   )
   sig := rule.FuncSignature{Args: []string{"int"}}
   r := &rule.InstFuncRule{SignatureContains: &sig}
   _, _ = funcDeclMatchesFilters(decl, r) // fatals
   ```

2. Run:

   ```bash
   go test ./tool/internal/ast/ -run TestFuncDeclMatchesFilters -v
   ```

3. See fatal:

   ```
   Unimplemented: signature filter: unsupported type node *dst.ChanType
   ```

**Option B - rule + setup (real-world):**

1. Add a target package with:

   ```go
   package main

   func Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) { return len(p), nil }
   ```

2. Create a rule:

   ```yaml
   read_hook:
     target: main
     func: Read
     signature_contains:
       args: [byte]
     before: BeforeRead
     path: example.com/hooks
   ```

3. Run `otelc setup` / `otelc go build` against that package.

4. Setup fatals while evaluating signature filters instead of matching `Read` or skipping it gracefully.

**Also affects:** `param: string` on `func(p []string)`, `signature` exact match on functions with slice/map/chan params, etc.

---

### Expected behavior

When a signature filter encounters a composite type in a function signature:

1. **No fatal error** -  setup/instrumentation must not abort.
2. For `signature_contains` / `param` / `result`: either return `false` (no match), or recurse into element types (e.g. `[]byte` contains `byte`) per documented “never match” / partial-match semantics.
3. For `signature` exact match: return `false` when composite types are present in the signature.
4. Behavior should align with `docs/rules.md`:

   > If a parameter or return value uses one of these forms, the filter will never match it.

   “Never match” must mean **skip / no match**, not **crash the tool**.

---

### Additional context

**Root cause:** `parsedTypeName.matches()` in `tool/internal/ast/typename.go:69–73` calls `util.Unimplemented(...)` for unsupported AST nodes instead of returning `false` or handling composite types.

**Impact:**

- Rule authors cannot safely use `signature_contains` to disambiguate overloaded function names when any candidate has `[]byte`, `chan`, `map`, or func-typed parameters - common in stdlib and networking code.
- Any instrumentation rule targeting packages with such signatures can crash `otelc setup` at load time.
- Existing golden tests only cover simple types (`string`, `int`, `error`); see `tool/internal/instrument/testdata/golden/func-sig-contains/`.

items.title: fix(ast): handle composite types in signature filters
items.body:
## Description

Signature sub-filters (`signature_contains`, `param`, `result`, `last_result`) previously called `util.Unimplemented` and fatally aborted `otelc setup` when scanning function signatures that use composite Go types (`[]T`, `chan T`, `map[K]V`, `func(...)`, etc.).

This PR fixes that crash by:

- Adding `matchesContainedIn()` in `tool/internal/ast/typename.go` to traverse composite types when evaluating contains-style filters
- Keeping `matches()` as exact-only matching for the `signature` exact-match path
- Replacing the fatal `Unimplemented` path with safe match/no-match behavior
- Adding regression tests for `chan`, `[]byte`, and exact vs contains semantics
- Updating `docs/rules.md` to document composite traversal behavior

## Motivation

Rule authors use signature filters to disambiguate overloaded function names (e.g. `signature_contains: {args: [byte]}` on `func Read(p []byte) (n int, err error)`). Before this fix, any such rule against a function with slice/chan/map params caused:

```
Unimplemented: signature filter: unsupported type node *dst.ChanType
```

That aborted the entire build instead of matching or skipping gracefully, contradicting the documented behavior that filters should not match composite types fatally.

Fixes #756

items.title: fix(runtime): flush telemetry on shutdown without terminating the process
items.body:
## Description

The auto-injected SIGINT/SIGTERM handler in `pkg/runtime` flushed telemetry and then called
`os.Exit(0)`, taking over the exit path of every instrumented binary. This PR keeps the flush
and drops the termination: the handler flushes the SDK, calls `signal.Stop` on its own channel,
and returns. No `os.Exit`, no re-raise.

`signal.Stop(sigCh)` replaces the previous global `signal.Reset(...)`, so an app-registered
handler stays intact. Since we stop listening after the first signal, a repeated signal still
reaches the app or the default disposition so "press Ctrl+C again to force quit" keeps working.

## Motivation

`os.Exit(0)` broke the transparency promise twice over:

1. **It raced the app's own shutdown.** `signal.Notify` is additive, so an app with its own
   SIGTERM handler runs concurrently with ours. The injected goroutine called `os.Exit(0)` as
   soon as the flush returned, and `os.Exit` skips deferred cleanup — cutting a graceful drain
   off mid-flight.
2. **It rewrote the exit code to 0.** A process killed by SIGTERM normally exits 143, so
   supervisors branching on exit status (`systemd Restart=on-failure`, …) misread an external
   kill as a clean stop.

## Note

For an app with **no** signal handler of its own, the first signal is now consumed by the flush
instead of killing the process; a second one terminates it. Apps that handle signals themselves
(the common case for servers) are unaffected.

## Tests

Two unit tests in `pkg/runtime/setup_test.go` cover the flush and error-log branches, reaching
their return proves the handler neither exits nor re-raises. The gRPC integration test now
asserts spans are flushed **and** the process is still alive. `demo/app/grpc/README.md` updated
to match.

Fixes #753

items.title: test(setup): pin.go orchestration entry points lack unit coverage
items.body:
## Description

The top-level orchestration functions in `tool/internal/setup/pin.go` have
no direct unit tests and currently sit at 0% coverage:

- `Pin` — build-lock wrapper around `pinLocked`
- `pinLocked` — dispatches between updating an existing tool file and
  generating a new one from the dependency graph
- `AutoPin` — tracks mutable files via the StateManager, then pins
- `prepareVendoredBuild` — forces module mode for vendored projects

Their helper functions (`updatePinnedProjects`, `matchInstrumentationImports`,
`ensureOtelcRequire`, `vendoringActive`, etc.) are well covered, but the
wiring that composes them is only exercised indirectly through the
integration/e2e suites.

## Impact

A regression in this wiring — wrong branch selection, a missing StateManager
guard, vendored-build args not rewritten — would not surface in the fast unit
run, only in the slow integration/e2e jobs (or in the field).

## Proposed change

Add unit tests covering:

- both branches of `pinLocked` (supplied `ModuleDirs` vs. discovery from cwd)
- `prepareVendoredBuild` for vendored and non-vendored modules
- `AutoPin`'s happy path and its missing-StateManager error path
- `Pin` end-to-end under the build lock

The package already has fixture helpers (`writeInstrumentationModule`,
`writeToolFile`, `NewStateManager`), so no new test infrastructure is needed.
