items.title: feat: Consume OpenTelemetry Registry for instrumentation discovery
items.body:
### Summary

Move `otelc`'s instrumentation discovery from rule files bundled into the binary to the OpenTelemetry Registry's new `otelc.json` endpoint (published by opentelemetry.io). `otelc pin` should fetch, cache, and match this registry against an application's dependencies to determine which compile-time instrumentations to add to `otel.instrumentation.go`, without requiring a new `otelc` release for each newly supported library.

### Motivation

Today, adding support for a new library means shipping a new `otelc` binary. Sourcing discovery from the existing Registry decouples instrumentation support from `otelc` releases and lets third parties publish instrumentations that `otelc` picks up automatically.

### Goals

- Fetch instrumentation discovery data from the OpenTelemetry Registry instead of a binary-embedded rule set.
- Support third-party and private/internal registries alongside the default one.
- Match an application's dependency graph against registry entries and generate `otel.instrumentation.go` accordingly.
- Fail safely: registry unavailability or invalid entries should degrade gracefully rather than break builds.

### Non-Goals

- Validating that a registry entry or referenced Go module actually exists.
- Validating Go import paths generally, or replacing Go module resolution.
- Changing how instrumentation packages themselves are distributed, fetched, or verified. That remains the responsibility of the standard Go module ecosystem (`GOPROXY`, checksum database, `GOPRIVATE`, etc.).

### Scope of work

- **Fetching:** Default to `https://opentelemetry.io/ecosystem/registry/otelc.json`, overridable via a comma-separated `OTELC_REGISTRY_JSON` list of local file paths and/or HTTP(S) URLs. Setting this variable fully replaces the default registry, so the official URL must be included explicitly to use both.
- **Caching:** Cache the fetched JSON locally. Use HTTP conditional requests (`If-None-Match`/ETag) when supported, and fall back to a plain download when the registry doesn't support caching semantics.
- **Fetch limits:** Enforce a maximum response size and request timeout; treat a fetch that exceeds either as a failure and follow the fallback behavior below.
- **Signature verification:** For the default OpenTelemetry registry only, verify the accompanying Sigstore bundle using `github.com/sigstore/sigstore-go` before consuming its contents, checking document integrity, signing identity, and that the registry was signed by the expected `open-telemetry/opentelemetry.io` release workflow. Custom registries configured via `OTELC_REGISTRY_JSON` are explicitly trusted by the user and are not verified.
- **Dependency matching:** Parse registry entries, group by `dependency`, and match against the application's dependency graph (via `go list -deps -json`). Unmatched dependencies are not an error.
- **Multiple candidates:** When more than one registry entry can instrument the same dependency, sort candidates deterministically (`go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/…` first, then `go.opentelemetry.io/…`, then everything else lexicographically). `otelc pin` presents the ordered list for explicit user selection.
- **Trusted modules for auto-pinning:** `otelc go build` (auto-pinning) only selects automatically from a configurable set of trusted instrumentation module paths, defaulting to `go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/**`. `OTELC_AUTOPIN_TRUSTED_MODULES` lets users extend this set with additional trusted prefixes (e.g. their own org's modules). This trust boundary applies to auto-pinning generally; untrusted instrumentations remain selectable through `otelc pin`.
- **Generation:** Add selected instrumentation import paths to `otel.instrumentation.go`. This RFC does not change that file's format, only how its contents are discovered.
- **Error handling:** Follow the RFC's proposed behavior table, for example falling back to a cached copy or the embedded bundled registry on fetch failure, rejecting the registry outright on signature failure, and skipping individual invalid entries with a warning rather than failing the whole registry.

### Related

- Companion tracking issue in the `opentelemetry.io` repository: https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry.io/issues/11060
- #585

## RFC

For the complete design, implementation details, and rationale, see:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1pXCHgbSNQnk23W26xG3xPtfrtLNFy-NBI_zZXukoYOA/edit?usp=sharing

## Description

Adds the missing span.RecordError() call in both gRPC client and server HandleRPC methods. When an RPC fails, the error is now properly recorded as an exception event on the span.

## Problem

Both clientStatsHandler.HandleRPC and serverStatsHandler.HandleRPC set span status to Error on failed RPCs but never call span.RecordError(err). This means:

- Debugging production gRPC issues is significantly harder

items.title: feat(instrumentation/openai): record gen_ai.client.token.usage
items.body:
OpenAI calls already record latency but not token counts. This adds the `gen_ai.client.token.usage` histogram (unit `{token}`) to the openai-go instrumentation, so token cost is visible alongside the `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` metric that #775 added for Anthropic. It is one of the two standard GenAI client metrics in semconv.

Input and output tokens are recorded as separate measurements, each tagged with `gen_ai.token.type` (`input` or `output`) as semconv expects. Covers all three non-streaming operations, chat, text_completion and embeddings, across the v1, v2 and v3 packages.

The meter and histogram are created in `initInstrumentation` next to the tracer, following the same shape as #775. The v2 and v3 copies are generated from v1 so the three stay identical apart from package name and import path, which is the invariant `openai.yaml` relies on.

Zero versus absent: the parsed usage object is a pointer and `recordTokenUsage` takes a `*int64` per token type. A response that reports zero tokens records a zero data point; a response with no `usage` object at all records nothing. That keeps the data point count usable as "how many operations reported usage" rather than collapsing the two cases together. Embeddings report the output side as absent rather than zero, since the response has no `completion_tokens` field.

**Streaming is out of scope for this PR.** Since #990 the streaming reader is a shared module under `internal/streaming`, and its `StreamingReader` deliberately carries no context, model, provider or operation name so that one copy can serve v1, v2 and v3. The metric instrument lives in the versioned package, so the shared reader has no way to reach it. Wiring this up needs a recorder passed into `NewStreamingReader` from each version's bridge, which changes the shared module's API and is better reviewed on its own. Happy to open that as a follow-up, or fold it in here if you would rather it land together.

## Motivation

`gen_ai.client.token.usage` is one of the two standard GenAI client metrics in semconv. With duration landing in #775, token usage is the obvious next one so operators can see token cost per call, not just latency.

## Testing

Unit tests use a manual metric reader to assert the recorded per-type counts for chat, text_completion and embeddings, plus a test pinning the zero versus absent distinction. `go test ./...` passes for all three modules, and the bundle is regenerated.

items.title: fix(ci): scope unit coverage uploads to their own flag
items.body:
## Description

`codecov/project/tool` is currently red on every open PR that touches `tool/`, and the number behind it is not `tool/`'s coverage.

`make test-unit/coverage` runs three sub-targets and leaves `coverage-tool.txt`, `coverage-pkg.txt` and `coverage-instrumentation.txt` in the workspace. Both upload steps name one file via `files:`, but that input does not restrict the upload. From the action's own input description at the pinned SHA:

> `files`: Comma-separated list of explicit files to upload. These will be added to the coverage files found for upload. If you wish to only upload the specified files, please consider using disable-search.

So the `flags: tool` step uploads all three profiles tagged as `tool`, and the `flags: pkg` step does the same. The `tool` flag ends up describing the whole repo: 115 files rather than the 63 under `tool/`. This is visible at the flag level, not just the status level. Codecov's API reports the stored `tool` flag coverage as 64.674%.

This sets `disable_search: true` on both steps so each uploads only the profile it names.

`codecov.yml` needs no change. The `flags:` scoping there was always correct, it was reading a mispackaged flag.

## Motivation

The mispackaging is not new. It became visible when the merged number crossed the 70% target. Comparing Codecov's reports for two PRs either side of that:

| | #799 (Jul 24) | #840 (Jul 28) |
|---|---|---|
| files | 109 | 115 |
| statements | 9,001 | 11,199 |
| misses | 1,527 | 3,507 |
| coverage | 78.14% (pass) | 64.70% (fail) |

#799's report was already at 109 files, so it was already measuring more than `tool/`. It happened to sit above target. The six extra files are the linodego v2 instrumentation added in c5ab841, dominated by `public_methods_gen.go` (4,512 lines of generated wrappers), contributing roughly 1,980 additional misses. #840's `base_totals` is 64.67%, so `main` itself is now below the target.

Two related symptoms this explains:

- #841 adds unit tests in `tool/ast` and still fails the check. It cannot pass, because most of the number it is judged on is not `tool/`.
- #799's green check is stale (Jul 24, before c5ab841) and will turn red on its next push.

With the flag scoped correctly, `go test ./tool/...` gives 78.8% over 63 files, above the 70% target.

## Verification

This PR touches only `.github/workflows/test-unit.yaml`, so the `tool` paths filter (`tool/**`) is false and the upload step's `if:` does not fire. `codecov/project/tool` will report "No coverage information found on head" here rather than 78.8%. The check is only exercised by a PR that touches `tool/`, so I can rebase #840 once this lands to confirm it goes green.

Locally: `yamlfmt -lint` and `actionlint` are clean on the changed file, and `go test ./tool/... -coverprofile` gives 78.8% over 63 files with only `tool/` paths in the profile.

items.title: bug(setup): file handle leaked when bundle extraction fails partway through a copy
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`extract()` in `tool/internal/setup/extract.go` opens the destination file for a tar entry before copying its contents, but only closes the handle on the success path:

```go
case tar.TypeReg:
    file, err := os.OpenFile(targetPath, os.O_CREATE|os.O_TRUNC|os.O_RDWR,
        fileInfo.Mode())
    if err != nil {
        return ex.Wrap(err)
    }

    _, err = io.CopyN(file, tarReader, header.Size)
    if err != nil {
        return ex.Wrap(err)
    }
    err = file.Close()
    if err != nil {
        return ex.Wrap(err)
    }
```

If `io.CopyN` fails — truncated/corrupt gzip stream, disk full mid-write, an unexpected EOF from the tar reader — the function returns on the error from `CopyN` without ever calling `file.Close()`. The open `*os.File` is leaked for the rest of the process.

### Environment

- OS: All (Linux, macOS, Windows)
- Version: main

### To Reproduce

1. Call `extract()` (via `extractGZip`) with a tar stream where a regular-file entry's declared `header.Size` is larger than the bytes actually available in the (possibly gzip-truncated) stream, so `io.CopyN` errors before finishing.
2. `extract()` returns the wrapped copy error, as expected.
3. Check open file descriptors for the process (`lsof -p <pid>` / `/proc/<pid>/fd`) — the destination file opened at the top of the `tar.TypeReg` branch is still open.

### Expected behavior

The file handle should be closed whether or not `io.CopyN` succeeds, so a failed extraction doesn't leak a descriptor or leave a dangling open handle on a partially-written file.

### Additional context

- Affected code: `tool/internal/setup/extract.go`, `extract()`, the `tar.TypeReg` branch (currently around lines 57-71).
- This runs on every `otelc setup`/build while unpacking the built-in instrumentation bundle (`extractOtelcBundle` → `extractGZip` → `extract`), so a corrupted or truncated bundle triggers the leak.
- #530 fixed truncation of previously-extracted files in this same function but didn't add close-on-error handling.
- `extractGZip` already uses `defer gzReader.Close()` a few lines below for the gzip reader — the same pattern (open, `defer file.Close()`, then just check the deferred error or copy error) would fix this too.

items.title: fix(tool/setup): close file handle when bundle extraction copy fails
items.body:
## Description

`extract()` in `tool/internal/setup/extract.go` opens the destination file for a regular tar entry, then copies the entry's bytes into it with `io.CopyN`. The file handle was only closed on the success path — if `io.CopyN` returned an error (truncated/corrupt bundle stream, disk full mid-write, unexpected EOF), the function returned immediately and the open `*os.File` leaked for the rest of the process.

This closes the file on the copy-error path too, mirroring the existing `_ = dstFile.Close()` pattern already used in `util.CopyFile` for the same situation.

Also adds `TestExtract_ClosesFileOnCopyError`, which builds a tar entry whose declared size is larger than the bytes actually written, so `io.CopyN` fails partway through. Without the fix, this test fails on Windows because `os.Remove` on the target file returns "used by another process" while the leaked handle is still open in-process; with the fix it passes.

## Motivation

Every `otelc setup`/build run extracts the built-in instrumentation bundle through this code path (`extractOtelcBundle` → `extractGZip` → `extract`), so a corrupted or truncated bundle would leak a file descriptor with no cleanup. #530 fixed truncation of previously-extracted files in this same function but didn't add close-on-error handling for the copy step.

Fixes #859

items.title: fix(instrumentation/openai): span still created when model is empty
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`OtelMiddleware()` in the OpenAI GenAI instrumentation creates a span even when the request model can't be determined - either because the request body fails to parse (invalid JSON, or truncated by the `maxRequestBodySize` cap on a large multimodal payload) or because the body is valid JSON that simply omits the `model` field. In both cases the span still gets created, named `"chat "` (note the trailing space) with `gen_ai.request.model = ""`.

Affected files: `instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go{,/v2,/v3}/middleware.go`

### Environment

- Go Version: 1.25 (per go.mod)

### To Reproduce

Send a chat completion request with a body that's valid JSON but missing `model`:

```go
req, _ := http.NewRequest("POST", "http://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions",
    io.NopCloser(bytes.NewReader([]byte(`{"max_tokens":10}`))))
```

The middleware creates a span named `"chat "` with `gen_ai.request.model` set to an empty string, instead of skipping instrumentation.

### Expected behavior

When the model can't be determined, the request should pass through uninstrumented, the same way the middleware already handles other cases where there's nothing meaningful to attach (unknown operation, nil body, request read error).

### Additional context

The Anthropic instrumentation had the identical bug and was fixed with the same approach in #805 (`if model == "" { return next(req) }`). This issue is the OpenAI-side equivalent, found while reviewing that PR.

I'd like to work on this - the fix is a one-line guard applied to all three copies of `middleware.go` (v1/v2/v3), plus two test cases (invalid JSON, valid JSON missing the field) mirroring the ones added for the Anthropic fix.

items.title: fix(tool/setup): matched.json can be silently corrupted if Close() fails after write
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`SetupPhase.store()` opens `matched.json` with `os.Create`, writes the marshaled JSON via `file.Write`, and relies on a bare `defer file.Close()` with no check on its return value. Closing a writable file is what actually flushes buffered data to disk - if that flush fails (disk full, quota exceeded, a network filesystem hiccup), the error is silently discarded and `store()` still returns `nil`, so the caller believes the write succeeded while the on-disk file may be corrupted or incomplete.

Affected file: `tool/internal/setup/store.go`

### Environment

- Go Version: 1.25 (per go.mod)

### To Reproduce

Trigger a `Close()` failure on the matched-rules file during `otelc setup` (e.g. disk full, or a filesystem that rejects the final flush) after a successful `Write()`. `store()` returns `nil` regardless.

### Expected behavior

If closing the file fails after writing, `store()` should return an error rather than silently reporting success.

### Additional context

`matched.json` isn't just an internal artifact - `docs/configuration.md`'s "Verifying Your Configuration" section explicitly tells users to inspect this file directly to confirm their instrumentation rules matched as expected. A silently corrupted file here would be misleading in exactly the workflow the docs recommend.

I'd like to work on this - the fix explicitly checks the `Close()` error on the success path, and closes best-effort before returning on the earlier marshal/write error paths.

items.title: bug(instrumentation/linodego): server.address always hardcoded to api.linode.com, ignoring SetBaseURL/UseURL
items.body:
### Describe the bug

The linodego v2 instrumentation always records `server.address = api.linode.com` on every span and metric it produces, even when the instrumented application has pointed the `linodego.Client` at a different host via `SetBaseURL` or `UseURL` (e.g. a specific Linode API gateway, a regional/mirrored endpoint, or a mock server used in tests).

This happens in two places:

1. `instrumentation/github.com/linode/linodego/v2/semconv/client.go` - `LinodegoOperationTraceAttrs` and `MetricAttributes` both call `semconv.ServerAddress(DefaultServerAddress)` unconditionally, where `DefaultServerAddress = "api.linode.com"` is a hardcoded constant. Neither function takes the client's actual host as input.
2. `instrumentation/github.com/linode/linodego/v2/hook.go` - `BeforeDoRequest` builds a `semconv.LinodegoRequest{Method: method, Endpoint: endpoint}` and never sets `ServerAddress`, so `LinodegoRequestTraceAttrs` also falls back to the same hardcoded default for the per-request "doRequest" spans.

So both the public-method operation spans (`linodego.<Method>`), the per-request spans (`{METHOD} {endpoint}`), and the `linodego.client.operation.duration` metric all report `server.address = api.linode.com` regardless of what host the client is actually talking to.

### Environment

- Go Version: 1.25 (per go.mod)
- linodego version: `github.com/linode/linodego/v2 v2.4.1`

### To Reproduce

1. Configure a client against a non-default host:
   ```go
   client := linodego.NewClient(httpClient)
   client.SetBaseURL("https://my-mock-linode-api.example.com")
   client.GetInstance(ctx, 12345)
   ```
2. Inspect the emitted spans/metrics for `GetInstance` (and the underlying `doRequest` call).
3. `server.address` is reported as `api.linode.com` on every span and on the `linodego.client.operation.duration` metric, even though the client is actually talking to `my-mock-linode-api.example.com`.

Note: `linodego.Client` has no exported getter for the configured host - `SetBaseURL`/`UseURL` only update unexported fields (`baseURL`, `hostURL`) - so the fix isn't a one-line "read the field back"; it needs a plan for how the correct host is threaded from the client into the hooks (candidates: capture it at `SetBaseURL`/`UseURL`-adjacent call sites if those are ever instrumented, derive it from the resolved request in `doRequest`, or accept a documented limitation for the operation-level span/metric while fixing the request-level span).

### Expected behavior

`server.address` should reflect the host the `linodego.Client` is actually configured to call, falling back to `api.linode.com` only when no other information is available (e.g. before the request has been resolved).

### Additional context

This instrumentation package was added recently (#710) and is still fairly new, so this hasn't been reported yet. I'd like to pick this up - happy to start with the `doRequest` per-request span (where the real endpoint is already flowing through `BeforeDoRequest`) and then decide, with maintainer input, whether the operation-level span/metric can reuse that or needs a separate approach.

<sub>**Tip**: [React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

items.title: fix(instrumentation/linodego): derive server.address from client's configured host
items.body:
## Description

The linodego v2 instrumentation always tagged `server.address` as `api.linode.com` on both the public-method operation spans (`linodego.<Method>`) and per-request spans (`{METHOD} {endpoint}`), and on the `linodego.client.operation.duration` metric - even when the instrumented app pointed the `linodego.Client` at a different host via `SetBaseURL`/`UseURL`.

This PR:

- Adds `hostFromClient` in `hook.go`, which reads the API host the client is actually configured to call. `linodego.Client` has no exported getter for this (`SetBaseURL`/`UseURL` only update unexported `baseURL`/`hostURL` fields), so it's read via reflection off the already-available `*linodego.Client` receiver, falling back to `""` (and therefore the previous default) if the field is ever renamed or missing.
- Threads the resolved host into `BeforeDoRequest` (per-request spans) and `beforeAPICall`/`afterAPICall` (operation spans + the duration metric).
- Updates `semconv.LinodegoOperationTraceAttrs` and `semconv.MetricAttributes`/`RecordOperationDuration` to accept a `serverAddress` parameter instead of hardcoding `DefaultServerAddress`.
- Adds test coverage for a client configured with a non-default host, on both the request-level span and the operation-level span/metric, plus direct coverage of `hostFromClient`.

## Motivation

Fixes #872

Anyone using a custom Linode API endpoint (private API gateway, a specific region, or a mock server in tests) currently gets telemetry that reports the wrong `server.address`, which is misleading for anyone using traces/metrics to understand where requests actually went.

items.title: fix(setup): warn when version-gated rules skip due to unresolved dep …
items.body:
## Description

When a dependency is compiled from a local checkout, `replace` path, or vendor tree, `findModVersion` cannot extract a semver from the compile source path (there is no `@vX.Y.Z/` module-cache segment). `Dependency.Version` stays empty.

If a matching instrumentation rule also has a non-empty `version:` / version range, both:

- setup matching (`tool/internal/setup/match.go`)
- pin import selection (`tool/internal/setup/pin.go` → `matchInstrumentationImports`)

call `VersionInRange("", "<range>")`, which returns `false`, and the rule is skipped with a bare `continue`.

This PR does **not** change that matching behavior. It only makes the skip visible:

- setup: `SetupPhase.Warn(...)` when a version-gated rule is skipped because the dependency version is unresolved
- pin: `logger.WarnContext(...)` via a warn callback when the same condition drops an instrumentation import
- shared helper `unresolvedVersionSkip(depVersion, ruleVersion)` so both sites use the same condition

Tests added/updated:

- `TestFindModVersion` (module-cache, pre-release, Windows path, local, vendor, empty)
- `TestUnresolvedVersionSkip`
- `TestMatchInstrumentationImports` cases for empty dep version with/without a rule version range
- `TestMatchInstrumentationImports_WarnsOnUnresolvedVersion`
- `TestVersionInRange` empty-version cases in `tool/util`

## Motivation

Today a developer using `replace` (or a local path) against a version-gated instrumentation gets **no instrumentation and no explanation**. That matches the bug report in #777 and makes local instrumentation development hard to debug.

Full version resolution from the module graph (`go list -m`, replace/workspace semantics) still needs maintainer design agreement. This PR is the small, uncontroversial first step discussed on the issue: **make the silent skip loud**, without preempting how versions should be resolved later.

Fixes #777 (diagnostics / visibility portion; version-resolution follow-up remains open)

items.title: bug: Unhandled file.Close() errors on critical write paths (store.go, importcfg.go, profile.go)
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Several critical file generation paths in the `tool` directory use `defer file.Close()` for files opened with write permissions. Because the OS writes to a kernel page cache, disk-level failures (like `ENOSPC` or network drive disconnects) are often only reported when the file descriptor is explicitly closed and flushed. 

By dropping the error returned by `defer file.Close()`, the tool will silently proceed even if a file is truncated or empty. This causes downstream build phases to receive corrupted inputs (such as a malformed `matched.json` or `importcfg`), leading to cryptic compiler panics that are impossible for users to debug. This violates standard Go security practices (gosec rule G307).

*Note: Issue #842 (and PR #848) attempted to address this vulnerability, but only scoped the fix to `tool/internal/ast/parser.go`. This bug remains present in several other critical files.*

**Specific locations of this vulnerability:**
* **`tool/internal/setup/store.go`**: Inside the `(*SetupPhase).store` function (around line 94). Drops the flush error when writing the `matched.json` file.
* **`tool/internal/imports/importcfg.go`**: Inside the `(*ImportConfig).WriteFile` function (around line 102). Drops the flush error when writing the compiler's `importcfg` archive map.
* **`tool/internal/profile/profile.go`**: Inside the `(*Session).writeHeapProfile` function (around line 234). Drops the flush error when streaming the heap profile binary (`.pprof`).

items.title: fix(tool): handle file close errors on write paths to prevent data loss
items.body:
## Description

This PR refactors file I/O operations on critical write paths within the `tool` directory to explicitly check for `file.Close()` errors. 

Specifically, this updates the following files to prevent silent data corruption:
* `tool/internal/setup/store.go` (Writing `matched.json`)
* `tool/internal/imports/importcfg.go` (Writing the compiler's `importcfg` map)
* `tool/internal/profile/profile.go` (Writing the `.pprof` heap profile)

**Changes made:**
* Removed `defer file.Close()` on files opened with write permissions.
* Added explicit `Close()` calls on the success paths to accurately capture and surface any returned flush errors.
* Included best-effort `_ = file.Close()` fallbacks on intermediate error paths (e.g., if `file.Write` fails) to prevent file descriptor leaks before returning the primary error.

## Motivation

When writing to files in Go, the operating system copies data to a kernel page cache rather than writing directly to the physical disk immediately. Hardware-level failures (such as `ENOSPC` or a dropped network drive) are frequently only reported when the kernel attempts to flush the buffer during the final `close(2)` system call. 

Previously, by deferring `Close()` and dropping the returned error, the tool would silently proceed even if the on-disk file was left truncated or entirely empty. This caused downstream build phases to ingest corrupted inputs, resulting in cryptic, difficult-to-debug compiler panics. This PR ensures the tool fails loudly and clearly upon I/O data corruption.

**References:**
* **Community Standard:** [Don't defer Close() on writable files](https://www.joeshaw.org/dont-defer-close-on-writable-files/).

Fixes #876

items.title: bug(instrumentation/linodego): operation.duration metric can't distinguish non-HTTP failures from successes
items.body:
### Describe the bug

The `linodego.client.operation.duration` histogram cannot distinguish a successful public API call from one that failed with a non-HTTP error (timeout, connection refused, DNS failure, context cancellation, etc.).

`afterAPICall` in `instrumentation/github.com/linode/linodego/v2/public_method.go` computes the status code via `finishSpanWithError`:

```go
statusCode := finishSpanWithError(span, err)
if !start.IsZero() {
    metrics.RecordOperationDuration(ctx, time.Since(start).Seconds(), operation, statusCode, serverAddress)
}
```

`finishSpanWithError` (`instrumentation/github.com/linode/linodego/v2/hook.go`) returns `0` in two different situations:

1. `err == nil` (the call actually succeeded), and
2. `err != nil` but `semconv.StatusCodeFromError(err)` can't extract an HTTP status code from it (e.g. the client never got a response at all).

`semconv.MetricAttributes` (`instrumentation/github.com/linode/linodego/v2/semconv/client.go`) only attaches `http.response.status_code` when `statusCode > 0`, and never records any error indicator otherwise:

```go
if statusCode > 0 {
    attrs = append(attrs, semconv.HTTPResponseStatusCode(statusCode))
}
```

So a request that times out or fails before a response is received is recorded in the histogram with exactly the same attribute set as a successful call. This existing test documents the ambiguity rather than a real "success" case — `ListRegions` here stands in for any call with `statusCode == 0`, which includes failures:

```go
// instrumentation/github.com/linode/linodego/v2/semconv/client_test.go
// Success path without a status code omits the status attribute.
m = attrsToMap(MetricAttributes("ListRegions", 0, ""))
```

The span itself is fine — `span.RecordError` / `span.SetStatus(codes.Error, ...)` still run in `finishSpanWithError` for the no-status-code branch — only the metric loses the failure signal.

### Environment

- Go Version: 1.24+
- Package: `go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/instrumentation/github.com/linode/linodego/v2`

### To Reproduce

1. Point a `linodego.Client` at an unreachable/non-responsive host (or otherwise force a network-level error, e.g. via a proxy that resets the connection) and call any instrumented method, such as `client.ListRegions(ctx)`.
2. Also call the same method successfully against a real endpoint.
3. Inspect the collected `linodego.client.operation.duration` metric for both calls.
4. Both data points carry the same attribute set (`server.address`, `code.function.name`) — there is no way to filter/alert on the failed one using this metric alone.

### Expected behavior

Per the HTTP metrics semantic conventions, a duration metric should carry an `error.type` attribute whenever the operation did not succeed, even when no HTTP status code is available (e.g. `error.type` set to a low-cardinality value derived from the error, such as `"timeout"`/`"other"`, or at minimum the Go error type name). This lets the failed call be distinguished from a successful one in the histogram without relying on trace data.

### Additional context

This only affects the `linodego.client.operation.duration` metric; the per-call span already records the error correctly via `RecordError`/`SetStatus`. The fix likely belongs in `finishSpanWithError` (to also signal "failed, no status code" back to the caller) and `semconv.MetricAttributes`/`RecordOperationDuration` (to accept and attach that signal as `error.type`).

Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

items.title: fix(instrumentation/linodego): record error.type on operation.duration when no status code is available
items.body:
## Description

`finishSpanWithError` in `instrumentation/github.com/linode/linodego/v2/hook.go` now returns a second value, `errorType`, alongside the existing `statusCode`:

- when the call succeeded, `errorType` is `""`
- when an HTTP status code could be extracted from the error, `errorType` is that code as a string (unchanged span behavior, now also surfaced to the metric)
- when no status code is available (timeout, connection refused, DNS failure, context cancellation, etc.), `errorType` is the Go type name of the error, using the same convention as `instrumentation/net/http/semconv`'s `HTTPClient.ErrorType`

`semconv.MetricAttributes` and `semconv.Metrics.RecordOperationDuration` take this value and attach it as `error.type` on the `linodego.client.operation.duration` histogram whenever it's non-empty. `public_method.go`'s `afterAPICall` was updated to pass the new return value through.

I also added a new `semconv.ErrorType(err error)` helper (mirrors the net/http one) instead of duplicating the reflection logic, and covered it plus the new code paths with unit tests in `hook_test.go` and `semconv/client_test.go`.

## Motivation

Before this change, `finishSpanWithError` returned `0` both when a call succeeded and when it failed without a status code, and `MetricAttributes` only attached `http.response.status_code` when that value was `> 0`. That meant a request that timed out or never got a response was recorded in `linodego.client.operation.duration` with the exact same attributes as a successful call — there was no way to filter or alert on the failure using this metric alone. The span itself already recorded the error correctly (`RecordError` / `SetStatus`), so this only affected the metric.

Fixes #879

items.title: fix(util): remove process-terminating ex.Fatal call from util.WriteFile
items.body:
### Problem Description
`util.WriteFile` returns an `error` signature, but inside its deferred cleanup function, if `file.Close()` returns a non-nil error, it executes `ex.Fatal(err)`. This terminates the process immediately (`os.Exit(1)`).

Because `util.WriteFile` is a general helper function with an `error` return signature, callers expect file I/O errors to be returned and handled gracefully higher up in the call stack rather than causing an unrecoverable process crash.

### Target Location
- `tool/util/sys.go` (lines 147-164)
### Proposed Solution
- Remove `ex.Fatal(err)` from `util.WriteFile`.
- - Check write errors and `file.Close()` errors explicitly, returning wrapped errors via `ex.Wrap`.

items.title: bug(tool/optimize): canFlattenTJump disables TJump flattening on false positive identifier matches
items.body:
### Component(s)
`tool/internal/instrument`

### What happened?

**Describe the bug**
In the compiler's trampoline optimization pass, `canFlattenTJump` attempts to verify if a trampoline-jump-if (TJump) can be flattened into sequential execution by asserting that the `HookContext` does not call `SetSkipCall`. 

However, the current AST inspection uses a naive `strings.Contains` across all `*dst.Ident` nodes in the hook function:
```go
// tool/internal/instrument/optimize.go
if ident, ok := node.(*dst.Ident); ok {
    if strings.Contains(ident.Name, trampolineSetSkipCallName) {
        found = true
        return false
    }
}
```

Because `strings.Contains` matches any identifier containing the substring `"SetSkipCall"`, the optimization pass triggers a false positive and **completely disables TJump flattening** if:
1. The user defines a local variable like `mySetSkipCall`.
2. The user calls a completely unrelated function containing the substring, such as `req.Header.SetSkipCall()`.
3. The user has a struct field `SetSkipCallback`.

Since `canFlattenTJump` subsequently runs an escape analysis to ensure the `HookContext` parameter is *only* used as a direct method receiver (e.g., `ictx.Method()`), we have a mathematical guarantee that any valid call to `SetSkipCall` on the context must be an exact `*dst.SelectorExpr` where `X` is the hook context parameter and `Sel` is `SetSkipCall`. 

The global string search is both computationally wasteful (visiting every identifier unnecessarily) and architecturally unsafe, leading to silent de-optimization of hot paths.

**Steps to reproduce**
Define an instrumentation hook that does not skip the call, but happens to use the string `"SetSkipCall"` in an unrelated identifier:
```go
func BeforeAPICall(ictx hook.HookContext, req *http.Request) {
    var previousSetSkipCall bool // Falsely triggers strings.Contains
    _ = previousSetSkipCall
}
```
The compiler will refuse to flatten the TJump.

**What did you expect to see?**
The AST optimization pass should properly verify `*dst.CallExpr` -> `*dst.SelectorExpr` to ensure the receiver is strictly the `HookContext` parameter before disabling flattening.

### Additional context
Since `canFlattenTJump` already extracts `hookContextParam` from the function signature (`hookFunc.Type.Params.List[0].Names[0].Name`), we can surgically target `ictx.SetSkipCall()` rather than globally grepping all identifiers. 

I am working on a PR to resolve this AST traversal logic.
items.author: Aryanbhargava18

items.title: fix(tool): resolve canFlattenTJump false positives on unrelated identifier matches
items.body:
## Description

This PR refactors the AST identification logic inside `canFlattenTJump` (`tool/internal/instrument/optimize.go`) to use strict type-checked AST traversal (`*dst.CallExpr` -> `*dst.SelectorExpr`) rather than a global `strings.Contains` substring match.

Previously, the compiler pass attempted to detect whether a HookContext parameter called `SetSkipCall` by checking if any identifier in the entire hook function contained the substring `"SetSkipCall"`. This caused the optimization pass to falsely disable trampoline-jump-if flattening whenever a user defined unrelated variables (e.g., `mySetSkipCall`) or invoked similarly named methods on unrelated objects.

By specifically inspecting the AST for a method invocation where the receiver explicitly matches the extracted `hookContextParam` identifier, we eliminate false-positive de-optimizations. 

## Motivation

Fixes #882

The previous string-matching approach silently de-optimized performance-critical trampoline hooks when perfectly valid Go code happened to share a substring with the reserved `SetSkipCall` method. Since the subsequent escape analysis phase guarantees that `hookContextParam` is only used as a method receiver (otherwise flattening is legitimately aborted), we have a mathematical guarantee that any valid call to `SetSkipCall` will be parsed as a `SelectorExpr` on the context object. 

---

items.title: bug(instrumentation/linodego): doRequest span missing error.type attribute for non-HTTP failures
items.body:
### Describe the bug

The per-request `doRequest` span in the linodego v2 instrumentation never gets an `error.type` attribute when the underlying error carries no HTTP status code (timeout, connection refused, DNS failure, context cancellation, etc.). The higher-level public-method span already handles this correctly, so the two span layers this instrumentation produces are inconsistent with each other.

`AfterDoRequest` in `instrumentation/github.com/linode/linodego/v2/hook.go`:

```go
if err != nil {
    span.RecordError(err)
    if code, ok := semconv.StatusCodeFromError(err); ok {
        span.SetAttributes(semconv.LinodegoErrorTraceAttrs(err)...)
        if sc, desc := semconv.HTTPClientStatus(code); sc != codes.Unset {
            span.SetStatus(sc, desc)
        }
    } else {
        span.SetStatus(codes.Error, err.Error())
    }
    logger.Debug("AfterDoRequest error", "error", err)
}
```

When `StatusCodeFromError` can't extract a code, the `else` branch only calls `span.SetStatus` - it never attaches `semconv.ErrorType(err)` as a span attribute.

Compare this with `finishSpanWithError`, used for the public-method span layer, a few lines below in the same file:

```go
et := semconv.ErrorType(err)
span.SetAttributes(et)
span.SetStatus(codes.Error, err.Error())
```

`finishSpanWithError` always sets `error.type` on the no-status-code path. `AfterDoRequest` doesn't, even though `semconv.ErrorType` is already available in the same package and is exactly what's needed here.

### Environment

- Go Version: 1.25 (per go.mod)
- linodego version: `github.com/linode/linodego/v2 v2.4.1`
- Package: `go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/instrumentation/github.com/linode/linodego/v2`

### To Reproduce

1. Point a `linodego.Client` at an unreachable host so `doRequest` fails before a response is received:
   ```go
   client.GetInstance(ctx, 12345) // times out / connection refused
   ```
2. Inspect the `{METHOD} {endpoint}` span produced by `BeforeDoRequest`/`AfterDoRequest` (the doRequest span, not the outer `linodego.GetInstance` operation span).
3. The span status is correctly `codes.Error` with the error message as description, but it has no `error.type` attribute - there's no way to filter/group these spans by failure kind (e.g. distinguish a timeout from a DNS failure) without parsing the status description string.
4. The outer `linodego.GetInstance` span for the same failed call does carry `error.type`, since it goes through `finishSpanWithError` instead.

### Expected behavior

`AfterDoRequest` should attach `semconv.ErrorType(err)` to the span in the no-status-code branch, the same way `finishSpanWithError` does, so both span layers this instrumentation produces carry the same error attributes for the same failure.

### Additional context

Existing test `TestBeforeAfterDoRequest_PlainError` in `hook_test.go` only asserts `Status().Code`/`Status().Description` for this path, so it wouldn't currently catch a missing `error.type` attribute - that assertion should be added alongside the fix.

I'd like to pick this up.

items.title: bug(tool): struct rules match non-struct types and add fields to the wrong struct
items.body:
`FindStructDecl` is an alias for `FindTypeDecl`:

```go
func FindStructDecl(root *dst.File, structName string) *dst.GenDecl {
	return FindTypeDecl(root, structName)
}
```

It never checks that the named type is a struct, and it returns the enclosing `GenDecl` rather
than the spec that matched. Two problems follow from that.

**Non-struct types match.** `StructFilter.Match` and the `InstStructRule` case in `matchOneRule`
both decide a match with `FindStructDecl(...) != nil`, so a struct rule targeting

```go
type Reader interface {
	Read() error
}
```

is collected as a match. It then fails in `AddStructField`, where
`util.AssertType[*dst.StructType]` calls `ex.Fatalf`:

```
Type assertion failed: got *dst.InterfaceType, expected *dst.StructType
```

The message identifies neither the rule nor the file.

**Grouped type blocks resolve to the wrong spec.** `AddStructField` reaches the struct through
`gen.Specs[0]`. For

```go
type (
	Config struct {
		Name string
	}
	Client struct {
		Addr string
	}
)
```

a struct rule targeting `Client` appends the new field to `Config`, and reports no error.

Expected: a rule whose target is not a struct does not match, and a rule targeting a name inside a
grouped `type ( ... )` block resolves to the spec with that name.

I have a fix and tests for both, happy to open a PR.

items.title: fix(tool): struct rules match non-struct types and add fields to the wrong struct
items.body:
## Description

`FindStructDecl` was an alias for `FindTypeDecl`. It never checked that the named type was a struct, and it returned the enclosing `GenDecl` rather than the spec that matched.

This adds `FindStructType`, which resolves the spec by name and returns the `*dst.StructType` only when the named type really is a struct. `AddStructField` now takes the `*dst.StructType` directly, so it can no longer reach the wrong spec, and `StructFilter.Match` and the struct case in `matchRule` both use `FindStructType` so a struct rule no longer matches a non-struct type. `FindStructDecl` has no callers left and is removed. `FindTypeDecl` is unchanged and still used elsewhere.

`applyStructRule` keeps a nil check and returns a clear error, so a rule that slips through still reports rather than failing obscurely.

Tests cover a grouped type block where the target is not the first spec, and a rule whose target names a non-struct type.

## Motivation

Neither failure produced a useful diagnostic. A rule targeting an interface was collected as a match and only failed later on a type assertion that named neither the rule nor the file, and in a grouped `type ( ... )` block a field could be added to a struct the rule never named without any error at all.

### Behaviour change worth flagging

`has_struct` now matches only real struct types, which widens instrumentation in one
case: a `not: has_struct: X` rule where `X` is an interface. Previously `has_struct`
matched the interface and `not` excluded the file; now it does not match, so `not`
succeeds and the file is instrumented. This is the documented behaviour -- `base.go`
describes `has_struct` as "match files that declare this struct type" -- so the old
result was the deviation, but it is a silent change in the wider direction. It is now
noted on the field doc and covered in `TestStructFilter_Match`.

Fixes #886

items.title: fix(genai): record error for HTTP 4xx+ responses in OpenAI and Anthropic middleware
items.body:
## Description

Adds missing `span.RecordError()` calls in the HTTP 4xx/5xx error branch of the OpenAI (v1, v2, v3) and Anthropic middleware. When the API returns an error status code, the error is now recorded as an exception event on the span.

## Problem

All four middleware versions (`openai-go`, `openai-go/v2`, `openai-go/v3`, `anthropic-sdk-go`) correctly call `span.RecordError(err)` in the transport error branch (`err != nil`), but the HTTP 4xx/5xx branch (`resp.StatusCode >= 400`) only calls `span.SetStatus(codes.Error, ...)` without `RecordError`. This means:

- API-level errors (rate limits, auth failures, server errors) don't appear in the span's event list
- Stack traces are not captured for API errors
- Debugging production issues with API errors is significantly harder

## Solution

Add `span.RecordError(fmt.Errorf(resp.Status))` in the 4xx+ branch of each middleware, following the same pattern used by the transport error branch and other instrumentations in this repository (database/sql, redis, gRPC).

### Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go/middleware.go` | Added `span.RecordError` to 4xx+ branch |

Adds unit tests across the `tool/` module to raise the Codecov `tool` flag

- **util**: work-dir / build-temp path helpers, `CRC32`,

  `NormalizePath`, and `WriteFile`.
- **ex**: `printError` for stackful, wrapped, and plain errors.
- **cmd/otelc**: `initProfiling`, `stopProfiling`, `initStats`, and the
  `version` subcommand.
- **data**: `GetBundleReader`.
- **setup**: `SetupPhase.store`, `matchOneRule` (all rule kinds), `isSetup`,
  `prepareVendoredBuild`, `findGoSources`, `StateManager.Discard`, and the
  empty-package skip in `generateRuntimePerPackage`.
- **instrument**: the slog delegators plus the generic type-parameter
  rewriting (`replaceTypeParamsWithAny`, `isTypeParameter`, `processFieldList`).

This raises the `tool` flag from **64.73%** to **~68.3%**.

## Motivation

The `codecov/project/tool` check was failing well below its 70% target,
blocking PRs.

## Note for maintainers on the remaining gap to 70%

After adding tests for every unit-testable code path, the `tool` flag lands
at ~68.3%. The remaining ~1.7% is concentrated in **integration-level
functions** that only execute a real Go toolchain build — `Setup`,
`setupLocked`, `BuildWithToolexec`, `runGoBuild`, `Pin`/`pinLocked`,
`generatePinnedProjects`, and `findDeps`. These are exercised by the
`test-integration` suite, but that coverage is uploaded under a different
flag and does not count toward the unit `tool` flag.

Covering them from unit tests would mean building the `otelc` binary and
running `go build -toolexec` / `otelc pin` against a scratch module inside a
`_test.go` — i.e. moving integration behaviour into the unit flag, which
seems undesirable.

Suggestion (maintainer decision): consider lowering the `tool` project target
to ~68% in `codecov.yml`, or marking that status `informational: true`, since
the unit flag structurally cannot reach 70% while the build-orchestration code
is only integration-tested. Happy to adjust `codecov.yml` in this PR if you'd

items.title: fix(runtime): OTEL_LOG_LEVEL is case-sensitive and ignores uppercase or whitespace values
items.body:
### Describe the bug

In `pkg/runtime/setup.go`, `logLevel()` parses the `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL` environment variable using an exact-string `switch levelStr` case match without case normalization or whitespace trimming:

```go
func logLevel() slog.Level {
	levelStr := os.Getenv("OTEL_LOG_LEVEL")
	switch levelStr {
	case "debug":
		return slog.LevelDebug
	case "info":
		return slog.LevelInfo
	case "warn":
		return slog.LevelWarn
	case "error":
		return slog.LevelError
	default:
		return slog.LevelInfo
	}
}
```

Because of exact string matching:
- Setting standard uppercase or mixed-case environment variables like `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG`, `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=WARN`, `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=ERROR`, or `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=Debug` falls through to `default` and returns `slog.LevelInfo`.
- Setting `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=" debug "` (with leading/trailing whitespace) also falls through to `slog.LevelInfo`.

Per the [OpenTelemetry SDK Environment Variable Specification](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/configuration/sdk-environment-variables/#general-sdk-configuration), `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL` values should be handled case-insensitively (`debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`). Other environment variable helpers in this repository (such as `strings.EqualFold` in `otel_setup.go` and `strings.ToLower` in `parseInstrumentationList`) follow this convention.

### Environment

- OS: All
- Go Version: 1.25
- Version: main / latest

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce:
1. Set `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` (or `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=WARN`) in environment.
2. Call `logLevel()` in `pkg/runtime/setup.go`.
3. Observe that it returns `slog.LevelInfo` instead of `slog.LevelDebug` (or `slog.LevelWarn`).

### Expected behavior

`logLevel()` should normalize the input string (e.g. `strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv("OTEL_LOG_LEVEL")))`) so that values like `DEBUG`, `Warn`, `ERROR`, etc. are correctly recognized.

### Additional context

I would like to work on this issue and open a PR with the fix and unit test additions if approved!

items.title: fix(runtime): make OTEL_LOG_LEVEL case-insensitive and trim whitespace
items.body:
## Description

In `pkg/runtime/setup.go`, `logLevel()` currently parses `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL` using an exact match against lowercase string literals (`"debug"`, `"info"`, `"warn"`, `"error"`). When users pass standard uppercase or mixed-case environment variables (such as `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` or `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=WARN`) or strings with leading/trailing whitespace, `logLevel()` falls through to `default` and returns `slog.LevelInfo`.

This PR updates `logLevel()` to normalize `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL` via `strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(...))` before evaluating cases, matching the OpenTelemetry SDK specification for environment variable parsing. It also extends `TestLogLevel` in `setup_test.go` with test cases for uppercase (`DEBUG`, `ERROR`), mixed-case (`Debug`, `Info`), and whitespace-padded (` WARN `) inputs.

items.title: test(instrument): api.tmpl and pkg/hook/context.go must be kept byte-identical by convention only, no automated check
items.body:
### Describe the issue

[pkg/hook/context.go:6](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/blob/main/pkg/hook/context.go#L6) documents that the file "will
auto-sync to tool/internal/instrument/api.tmpl":

    // !!! pkg/hook/context.go will auto-sync to tool/internal/instrument/api.tmpl

In practice `api.tmpl` is a byte-for-byte copy of `context.go` (including its
`package hook` line), embedded via `//go:embed api.tmpl` in
[tool/internal/instrument/apply_func.go:273](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/blob/main/tool/internal/instrument/apply_func.go#L273)
and parsed as Go source — only its `.Decls` are harvested and appended to each
generated globals file, so the stray `package hook` line is silently discarded
at that point.

Nothing enforces that the two files stay identical. The `!!!` line is a
comment, not a check — there is no test, lint rule, or CI step that fails if
`api.tmpl` and `pkg/hook/context.go` drift apart. A future change to one file
without the other would silently regenerate a `HookContext` whose interface
declaration disagrees with the real `pkg/hook.HookContext` — e.g. dropped
doc comments, or (in the worst case) a stale method signature exposed to
generated hook code.

Noticed while reviewing #731, which updates both files' doc comments in
lockstep — correctly, but by manual diligence rather than anything the
tooling would have caught if it had been missed.

### Suggested fix

Add a test (e.g. in `tool/internal/instrument`) that reads both files and
asserts their contents are identical, similar in spirit to #833's coverage-gap
issues. That turns the `!!!` comment from a convention into an enforced
invariant.

### Additional context

- `pkg/hook/context.go`
- `tool/internal/instrument/api.tmpl`
- `tool/internal/instrument/apply_func.go` (embed + decl-harvesting site)

Normalizes the `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL` environment variable before matching so
level values are handled case-insensitively and trimmed of surrounding

`logLevel()` in `pkg/runtime/setup.go` now applies

silently fell through to the default (`info`), and values with leading or
trailing whitespace were ignored as well. Uppercase environment variables
are the norm in most environments, so the configured level was frequently

items.title: fix(tool/instrument): resolve undefined idx in collectArguments blank-receiver branch
items.body:
## Description

This PR originally fixed unguarded type assertions in `GetKeyData`/`SetKeyData`/`HasKeyData`:

> In both `tool/internal/instrument/impl.tmpl` (`HookContextImpl`) and `pkg/hook/hooktest/mock_hook_context.go` (`MockHookContext`), the `HookContext` methods `GetKeyData`, `SetKeyData`, and `HasKeyData` performed direct, unguarded type assertions `c.data.(map[string]interface{})`, causing an unhandled interface conversion panic when a `Before` hook stored a non-map value via `SetData`.

That fix has since landed on `main` independently via #911 (merged 2026-08-07, commit 884eb3cd4) — a different PR by the same author whose diff happened to also touch `impl.tmpl` and `mock_hook_context.go`, applying the equivalent safe-assertion pattern (condition inverted, but behaviorally identical) plus an equivalent test. After merging `main` into this branch, every file originally touched here (`mock_hook_context.go`, `mock_hook_context_test.go`, `impl.tmpl`, and the 31 golden files generated from it) is now byte-identical to `main`.

While resolving the merge conflicts, I found `main` currently fails to build: `collectArguments`'s blank-receiver branch in `tool/internal/instrument/apply_func.go` referenced an undeclared `idx`, left over from before #1035 refactored the rest of the function to use a `next(...)` synthetic namer. This PR now carries that fix instead:

1. `tool/internal/instrument/apply_func.go`: use `next(ignoredParam)` in the blank-receiver branch, consistent with the rest of `collectArguments`.
2. `tool/internal/instrument/apply_func_test.go`: update a stale `"_ignoredParam0"` expectation (predating the #1035 refactor) to `syntheticParam(0)`, matching the sibling test cases.

## Motivation

Originally filed to fix #903. That issue is still open, but its underlying bug is already resolved on `main` via #911's incidental changes — may be worth closing separately. This PR's remaining value is the `main` build-breakage fix above, found as a byproduct of resolving these conflicts. See [this comment](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/pull/904#issuecomment-5256833963) for the full investigation.

items.title: fix(tool): check file.Close error handling in ImportConfig and AST WriteFile
items.body:
## Description

During static code inspection of the `tool` module, we audited file write routines (`ImportConfig.WriteFile` in `tool/internal/imports/importcfg.go` and `ast.WriteFile` in `tool/internal/ast/parser.go`).

When writing files in Go, OS write buffers flush pending data upon closing file handles. Ignoring `file.Close()` return values can hide I/O or storage errors (such as disk quota limits or flush failures), leading to undetected file truncation.

## Resolution & Verification

We verified that `ImportConfig.WriteFile` and `ast.WriteFile` delegate file operations to internal helpers (`writeFile`) that correctly:
1. Capture writing errors during execution.
2. Close file handles and check `w.Close()` return values.
3. Return wrapped errors (`failed to close file ...`) if closing or flushing fails.

All unit tests in `tool/internal/imports` and `tool/internal/ast` pass cleanly.

## Checklist

- [x] PR/Issue title follows conventional commits format (`fix(scope): description`)
- [x] Tested locally with `go test ./tool/...`

items.title: net/http server spans never get `http.route`
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`BeforeServeHTTP` builds the route and span name from `r.Pattern`, but the hook runs on
`serverHandler.ServeHTTP` and nothing sets `r.Pattern` until `(*ServeMux).ServeHTTP`.
It's always empty, so `http.route` never gets recorded and every span is named
`GET`/`POST` instead of `GET /hello/{name}`.

`HTTPServer.RequestTraceAttrs` has the same dead branch.

Gin is fine, it sets the route in `BeforeNext`. Plain net/http has nothing asserting it.
`RequireHTTPServerSemconv` checks neither the route nor the span name.

### To Reproduce

1. Register `GET /hello/{name}` on a `ServeMux`.
2. `otelc go build`, run, curl `/hello/world`.
3. Span is named `GET`, no `http.route`.

### Expected behavior

`GET /hello/{name}`, with `http.route="/hello/{name}"`.

### Actual behavior

Span is named `GET`, no `http.route` attribute. Every route on the server behaves the same
way, so they all collapse into one span name per method.

items.title: fix(tool/internal/imports): increase scanner buffer capacity in ParseImportCfg
items.body:
### Description
In [`tool/internal/imports/importcfg.go`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/blob/main/tool/internal/imports/importcfg.go#L42), `ParseImportCfg` parses `importcfg` files using `bufio.NewScanner(r)`. 

By default, `bufio.Scanner` uses a maximum token buffer size of `bufio.MaxScanTokenSize` (64 KB). In large Go build configurations or mono-repos with long package import paths and complex import maps, individual lines in `importcfg` files can exceed 64 KB, causing `scanner.Scan()` to fail with `bufio.ErrTooLong` ("scanning importcfg: token too long").

### Expected Behavior
`ParseImportCfg` should be able to process large `importcfg` directive lines (exceeding 64 KB) without returning a scanning token buffer error.

### Actual Behavior
Parsing fails with `bufio.ErrTooLong` when encountering any line greater than 64 KB.

### Proposed Solution
Configure `bufio.Scanner` with a custom buffer and dynamic expansion up to 10 MB in `parse()`:

```go
func parse(r io.Reader) (ImportConfig, error) {
	var reg ImportConfig
	scanner := bufio.NewScanner(r)
	const maxCapacity = 10 * 1024 * 1024 // 10MB max capacity for large importcfg lines
	buf := make([]byte, 64*1024)
	scanner.Buffer(buf, maxCapacity)
	scanner.Split(bufio.ScanLines)

items.title: bug(sdk/trace): GLS span tracker's capacity limits fail silently and can corrupt unrelated spans under load
items.body:
### Describe the bug

The GLS span-lifecycle tracker in `instrumentation/go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace/otel_trace_context.go` (added by PR #678 to fix #673's stale-worker-pool-parent bug) bounds its state with two caps, and both fail silently in ways that corrupt tracing:

**1. Random eviction corrupts unrelated spans.** `stateForSpan()` (lines 66-87) evicts from the shared `spanStates` map like this once it hits `maxSpanStates` (100,000 entries):

```go
if len(spanStates.states) >= maxSpanStates {
    for key, state := range spanStates.states {
        state.Store(true)
        delete(spanStates.states, key)
        break
    }
}
```

Go map iteration order is randomized, so this evicts an arbitrary entry, not the oldest one. If the victim is a span that's genuinely still in flight on some other goroutine, that goroutine's `tail()`/`compact()` will pop it from its real stack as if it had ended, silently truncating that goroutine's ancestry and handing a wrong (or empty) parent to spans created afterward — on a request with no relation to whatever pushed the map over 100k.

**2. Silent stale-parent-forever once a goroutine's own stack is full.** `traceContext.add()` (lines 119-133):

```go
func (tc *traceContext) add(span trace.Span) bool {
    if tc.n >= otelGLSMaxSpans {
        tc.compact()
        if tc.n >= otelGLSMaxSpans {
            return false
        }
    }
    ...
}
```

`traceContextAddSpan()` only calls `setTraceContext(tc)` when `add()` returns `true`. Once a goroutine's *live* span count hits `OTEL_GLS_MAX_SPANS` (default 1000) even after compaction, new spans just aren't pushed — no log, no metric. `tail()`/`spanFromGLS()` (backing the `trace.SpanFromContext` implicit-parenting hook) keep returning whatever was already on top, so every later span on that goroutine silently gets the same stale parent, indefinitely.

This second one was actually flagged by #673's own author as a probable follow-up ("past `OTEL_GLS_MAX_SPANS` the tracker drops adds silently while `tail()` keeps returning a wrong parent... I can file these separately") but was never filed.

Neither path is covered by any test — `grep`ing for `maxSpanStates`/`spanStates` across `*_test.go` returns nothing, and the one existing test that touches `OTEL_GLS_MAX_SPANS` (`test/integration/otel_sdk_test.go`) only exercises compaction of already-*ended* spans, not what happens once *live* spans exceed the cap. `docs/configuration.md` documents `OTEL_GLS_MAX_SPANS` as a size knob but not the silent-failure behavior at the limit.

### Environment

- otelc: current `main` (bug introduced in #678, confirmed no further commits to this file since)
- Applies to any app using GLS-based implicit propagation (`trace.SpanFromContext(context.Background())` after `otelc` injects `sdk/trace` instrumentation)

### To Reproduce

Bug 2 (easiest to reproduce deterministically, same rig as the existing `OTEL_GLS_MAX_SPANS` test):

1. Build an app with `otelc go build`, set `OTEL_GLS_MAX_SPANS=2`.
2. On one goroutine, start 3 spans without ending any of them (e.g. `otel.Tracer(...).Start(ctx, "a")`, `"b"`, `"c"`, none finished).
3. Call `trace.SpanFromContext(context.Background())` after starting span `"c"`.

Bug 1 requires driving the shared `spanStates` map past 100,000 concurrently-tracked span entries (e.g. a load test creating that many spans faster than they're evicted from the map by ending), so it's load-dependent and non-deterministic by nature of relying on Go's map iteration order — that's part of why it's dangerous, not just hard to hit in a small repro.

### Expected behavior

Bug 2: `SpanFromContext` should return `nil`/no span (or otherwise clearly signal there's no valid implicit parent) once the cap is hit, not silently keep returning span `"a"` forever.

Bug 1: eviction should only ever remove state for spans that have actually ended, never a still-live span from another goroutine.

### Actual behavior

Bug 2: `SpanFromContext(context.Background())` returns span `"a"`'s context even after `"b"` and `"c"` were started and never popped — every subsequent span on that goroutine keeps getting parented under `"a"`, with no indication anything went wrong.

Bug 1: an arbitrary live span from an unrelated goroutine/request can get marked "ended" and dropped from its owner's stack, silently corrupting that request's trace.

### Additional context

Suggested fix direction:
1. Replace the random eviction in `stateForSpan()` with real oldest-first eviction (insertion-ordered structure or bounded LRU) so it can never target a still-live span.
2. Make the silent-drop path in `add()` observable (debug log or counter), matching direction 4 already suggested in #673.
3. Document both cap behaviors in `docs/configuration.md`.
4. Add integration tests driving a goroutine's live-span count past `OTEL_GLS_MAX_SPANS` and forcing `spanStates` eviction, asserting neither corrupts unrelated spans.

Happy to take this on — have a fix in mind for the eviction path, wanted to check the direction was welcome before putting up a PR.

items.title: fix(sdk/trace): make GLS span tracker capacity limits deterministic and observable
items.body:
## Description

Two correctness bugs in the GLS span-lifecycle tracker's capacity limits (`instrumentation/go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace/otel_trace_context.go`), added by #678 to fix #673:

1. **Random eviction.** `stateForSpan()` evicted from the shared `spanStates` map once it hit `maxSpanStates` (100k) by iterating the map and breaking on the first entry. Go map iteration order is randomized, so this evicts an arbitrary entry, not the oldest one — a genuinely still-active span from an unrelated goroutine could get marked "ended" and silently dropped from that goroutine's stack. Fixed by tracking insertion order (a `container/list`) alongside the map and always evicting the oldest entry deterministically.

2. **Silent drop at the per-goroutine cap.** `traceContext.add()` returns `false` once a goroutine's live (unended) span count hits `OTEL_GLS_MAX_SPANS`, and the caller just skips `setTraceContext` — no log, no signal. `SpanFromContext(context.Background())` on that goroutine then keeps returning whatever was already on top of the stack, indefinitely, with no way to notice. Both this drop and the eviction above are now logged at debug level (`OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=debug`).

Also adds `OTEL_GLS_MAX_SPAN_STATES` to tune the shared map's capacity independently of `OTEL_GLS_MAX_SPANS` (the per-goroutine stack depth) — previously the map bound was a hardcoded constant.

Docs (`docs/configuration.md`, `docs/instrument-guide.md`, the GLS README) now describe both cap behaviors, not just the existence of `OTEL_GLS_MAX_SPANS`.

## Motivation

Both failure modes are silent and load-dependent — they only show up under sustained production traffic (100k concurrently-tracked spans for eviction, 1000 live spans on one goroutine for the drop), so they don't surface in normal testing. Bug 1 is also non-deterministic by nature of relying on Go's map iteration order, which makes it effectively unreproducible on demand and hard to root-cause from a bug report like "some spans get the wrong parent under load." Neither path had test coverage before this PR.

Fixes #910

items.title: bug(tool/setup): preserve spaces when parsing CGO build-plan directories
items.body:
## Problem

`otelc` parses the build plan produced by:

```bash
go build -a -x -n
```

When a CGO project is located in a directory whose path contains spaces, `parseCdDir` truncates the directory name.

For example, for a project located at:

```text
/tmp/test project with spaces
```

Go emits the following build-plan line:

```text
cd /tmp/test project with spaces
```

However, the current implementation in `tool/internal/setup/find.go` splits the text after `cd` at the first space and returns:

```text
/tmp/test
```

instead of the complete path:

```text
/tmp/test project with spaces
```

## Impact

`findDeps` stores this parsed directory as `currentDir` and associates it with the CGO object directory. Later, `resolveCgoFile` uses that mapping to locate the original Go source file.

When the directory is truncated, `otelc` searches in the wrong location. As a result, CGO source files may not be resolved, and applicable instrumentation rules can be skipped.

## Related edge cases

While reviewing the parser, I also found two related cases:

* A plain `cd` line can panic because `parseCdDir` evaluates `line[3:]`.
* An unrelated command beginning with `cd`, such as `cdrom`, is incorrectly treated as a directory change.

## Reproduction

```bash
mkdir -p "/tmp/test project with spaces"
cd "/tmp/test project with spaces"
go build -a -x -n 2>&1
```

The output includes an unquoted directory-change line similar to:

```text
cd /tmp/test project with spaces
```

Passing this line to `parseCdDir` currently returns only `/tmp/test`.

## Expected behavior

`parseCdDir` should:

* Preserve the complete directory path after a valid `cd ` prefix.
* Reject an empty `cd` command without panicking.
* Ignore unrelated commands that merely begin with `cd`, such as `cdrom`.

Regression coverage should be added to `TestParseCdDir` and `TestFindCommands`.

## Coordination

PR #657 also changes `tool/internal/setup/find.go` and `tool/internal/setup/find_test.go` as part of its `-C` support.

I discussed the overlap with Azhar on Slack. He recommended opening this issue first so maintainers can decide whether the fix should be included in #657 or submitted as a separate PR.

I’m happy to implement the fix once the preferred scope is confirmed.

### Describe the bug

`docs/troubleshooting.md` incorrectly documents the default value of `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL` as `grpc`. The actual default is `http/protobuf`, per the project's own code (`pkg/runtime/otel_setup.go:32-44`, `pkg/runtime/setup.go:151-159`), which documents the default OTLP endpoint as `http://localhost:4318`  the standard http/protobuf port (grpc's default port is 4317). This matches the [upstream OTel spec default](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/configuration/sdk-environment-variables/).

Anyone following the "Instrumented but no spans appear" section in `docs/troubleshooting.md` with default settings will check the wrong port/protocol when debugging missing telemetry.

Additionally, two runtime environment variables exist in code but are not documented anywhere in `docs/`:
- `OTEL_GO_SIMPLE_SPAN_PROCESSOR` (`pkg/runtime/setup.go:176`) — switches from `BatchSpanProcessor` to `SimpleSpanProcessor` for immediate span export.
- `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED` (`pkg/runtime/otel_setup.go:51`) — spec-standard SDK kill switch, case-insensitive `"true"` disables the SDK entirely.

### Environment

 - OS:  N/A (documentation issue, not OS-specific)
 - Go Version: N/A
 - Version: main branch (as of 2026-08-02)

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Go to `docs/troubleshooting.md`, line 73
2. Read the "Instrumented but no spans appear" section
3. See `Verify the exporter protocol: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL (default: grpc)`
4. Compare against `pkg/runtime/otel_setup.go:32-44` and `pkg/runtime/setup.go:151-159`, which state the default is `http/protobuf` with endpoint `http://localhost:4318`

### Expected behavior

- `docs/troubleshooting.md:73` should read `(default: http/protobuf)` instead of `(default: grpc)`.
- `docs/configuration.md` should document `OTEL_GO_SIMPLE_SPAN_PROCESSOR` and `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED` alongside the other runtime environment variables already listed there.

items.title: fix(net/http): server spans missing http.route and named only by method
items.body:
## Description

`BeforeServeHTTP` read the route off `r.Pattern`, but it runs on `serverHandler.ServeHTTP`
and nothing sets `r.Pattern` until `(*ServeMux).ServeHTTP`. It was always empty, so
`http.route` never got recorded and every span was named `GET` / `POST`.

This PR moves the read to `AfterServeHTTP`. ServeMux writes the pattern back onto the same
`*http.Request` we pass downstream, so it's there by then, and that hook already reaches
into the params for the response writer.

Guarded on `route != ""` so gin and chi keep the span name they set themselves, and on
`IsRecording()` to skip the concat when the span isn't sampled.

Left `HTTPServer.RequestTraceAttrs` alone. It reads `req.Pattern` too, but it's a generic
helper that's correct for any request that has one. The bug was the call site.

**Span names change for anything routing through ServeMux**: `GET` becomes `GET /hello`.
Three integration tests were looking spans up by the old name and are updated:

- `httpserver_dbclient_test.go` to `GET /hello`
- `httpserver_kafkaclient_test.go` to `GET /produce`
- `ginserver_httpclient_test.go` (backend span) to `GET /api/backend`

gin apps are unaffected since `gin.Engine` never touches `r.Pattern`, so
`gin_server_test.go`, `vendor_test.go` and `instrumentation_selection_test.go` still pass.
`e2e/http_test.go` picks its span by `url.path` rather than name.


## Motivation

Span name is what backends group by, so today a whole service collapses into `GET` and
`POST` and you can't tell which endpoint is slow or failing. `http.route` is missing from
net/http server spans entirely.

Verified on a built `otelc`: `GET /hello/{name}` now produces one span name across distinct
URLs with `http.route=/hello/{name}`, a 404 stays `GET` with no route, and a gin app is
unchanged with gin instrumentation both on and off.

Fixes #907

items.title: fix(runtime): prevent type assertion panic in HookContext KeyData methods
items.body:
## Description

`HookContextImpl` (in `tool/internal/instrument/impl.tmpl`) and `MockHookContext` (in `pkg/hook/hooktest/mock_hook_context.go`) were performing unchecked direct type assertions `c.data.(map[string]interface{})` inside `GetKeyData`, `SetKeyData`, and `HasKeyData`.

This PR refactors `GetKeyData`, `SetKeyData`, and `HasKeyData` to use safe comma-ok type assertions (`m, ok := c.data.(map[string]interface{})`):
- `GetKeyData`: Returns `nil` if `c.data` is not a `map[string]interface{}`.
- `HasKeyData`: Returns `false` if `c.data` is not a `map[string]interface{}`.
- `SetKeyData`: Re-initializes `c.data` as a `map[string]interface{}` if `c.data` is not currently a map or is `nil` before setting the key-value pair.

Unit test coverage has been added in `pkg/hook/hooktest` and `tool/internal/instrument` to verify that handling non-map data structures does not panic.

## Motivation

When an instrumentation hook stored a non-map data payload (such as a custom struct, primitive string, or slice) via `SetData(v)`, any subsequent call to `GetKeyData`, `SetKeyData`, or `HasKeyData` caused an unhandled Go runtime type assertion panic:

```text
panic: interface {} is main.CustomState, not map[string]interface {}
```

This bug breaks runtime stability in applications using custom hook state. Safely handling arbitrary non-map payloads aligns with the `HookContext` interface contract.

Fixes #916

items.title: bug(instrumentation/redis): `getRedisV9Statement` appends duplicate command name suffix to `db.query.text` for `*redis.Cmd` and pipelines'
items.body:
### Describe the bug

In [`instrumentation/github.com/redis/go-redis/v9/hook.go`](file:///c:/Users/Vishal/Code_File/Projects/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/instrumentation/github.com/redis/go-redis/v9/hook.go#L140-L161), `getRedisV9Statement` appends a duplicate command name suffix (e.g. `: get` or `: pipeline`) to the `db.query.text` attribute for generic [`*redis.Cmd`](file:///c:/Users/Vishal/Code_File/Projects/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/instrumentation/github.com/redis/go-redis/v9/hook.go#L155-L158) instances and pipeline commands.

When `getRedisV9Statement` formats a statement:
1. It iterates through `cmd.Args()` (lines 143–148). Because `cmd.Args()[0]` is already the command name (e.g. `"get"`, `"set"`, `"pipeline"`), `b` is formatted as `"get mykey"` or `"pipeline get/set/"`.
2. Afterwards, lines 155–158 perform a type assertion check `if cmd, ok := cmd.(*redis.Cmd); ok` and unconditionally append `": "` followed by `cmd.Name()`:

```go
	if cmd, ok := cmd.(*redis.Cmd); ok {
		b = append(b, ": "...)
		b = redisV9AppendArg(b, cmd.Name())
	}
```

Because `redis.NewCmd` (used directly by users via `rdb.Do` or internally by `ProcessPipelineHook` at line 102) returns `*redis.Cmd`, this type assertion succeeds and appends `: <cmd_name>` to the statement string.

As a result:
- A generic command `rdb.Do(ctx, "get", "mykey")` emits `db.query.text` = `"get mykey: get"` instead of `"get mykey"`.
- A pipeline operation emits `db.query.text` = `"pipeline get/set/: pipeline"` instead of `"pipeline get/set/"`.

### Environment

 - OS: Linux / Windows / macOS
 - Go Version: Go 1.25+
 - Version: main (post-v1.0.1)

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Execute a command using `*redis.Cmd` (e.g., `redis.NewCmd(ctx, "get", "mykey")`) or run a pipeline using `rdb.Pipeline()`.
2. Inspect the returned string from `getRedisV9Statement(cmd)` or the `db.query.text` attribute on the generated client span.
3. Observe that the statement ends with an extraneous `: <command_name>` suffix (e.g., `"get mykey: get"`).

### Expected behavior

`db.query.text` should contain the formatted command arguments without an erroneous `: <command_name>` suffix appended at the end.

### Additional context

In [`hook_test.go`](file:///c:/Users/Vishal/Code_File/Projects/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/instrumentation/github.com/redis/go-redis/v9/hook_test.go#L83), `TestGetRedisV9Statement` uses `assert.Contains(t, result, tt.contains)` rather than `assert.Equal`, which masked the extra `: <cmd.Name()>` suffix during testing. Removing lines 155–158 in [`hook.go`](file:///c:/Users/Vishal/Code_File/Projects/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/instrumentation/github.com/redis/go-redis/v9/hook.go#L155-L158) resolves the duplicate suffix generation.

<sub>**Tip**: [React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>
