items.title: bug(instrumentation/logrus): unbounded memory leak in hookInitMap/fieldInitMap dedup maps
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`instrumentation/github.com/sirupsen/logrus/logrus_hook.go` tracks which `*logrus.Logger` instances already have the trace-correlation hook attached using two package-level maps keyed by logger pointer:

```go
hookInitMap   = make(map[*logrus.Logger]bool)
fieldInitMap  = make(map[*logrus.Logger]bool)
```

`AfterLogrusNew` (wired via `otelc.yaml` to fire after every call to `logrus.New()` anywhere in the instrumented binary) and `AfterLogrusWithField` (fires after every `WithField` call) each insert into their map and never delete from it:

```go
func AfterLogrusNew(ictx hook.HookContext, logger *logrus.Logger) {
    ...
    hookInitMap[logger] = true // never removed
}

func AfterLogrusWithField(ictx hook.HookContext, entry *logrus.Entry) {
    ...
    fieldInitMap[entry.Logger] = true // never removed
}
```

Go map keys are strong references, so every distinct `*logrus.Logger` ever constructed via `logrus.New()` (or reachable via `.WithField()`) becomes permanently unreclaimable by the GC for the lifetime of the process — there is no delete, no LRU, no weak reference, and no bound on map size anywhere in the file.

Grep confirms no `delete(hookInitMap` / `delete(fieldInitMap` exists in the package:

```
instrumentation/github.com/sirupsen/logrus/logrus_hook.go
```

The existing unit tests only catch idempotency for a *single, reused* logger pointer, via a test-only `resetHookState()` helper that manually clears both maps between test cases (`logrus_hook_test.go:16-22`) — there is no test that exercises many distinct loggers, so the unbounded growth isn't caught by CI.

### Environment

 - OS: any (not platform-specific)
 - Go Version: 1.25.0
 - Version: main @ 1ae6900

### To Reproduce

1. Instrument and build any Go service that creates `*logrus.Logger` instances dynamically at runtime rather than reusing one global logger — e.g. a per-request/per-tenant logger, or a worker pool doing `logrus.New()` per job:
   ```go
   for {
       logger := logrus.New() // fires AfterLogrusNew every time
       logger.Info("handling request")
       // logger goes out of scope here in normal Go code,
       // but hookInitMap[logger] keeps it alive forever
   }
   ```
2. Run the instrumented binary under a heap profiler (or just watch RSS) while the loop above runs.
3. Observe that `map[*logrus.Logger]bool` retains a reference to every logger ever created, so none of them (or their `Out`/`Formatter`/`Hooks`/mutex) are ever collected.

### Expected behavior

The dedup map(s) should not cause unbounded process memory growth. Options include keying off something that doesn't pin the logger (e.g. checking the hook is already registered by inspecting `logger.Hooks` directly instead of a side map, which is already partially done via `entry.Logger.Hooks == nil` checks elsewhere in the file), or using `weak.Pointer` (Go 1.24+, this repo targets 1.25), or documenting/bounding the expected logger cardinality.

### Additional context

- This is distinct from #995 / #773 (trace ID not injected without a direct `sdk/trace` import) and from #752 (nil-map panic on `AfterLogrusNew` firing during logrus's own package init via `go:linkname`) — those are about correctness/ordering, this is a resource-leak in the otherwise-working path.
- Affected file: `instrumentation/github.com/sirupsen/logrus/logrus_hook.go:30-31,61-69,77-89`

### Describe the bug

For chat completions, `parseChatRequest` only looks at `max_tokens`. Modern OpenAI chat requests (and the official Go SDK) usually send `max_completion_tokens` instead,  `max_tokens` is deprecated and doesn't work on o-series models.

So if an app sets `MaxCompletionTokens`, the JSON on the wire has `max_completion_tokens`, we ignore it, and the span never gets `gen_ai.request.max_tokens`.

Same in v1, v2, and v3.

### To Reproduce

Send a chat completion body like:

```json
{"model":"o1-mini","max_completion_tokens":100}
```

Span is created, but there's no `gen_ai.request.max_tokens` attribute.

With the old field it works:

```json
{"model":"gpt-4","max_tokens":100}
```

### Expected behavior

Either JSON field should set `gen_ai.request.max_tokens`. If both are present, prefer `max_completion_tokens`.

Happy to send a PR for v1/v2/v3 + tests.

## Description
`AstParser.FindPosition` in `tool/internal/ast/parser.go` returns `token.Position{Filename: "", Line: -1, Column: -1}` when a node is absent from the decoration AST node map.

In standard Go (`go/token`), an invalid position is conventionally represented by the zero value `token.Position{}` (`Line: 0, Column: 0`). `pos.IsValid()` is defined as `pos.Line > 0`, so returning negative line numbers breaks standard position validation and diagnostic error formatting.

## Location
- `tool/internal/ast/parser.go:90`
## Proposed Fix
Return standard `token.Position{}` when `astNode == nil` and update unit tests to assert `token.Position{}` and `!pos.IsValid()`.

items.title: bug: `net/http` records unknown HTTP methods as `GET` instead of `_OTHER`
items.body:
### Description

Span attributes for unknown / empty HTTP methods fall back to `GET` in both the server and client helpers:

```go
// instrumentation/net/http/semconv/server.go (same pattern in client.go)
return semconv.HTTPRequestMethodGet, orig
```

So a request with method `CUSTOM` ends up as:

- `http.request.method` = `GET`
- `http.request.method_original` = `CUSTOM`

That’s incorrect telemetry as unknown traffic gets mixed into real GETs.

Metrics already handle this correctly via `StandardizeHTTPMethod` (`CUSTOM` / `""` → `_OTHER`). Spans don’t. Upstream `otelhttp` returns `HTTPRequestMethodOther` here.

### Spec

[HTTP spans](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/http/http-spans/) (v1.37.0, what we pin):

> If the HTTP request method is not known to instrumentation, it MUST set the `http.request.method` attribute to `_OTHER`.

And for span names:

> In other cases (when `{http.request.method}` is set to `_OTHER`), `{method}` MUST be `HTTP`.

We still put the raw method in the span name (`FOOBAR /path`, client span `FOOBAR`), including when gin renames the span after route match.

### Expected

| method | `http.request.method` | `http.request.method_original` | span name |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `CUSTOM` | `_OTHER` | `CUSTOM` | `HTTP` / `HTTP {route}` |
| `""` | `_OTHER` | omitted | `HTTP` |
| `get` | `GET` | `get` | `GET` / `GET {route}` |
items.author: Anshumancanrock

items.title: fix(net/http): set `http.request.method=_OTHER` for unknown methods
items.body:
## Summary

Unknown / empty HTTP methods were recorded as `GET` on spans. That breaks the HTTP semconv MUST and mixes custom traffic into real GET counts.

This pr aligns span attributes and span names with the spec and with upstream `otelhttp`:

- unknown / empty → `http.request.method=_OTHER`
- keep `http.request.method_original` when the raw method is non-empty
- span name uses `HTTP` (or `HTTP {route}`) when the method is `_OTHER`
- shared helpers so server/client don’t drift; gin route rename uses the same naming

Fixes #1011 

Metrics were already correct via `StandardizeHTTPMethod`.

## Test plan

- [x] `go test` in `instrumentation/net/http/semconv` (`CUSTOM`, empty, lowercase known method, span names)
- [x] `go test` in `instrumentation/net/http/{client,server}`
- [x] `go test` in `instrumentation/github.com/gin-gonic/gin`

items.title: bug(tool): synthetic parameter/return names can collide with existing vars or shadow global identifiers
items.body:
### Describe the bug

When the tool generates synthetic names for unnamed or blank (`_`) parameters and return values, the generated names (e.g. `_ignoredParam0`, `_unnamedRetVal0`) can currently collide with existing names in the function signature, as well as shadow identifiers declared at package scope or in the function body.

PR #729 attempts to address this with `syntheticNamer`, but it only checks for collisions against names in the function signature (receiver, params, results). It doesn't account for:

- Package-level variables/constants/functions
- Local variables declared in the function body
- Imported package names

This was previously discussed in [#799 (comment)](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/pull/799#discussion_r3689788318). The `syntheticNamer` approach in #729 is an incomplete fix for the same problem.

### Environment

- OS: any
- Go Version: any
- Version: current main

### To Reproduce

1. Have a Go file with a package-level variable or local variable whose name matches a synthetic name, or a function signature with a colliding parameter name:

```go
package main

var _ignoredParam0 = "important"

func foo(_ int, _ignoredParam1 string) {
    println(_ignoredParam0) // expects the global
}
```

2. Apply a func rule that targets `foo`. The tool renames the blank param to `_ignoredParam0`, shadowing the global. It might also generate `_ignoredParam1` for another param, causing a direct signature collision.

3. The instrumented code now prints the parameter value instead of the global.

### Expected behavior

Synthetic names should not collide with any identifier visible in the function's scope. The generated name should be unique enough that shadowing is not a realistic concern.

### Additional context

One approach: use a hash (see `InstFuncRule.Identity`) in the synthetic identifier names, like `_param_a1b2c3d4_0`. This makes collisions nearly impossible without needing to resolve every identifier in scope.

Note that raw rules currently hardcode synthetic names like `_unnamedRetVal0` in YAML (see `instrumentation/runtime/otelc.yaml`). If the naming scheme changes, those rules break. However, there is already a planned followup PR to expand func template variables to raw rules ([hannahkm/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation#1](https://github.com/hannahkm/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/pull/1)) which would solve this by allowing rule authors to use `{{.FuncReturn 0}}` instead, and the internal naming scheme can safely change.

Related:
- #729 -- introduces `syntheticNamer` (incomplete fix)
- [hannahkm/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation#1](https://github.com/hannahkm/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/pull/1) -- planned PR to add template vars to raw rules (prerequisite for changing the naming scheme)
- [#799 (comment)](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/pull/799#discussion_r3689788318) -- original discussion about this problem
items.author: amazingakai

items.title: bug(pkg/runtime): process shutdown hijack via os.Exit(0), hot-path allocation churn in Instrumented(), and uncoordinated SDK disablement
items.body:
### Describe the bug

A technical audit of `pkg/runtime` revealed three interconnected defects in runtime process lifecycle, signal handling, and hot-path configuration evaluation that impact production applications compiled with `otelc`:

1. **Process Shutdown Hijack (`os.Exit(0)`) in `setupSignalHandler()`**:
   In `pkg/runtime/setup.go` (lines 320–344), `setupSignalHandler()` registers a signal channel for `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM`. When a signal is caught, the background goroutine flushes OTel SDK providers and calls `os.Exit(0)`. In Go, `os.Exit` does not run `defer` statements in `main()`, nor does it allow the user application's own `signal.Notify` handlers (e.g., HTTP server `Shutdown()`, gRPC graceful stop, K8s pod termination handlers, or database connection pool drainers) to execute. The auto-instrumentation effectively steals process lifecycle control from the host application.

2. **High-Frequency Allocation Churn & OS Env Lookups on Hot Paths**:
   In `pkg/runtime/otel_setup.go` (lines 75–108), `Instrumented(name)` is called by every instrumentation hook (HTTP handlers, SQL queries, gRPC calls, Redis operations) on every single request. On every call, `Instrumented()` executes `os.Getenv("OTEL_GO_ENABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS")` and `os.Getenv("OTEL_GO_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS")`, invoking `parseInstrumentationList()` which allocates a new string slice (`result := append(...)`), iterates via `strings.SplitSeq`, and runs `strings.ToLower` and `strings.TrimSpace`. On high-throughput services executing 50,000+ ops/sec, this produces hundreds of thousands of environment lookups and heap allocations per second on hot execution paths.

3. **Inconsistent `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED` Evaluation**:
   When `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true` is set, `SetupOTelSDK()` returns early without initializing SDK providers. However, `Instrumented(name)` does not check `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED`. Hook enablers calling `runtime.Instrumented("sql")` continue to return `true` when `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true`. Hooks continue executing, creating `HookContext` objects, parsing parameters, and attempting to obtain tracers from `otel.GetTracerProvider()`, incurring unnecessary overhead despite the SDK being explicitly disabled.

### Environment

 - OS: Linux / All
 - Go Version: 1.25 / 1.26
 - Version: v0.0.0 (main branch)

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. **Signal Hijack**: Build an HTTP application instrumented with `otelc` that registers a custom `signal.Notify(ch, syscall.SIGTERM)` handler to log `"App shutting down"` and sleep 2 seconds. Send `SIGTERM`. Observe that `"App shutting down"` is never printed because `otelc` calls `os.Exit(0)` immediately after flushing telemetry.
2. **Allocation Churn**: Run a benchmark invoking `runtime.Instrumented("nethttp")` in a tight loop. Observe non-zero heap allocations per op in `go test -benchmem`.
3. **OTEL_SDK_DISABLED**: Set `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true` and invoke `runtime.Instrumented("database")`. Observe that it returns `true`.

### Expected behavior

1. **Non-Destructive Signal Handling**: `setupSignalHandler()` flushes OTel telemetry on `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM` and then un-registers or relays the signal so the host application's signal handlers and `main()` function can complete their own graceful shutdown without forcing `os.Exit(0)`.
2. **Zero-Allocation Hot-Path Enablers**: `Instrumented()` uses an atomic, thread-safe configuration cache (`atomic.Pointer` or `sync.RWMutex`) for parsed `OTEL_GO_ENABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS` and `OTEL_GO_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS` to perform O(1) lock-free lookups with 0 heap allocations on hot paths.
3. **Symmetrical `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED` Short-Circuiting**: `Instrumented()` returns `false` immediately whenever `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED` is set to `"true"`.

### Additional context

**Proposed High-Level Implementation Plan**:
1. `pkg/runtime/otel_setup.go`: Introduce an `instrumentationState` struct holding an `atomic.Bool` for `sdkDisabled` and a `map[string]bool` cache of enabled/disabled instrumentation names. Re-evaluate state on startup or environment change, updating an `atomic.Pointer[instrumentationState]`. Update `Instrumented(name)` to read from the atomic pointer.
2. `pkg/runtime/setup.go`: Modify `setupSignalHandler()` to remove `os.Exit(0)`. After calling `Shutdown(ctx)`, call `signal.Stop(sigCh)` so subsequent signals pass directly to user handlers.
3. `pkg/runtime/setup_test.go` & `otel_setup_test.go`: Add benchmark tests (`BenchmarkInstrumented`) and unit tests for signal propagation and SDK disablement.
items.author: bhuvan-somisetty

items.title: fix(pkg/runtime): cache parsed instrumentation lists in Instrumented() to cut hot-path allocations
items.body:
Fixes #1015

## Description

This PR reduces per-call allocation overhead in \`pkg/runtime.Instrumented()\`, which is on the hot path for every instrumented call (database queries, HTTP/gRPC requests, etc).

The signal-handling portion originally proposed here is no longer part of this PR: #759 landed on \`main\` with a proper fix for the same `os.Exit`-in-signal-handler problem (first-signal shutdown, second-signal escalation, with subprocess tests). This branch is rebased onto that, so \`pkg/runtime/setup.go\` has no diff here.

What's left, scoped to \`pkg/runtime/otel_setup.go\`:

1. **Lock-Free Atomic Caching for `Instrumented()`**:
   - Replaces per-hook `parseInstrumentationList` string slice allocations with an `atomic.Pointer[configCache]`.
   - `Instrumented(name)` still reads `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED`, `OTEL_GO_ENABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS`, and `OTEL_GO_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS` via `os.Getenv` on every call (this is not cached — see doc comment). What's cached is the parsed-list -> `map[string]struct{}` conversion, so repeated calls skip re-splitting and re-allocating those lists as long as the env vars haven't changed.
   - Benchmarked: for callers who configure `OTEL_GO_ENABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS`/`OTEL_GO_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS`, allocations drop from 4-7 down to 1 per call, and calls get 42-58% faster. The unset (default) case gets ~20ns slower per call due to the extra `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED` lookup and atomic load, which is negligible next to the cost of the instrumented call itself.

2. **Symmetrical `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED` Short-Circuiting**:
   - Ensures `Instrumented()` respects `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true` and immediately returns `false`, preventing hook execution and parameter parsing when the SDK is explicitly disabled.

3. **Testing**:

items.title: bug(instrumentation): GenAI middleware omits error.type on transport failures
items.body:
### Describe the bug

OpenAI and Anthropic GenAI middleware set span status + `RecordError` on transport failures (`next(req)` returns `err != nil`), but never set `error.type`.

HTTP 4xx/5xx responses do set `error.type`. Transport / dial failures don't. Same middleware, inconsistent error paths.

```go
resp, err := next(req)
if err != nil {
    span.SetStatus(codes.Error, err.Error())
    span.RecordError(err)
    // missing: error.type
    span.End()
    return resp, err
}
```

Affects:

- `instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go` (v1 / v2 / v3)
- `instrumentation/github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-go`

GenAI span semconv marks `error.type` as conditionally required when the operation ends in an error. `RecordError` only adds an exception event, it does not set the span attribute. GenAI middleware also suppresses nested HTTP client instrumentation, so nothing else fills this in.

### To Reproduce

1. Hit OpenAI or Anthropic middleware with a chat/messages request that starts a GenAI span (valid model in the body).
2. Make `next(req)` fail with a transport error (e.g. connection refused / dial failure) instead of returning an HTTP response.
3. Inspect the ended GenAI span.

See error: span status is `Error` and there is an `exception` event, but no `error.type` attribute.

Existing coverage already exercises this path without asserting the attribute:

- OpenAI: `TestOtelMiddleware_NextError`
- Anthropic: `TestOtelMiddleware_TransportError`

### Expected behavior

Transport failures should set `error.type` on the GenAI span (low-cardinality type string, same idea as `HTTPClientErrorType` in `instrumentation/net/http/semconv/client.go`), consistent with the HTTP error path and GenAI semconv.

items.title: test(integration): missing trace-root assertions in propagation tests
items.body:
## Problem

Three `//go:build integration` propagation tests under `test/integration/` assert
parent/child span relationships but never assert that the *initiating* span is
actually the trace root. This is the same coverage gap that was fixed for the
`test/e2e/` suite in #963 (fixing #960) — it just wasn't fixed for the sibling
`test/integration/` suite, which has near-identical test bodies.

Without this assertion, a bug that gives the root span a bogus non-empty
`ParentSpanID` (e.g. a stray injected parent context, or a propagator that
incorrectly extracts a parent from an unrelated header) would slip through
these tests undetected, since only the *relative* parent/child links are
checked, never that the chain terminates.

The codebase already has precedent for this exact assertion style in
`test/integration/otel_sdk_test.go:46`:
```go
require.True(t, workerSpan.ParentSpanID().IsEmpty(), ...)
```

## Affected tests

- `test/integration/grpcserver_dbclient_test.go` — `grpcServerSpan` (the gRPC
  frontend) is the trace-initiating span (the test calls it directly via an
  uninstrumented `grpc.NewClient`), but nothing asserts it's the root.
- `test/integration/httpserver_dbclient_test.go` — same gap for
  `httpServerSpan`.
- `test/integration/ginserver_httpclient_test.go` — same gap for
  `ginServerSpan`.

(Note: unlike the `test/e2e/` versions, these `test/integration/` tests have
no separate instrumented client app — the test process itself makes the
initial call — so the root span here is the *server* span, not a client
span.)

## Proposed fix

Add one `require.True(t, <span>.ParentSpanID().IsEmpty(), "<span> must be the
trace root")` assertion to each of the three tests, following the exact
pattern used in #963 and in `otel_sdk_test.go`.

items.title: fix(instrumentation): set error.type on GenAI transport failures
items.body:
Fixes #1017

## Problem

OpenAI and Anthropic GenAI middleware set span status and call `RecordError` when `next(req)` returns an error, but never set `error.type`. The HTTP 4xx/5xx path in the same middleware does set it, so the two error paths were inconsistent.

GenAI semantic conventions make `error.type` conditionally required when an operation ends in an error. `RecordError` only adds an exception event, not the span attribute, and the middleware suppresses nested HTTP client instrumentation, so nothing else fills it in.

## Change

Adds an `ErrorType` helper to each GenAI semconv package that derives the fully qualified error type name and falls back to `_OTHER`. This mirrors the existing convention in `instrumentation/net/http/semconv`, so `error.type` stays consistent across instrumentations. Each instrumentation is its own Go module, so the helper cannot be shared.

Wired into the transport-error path of all four middlewares:

- `instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go` (v1, v2, v3)
- `instrumentation/github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-go`

## Tests

- `TestErrorType` in each semconv package covers the nil, builtin-pointer, named-type and wrapped-error cases, plus a typed-nil case that would otherwise panic.
- The three existing `TestOtelMiddleware_NextError` tests now assert `error.type` and the error status code.
- New `TestOtelMiddleware_TransportErrorSetsErrorType` for anthropic-sdk-go.

I confirmed each test fails without the middleware change and passes with it, so they exercise the fix rather than the surrounding behaviour.

`go test ./...` passes in all four modules, and `golangci-lint` (v2.11.3, repo config) reports no new findings.

items.title: bug(tool/internal/ast): scanArgs splits directive args on quote-unaware colons and accepts empty keys
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`scanArgs` in `tool/internal/ast/directive.go` splits each token with
`strings.Cut(tok, ":")`, but `tokenize` deliberately keeps the quote characters in
the token. The split is therefore quote-unaware, and the resulting key is never
validated, so malformed directives parse successfully into malformed args.

Verified against `ParseDirectiveArgs` on main:

| input after `//otelc:span ` | parsed | error |
|---|---|---|
| `"key:value"` | `{Key: "key, Value: value"}` | none |
| `:v` | `{Key: "", Value: v}` | none |
| `"k":v` | `{Key: "k", Value: v}` | none |

For contrast `k:"a:b"` parses correctly to `{Key: k, Value: a:b}`, because there
the first colon falls outside the quotes. That is why this is easy to miss.

### Why it matters

Quoting the whole argument (`//otelc:span "span.name:my op"`) is a natural
mistake, and it currently produces an attribute key of `"span.name` rather than
an error. The empty-key case is worse: `:v` yields an arg with no key at all.
Both flow downstream instead of being rejected at parse time, and
`scanArgs` already rejects other malformed input, so the missing colon case
errors while these do not.

### Suggested fix

Reject a token whose colon falls inside a quoted region, and reject an empty key,
in the same place the existing "missing colon separator" and "single-quoted
values are not supported" checks live.

### Notes

I checked for existing reports and found none; the code came in with #375 and
the validation was not discussed there. Happy to fix this, but per the intake
discussion in #973 I will wait to be assigned before opening a PR.

items.title: feat(instrumentation/http): enable metrics collection for HTTP client…
items.body:
## Description

`instrumentation/net/http/semconv/client.go` already defines the metric instruments for the HTTP client, but nothing ever used them. The hook called the package-level helpers (`HTTPClientRequestTraceAttrs`, `HTTPClientStatus`, and so on), and those go through `defaultHTTPClient`, which is built with a nil meter. So the instruments existed and were never recorded to.

This PR wires them up:

- `initInstrumentation` now builds a `semconv.HTTPClient` from the global meter provider, the same way `google.golang.org/grpc/client` does.
- `BeforeRoundTrip` stores `req.ContentLength` alongside the span and start time.
- `AfterRoundTrip` calls `RecordMetrics`, so `http.client.request.duration`, `http.client.request.body.size` and `http.client.response.body.size` get recorded.
- The trace attribute calls move from the package-level helpers to the instance methods, since we now have an instance.

Only three of the six instruments are recorded. `active_requests`, `open_connections` and `connection.duration` need connection-level information that isn't available from inside `RoundTrip` — that would need `httptrace` hooks, which felt like a separate change. `NewHTTPClient` still creates all six, which is existing behaviour I didn't touch, but I'm happy to gate the unused three if you'd rather not register instruments that are never written to.

## Motivation

HTTP is the most used instrumentation here and it only emits traces today, while gRPC already emits both. The metric side was already written, just not connected.

No existing issue covers this — @Labreo asked about that above. Happy to open one if you'd prefer it tracked there first.

## Notes

Three tests added: metrics recorded on success, behaviour when the request fails, and graceful degradation when there is no meter (so a nil meter can't panic in a user's app).

CI is currently red on this branch because `main` doesn't compile (`undefined: idx` in `tool/internal/instrument/apply_func.go`). That's unrelated to this PR — #904 fixes it, and I'll rebase once that lands.

items.title: GenAI spans miss server.address and server.port when HTTP instrumentation is suppressed

### Description

OpenAI (v1/v2/v3) and Anthropic create a GenAI client span and suppress the nested `net/http` client span to avoid duplicates. That HTTP span is where `server.address` / `server.port` would normally come from, and the GenAI span does not set them either.

- `server.address` from the parsed hostname (`req.URL.Hostname()`)
- `server.port` when required by GenAI SemConv

Cover OpenAI v1/v2/v3 + Anthropic, including custom base URLs and non-default ports.

items.title: bug(instrumentation): GenAI client duration metric omissions (OpenAI and Anthropic)
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Hey folks, I noticed a couple of gaps in how we're handling the `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` metric across the GenAI middlewares. 

According to the GenAI Semantic Conventions, `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` is a Recommended (SHOULD) metric, and `error.type` is a Conditionally Required attribute on it when the operation ends in an error. Right now, neither middleware gets this quite right:

1. **OpenAI (`github.com/openai/openai-go`)**: The duration metric is completely missing. The middleware currently only records spans, and there is no meter or metric recording implemented at all.
2. **Anthropic (`github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-go`)**: The duration metric exists, but it never gets the `error.type` attribute when the operation fails. The code defers adding this with a `// TODO(#679)` comment (which was added back in #775), so that gap is still open.
Related but minor issue:
When `error.type` *is* emitted (on spans for HTTP errors), the format doesn't match between the two middlewares. OpenAI uses the numeric status code (e.g. `"404"`), while Anthropic uses the full status string (e.g. `"404 Not Found"`). Figured it was worth mentioning here since it's a related parity issue!

### Environment

 - OS: macOS (but applies everywhere)
 - Go Version: 1.23
 - Version: `main` (cde2de2)

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Instrument an app with `github.com/openai/openai-go`.
2. Make a request to the API and check the exported metrics,`gen_ai.client.operation.duration` is missing.
3. Instrument an app with `github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-go`.
4. Trigger a failure (like an invalid API key).
5. Check the exported `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` metric,it's there, but `error.type` is missing.

### Expected behavior

- The `github.com/openai/openai-go` instrumentation should emit the `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` metric.
- The `github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-go` instrumentation should include the `error.type` attribute on the duration metric when requests fail.
- Ideally, the `error.type` value format should be consistent across both middlewares.

### Additional context

The deferred Anthropic `error.type` on the metric is commented here:
https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/blob/cde2de202279c67ad3a9da3db86e3f42b31495c6/instrumentation/github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-go/middleware.go#L130

items.title: fix(instrumentation): record penalties on openai completion requests
items.body:
## Description

`parseCompletionRequest` parsed only `model`, `max_tokens`, `temperature` and `top_p`. `CompletionNewParams` also carries `FrequencyPenalty` and `PresencePenalty`, serialised as `frequency_penalty` and `presence_penalty`:

```go
// openai-go/v3@v3.49.0 completion.go
FrequencyPenalty param.Opt[float64] `json:"frequency_penalty,omitzero"`
PresencePenalty  param.Opt[float64] `json:"presence_penalty,omitzero"`
```

`parseChatRequest` already records both. So for two otherwise identical requests, the chat span reports the sampling penalties and the legacy completions span silently does not.

Both attributes are already defined in `semconv` (`GenAIRequestFrequencyPenalty`, `GenAIRequestPresencePenalty`) and already emitted on the chat path, so this introduces no new attribute — the completions path just stopped short of the fields it was already shaped to read.

Parsed as `*float64` to match the surrounding fields, so an omitted penalty stays absent rather than being reported as `0` — `0` is a meaningful value for both parameters, and `omitempty` on a non-pointer would make "explicitly zero" and "not sent" indistinguishable.

Applied to v1, v2 and v3, which all had the same gap.

## Motivation

Anyone comparing chat and completions traffic on `gen_ai.request.frequency_penalty` or `gen_ai.request.presence_penalty` sees completions requests as if the penalties were never set. The gap is invisible in the span — nothing signals the attribute was dropped rather than unset.

I found this while reading the request-parsing paths, after building a benchmark harness that measures how tool and instrumentation shape affects an LLM agent's behaviour, where request-side sampling parameters are exactly the sort of thing you need recorded to compare runs.

## Testing

Two tests per version:

- `TestParseCompletionRequest_Penalties` — a completions body with `frequency_penalty: 0.5` and `presence_penalty: -0.25` produces both attributes with those values.
- `TestParseCompletionRequest_PenaltiesOmitted` — a body without them produces neither, so absent stays absent.

Confirmed these are real regression tests. Against unpatched `parseCompletionRequest`:

```
--- FAIL: TestParseCompletionRequest_Penalties (0.00s)
    Error: map[attribute.Key]attribute.Value{} does not contain "gen_ai.request.frequency_penalty"
```

With the change, all three modules pass:

```
ok  go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go      7.111s
ok  go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go/v2   6.387s
ok  go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/instrumentation/github.com/openai/openai-go/v3   6.950s
```

`make` is not available on my machine (Windows), so I ran `go test ./...` per module and verified every changed file is `gofmt` clean rather than running `make format` / `make test`. Worth a second pair of eyes on the lint job.

items.title: bug(instrumentation/logrus): AfterLogrusNew panics with "assignment to entry in nil map" during logrus's own package init
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Building and running an otelc-instrumented app that has `github.com/sirupsen/logrus` anywhere in its dependency graph, even if the application never calls a single logrus function, currently prints this before any application code runs:

```
failed to exec After hook AfterLogrusNew
assignment to entry in nil map
```

The panic fires before `main()`, from logrus's own package-level `var std = New()` initializer, and is silently recovered by the generated hook trampoline (`tool/internal/instrument/impl.tmpl`), so the process keeps running but every user sees this panic-looking message on every startup.

### Cause

`AfterLogrusNew` (the compile-time hook on `logrus.New()`, wired via `//go:linkname`) fires while logrus's own `var std = New()` package-level initializer runs. `go:linkname` doesn't create a normal Go import edge, so Go's init-order guarantees don't apply here: the hook implementation package's own state (`hookInitMap` in `instrumentation/github.com/sirupsen/logrus/logrus_hook.go`) is not guaranteed to be initialized yet when the hook fires. The resulting nil-map write panics.

### Environment

- OS: any (not platform-specific)
- Go Version: 1.25.0
- Version: main

### To Reproduce

This is not specific to any particular usage pattern. It reproduces unconditionally, even when the application code never references `github.com/sirupsen/logrus` at all:

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	_ "github.com/sirupsen/logrus"
)

func main() {
	fmt.Println("app never touches logrus directly")
}
```

Built and run with `otelc go build -a`:

```
$ /tmp/logrusblankimport-repro
failed to exec After hook AfterLogrusNew
assignment to entry in nil map
{"time":"...","level":"INFO","msg":"trace provider initialized with auto-export"}
...
app never touches logrus directly
```

A skipped regression test documenting this panic was added in #752 (`test/integration/logs_test.go`, subtest `"AfterLogrusNew hook does not panic during logrus init"`).

### Expected behavior

`AfterLogrusNew` should not panic regardless of when it fires relative to the hook implementation package's own init.

items.title: feat(tool): add struct_literal selector and set_fields modifier
items.body:
## Description

Adds a `struct_literal` selector that matches composite literals of a given type, and a `set_fields` modifier that sets fields on the matched literal.

A field takes a `value`, a `wrap` template that transforms whatever the literal already assigns, or both. Both is useful because a field is often present in some literals and absent in others:

```yaml
instrument_vault_config:
  target: example.com/app
  where:
    struct_literal: github.com/hashicorp/vault/api.Config
  do:
    - set_fields:
        field:
          - name: HttpClient
            wrap: "vaulttrace.WrapHTTPClient({{ . }})"
            value: "vaulttrace.NewHTTPClient()"
```

Two limits worth calling out: it matches only qualified literals (`pkg.Type{...}`), following the same restriction `function_call` already has, and it sets named fields rather than rewriting a literal as a whole, so it cannot reorder or drop elements.

## Motivation

Some libraries offer no constructor to hook. Their configuration type is written as a literal at each use site, so there is nothing for `inject_hooks` or `wrap_call` to match and the value cannot be reached at all today. `hashicorp/vault`'s `api.Config` is one example: the HTTP client it holds is the only place tracing can be injected, and the type is commonly built inline.

Opening as a draft: happy to change the selector name, the modifier name, or the `value`/`wrap` shape before this is reviewed in earnest.

Fixes #1001

items.title: bug(tool): imports injected during toolexec fail to build unless explicitly registered by setup in otelc.runtime.go
items.body:
### Describe the bug

When `otelc` injects new imports into a package during the `toolexec` phase, the build will fail with a linker error if those imported packages aren't already part of the application's standard build graph.

This happens because standard `go build` finalizes its action graph before `toolexec` runs. If an injected import wasn't known to `go build` beforehand, it never gets compiled into a `.a` archive.

Currently, **func rules** bypass this issue entirely because the `setup` phase analyzes them and generates an `otelc.runtime.go` file containing dummy imports for all the hook packages (e.g., `import _ "go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/instrumentation/..."`). This forces `go build` to include them in the build graph.

However, this pre-registration isn't universally applied to other mechanisms, like `add_file` rules. If an `add_file` rule injects a file that relies on a third-party module (even if tracked in `go.mod`), the setup phase does not add those imports to `otelc.runtime.go`, leading to a linker failure.

**Root Cause**
Any import edge introduced dynamically during `toolexec` is completely invisible to the Go toolchain's build planner. While `apply_file.go` currently parses the injected file's AST and successfully updates `importcfg` during the `toolexec` phase, this happens **too late**. The compiler/linker still cannot find the `.a` archive because `go build` never executed a compile action for it when it finalized the build graph before `toolexec` even started.

### Environment

 - OS: All
 - Go Version: 1.25+
 - Version: `main`

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Initialize a minimal project (`go mod init example.com/myapp`).
2. Add a dependency to `go.mod` using a tools file to prevent it from being pruned:
   ```go
   // tools.go
   //go:build tools
   package tools
   import _ "github.com/google/uuid"
   ```
3. Create the target file to be injected (`subpkg/extend.go`) that uses the dependency:
   ```go
   //go:build ignore
   package subpkg
   import "github.com/google/uuid"
   // ...
   ```
4. Define a rule in `otelc.yaml` to inject the file:
   ```yaml
   inject-extend-main:
     target: main
     do:
       - add_file:
           file: extend.go
           path: example.com/myapp/subpkg
   ```
5. Run `otelc --rules otelc.yaml go build .`

**Actual Behavior:**
The build fails during the linking phase with an error indicating the package archive is missing:
```
cannot find package github.com/google/uuid (using -importcfg)
/usr/local/go/pkg/tool/linux_amd64/link: cannot open file : open : no such file or directory
```

### Expected behavior

The file is injected and the dependency is successfully resolved, compiled, and linked into the final binary (just like hook dependencies for func rules).

### Additional context

Currently, this issue doesn't affect `func` rules because their hook dependencies are automatically extracted and pre-registered in `otelc.runtime.go` during the setup phase. The fix will likely involve exploring how to generalize this dependency discovery process so that *all* rule types (especially code-injecting ones like `add_file`) have their imports discovered and registered into the build graph before `toolexec` begins.

<sub>**Tip**: [React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with  to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

items.title: fix(tool): register add_file imports in otelc.runtime.go during setup
items.body:
## Description

`add_file` (and other rules that inject imports) can pull in packages that aren't part of the app's normal build graph. Before this change, those packages were only patched into `importcfg` during toolexec, too late for `go build` to compile them, so the linker failed.

This PR fixes that by discovering those imports during setup and blank-importing them in `otelc.runtime.go`, the same way we already do for func-rule hook packages. That forces `go build` to compile them up front.

Also applies optional top-level `imports:` on `add_file` rules when the file is injected (this was documented but not implemented).

## Motivation

Repro from #1032: an `add_file` rule injects a `//go:build ignore` file that imports e.g. `github.com/google/uuid`. Setup only blank-imported the rule's `path` package (often just a stub), so `uuid` never got a compile action. Build then failed with:

```
cannot find package github.com/google/uuid (using -importcfg)
```

Func rules didn't hit this because their hook packages were already registered in `otelc.runtime.go`. This generalizes that for `add_file` and other import-injecting rules.

Fixes #1032

items.title: refactor(test): replace log.Fatal with graceful shutdown in example apps
items.body:
## Description

This PR refactors all `main.go` files inside the `test/apps/` directory to replace calls to `log.Fatal` and `log.Fatalf` with a graceful shutdown pattern. 

Specifically, the core application logic has been moved from `main()` to a `run() error` function. The new `main()` wrapper executes `run()`, logs any returned errors using `log.Printf`, and subsequently exits with `os.Exit(1)`.

## Motivation

Sample apps and tests previously used `log.Fatal` or `log.Fatalf` to exit upon error. `log.Fatal` immediately calls `os.Exit(1)`, which prevents any deferred functions (such as `defer provider.Shutdown()`) from running. 

This meant that traces generated just prior to an error might not be properly flushed to the backend before process termination. This refactor ensures all `defer` statements are respected while preserving the non-zero exit code behavior on failure.

items.title: fix(tool/internal/instrument): resolve file rule path directly to prevent filename suffix collision
items.body:
## Description

This PR updates `applyFileRule` in `tool/internal/instrument/apply_file.go` to directly resolve the target file via `filepath.Join(rule.ResolvedPath, rule.File)` and verify its existence with `util.PathExists(file)`, instead of listing all directory files with `util.ListFiles` and matching with `strings.HasSuffix`.

Unit tests have been added to `tool/internal/instrument/apply_file_test.go` covering:
- Successful file rule application and package renaming.
- Verifying that files sharing common suffixes (e.g. `custom_helper.go` vs `helper.go`) do not cause accidental collisions.
- Clear error handling for missing files.
- Subdirectory relative path support.

## Motivation

Previously, `applyFileRule` scanned all files in `rule.ResolvedPath` with `util.ListFiles` and found the target file using `strings.HasSuffix(file, rule.File)`. Because `strings.HasSuffix` does not respect path segment boundaries, any file sharing a suffix (e.g., `my_hook.go` when `hook.go` is specified) could be chosen if enumerated first during directory traversal. Directly constructing and validating `filepath.Join(rule.ResolvedPath, rule.File)` eliminates false suffix collisions and avoids unnecessary directory walks.

Fixes #1039

items.title: bug(tool/internal/instrument): directive rule injects its imports even when no function matches
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`applyDirectiveRule` in `tool/internal/instrument/apply_directive.go` adds the rule's
`imports:` to the target file *before* it looks for the functions the directive annotates:

```go
func (ip *InstrumentPhase) applyDirectiveRule(ctx context.Context, r *rule.InstDirectiveRule, root *dst.File) error {
	if err := ip.addRuleImports(ctx, root, r.Imports, r.Name); err != nil {   // <- import added here
		return err
	}
	tmpl, err := fasttemplate.NewTemplate(r.Template, "{{", "}}")
	...
	funcs := ast.FindFuncsByDirective(root, r.Directive)                       // <- match computed here
```

`ast.FindFuncsByDirective` only matches a directive that is a *leading* comment on a
top-level `FuncDecl`. If the same comment appears anywhere else in the file — inside a
function body, on a `GenDecl`, on a struct field — `funcs` is empty and nothing is
injected. The import is already in the AST at that point, and `instrument()` writes the
file out regardless, so the user's package ends up with:

```
main.go:6:8: "fmt" imported and not used
```

in code they did not write and cannot easily trace back to a rule.

The other rule types already guard against this. `apply_call.go` has an explicit
`if !appendModified && !replaceModified { return nil }` before its `addRuleImports` call;
`apply_struct.go` and `apply_decl.go` both locate their target and return early when it is
missing, before touching imports. `apply_directive.go` is the only one without the guard.

There is a second, quieter symptom in `applyOneRule` (`tool/internal/instrument/instrument.go`):

```go
case *rule.InstDirectiveRule:
	return true, ip.applyDirectiveRule(ctx, rt, root)
```

It reports `true` ("a globals file is needed") unconditionally, so a directive rule that
matched nothing still makes `instrument()` call `writeGlobals` and emit the `HookContext`
interface into the target package.

### Environment

- OS: Linux / any
- Go Version: 1.25
- Version: main (efb163d)

### To Reproduce

1. Write a source file where the directive is not a leading comment on a top-level func:

   ```go
   package main

   func main() {
   	//otelc:span
   	value := 1
   	println(value)
   }
   ```

2. Apply a directive rule that carries a non-empty `imports:` map:

   ```yaml
   span_directive_no_match:
     target: main
     where:
       directive: "otelc:span"
     do:
       - expand_directive:
           template: |-
             fmt.Println("span start: {{FuncName}}")
     imports:
       fmt: "fmt"
   ```

3. Build. The compile fails with `"fmt" imported and not used`.

### Expected behavior

A directive rule that matches no function should be a no-op: no imports injected, no
globals file emitted, and the target file unchanged.
items.author: darkraider01

items.title: bug(tool/internal/instrument): decl rule replace/wrap rewrites every name in a multi-name var/const declaration
items.body:
### Describe the bug

A decl rule targets one identifier, but `applyDeclRule` in
`tool/internal/instrument/apply_decl.go` rewrites every name declared in the same
`ValueSpec`.

`ast.FindNamedDecl` / `findValueDecl` return the whole `*dst.ValueSpec` that contains the
matched name and discard which name it was. `applyDeclRule` then has no way to tell the
targeted name from its siblings, and the replace path assigns to all of them:

```go
// Assign the expression to all names in the spec.
spec.Values = make([]dst.Expr, len(spec.Names))
for i := range spec.Values {
	spec.Values[i] = util.AssertType[dst.Expr](dst.Clone(expr))
}
```

`wrapDeclValues` has the same shape — it loops over every entry in `spec.Values`.

So given

```go
var readTimeout, writeTimeout = 5 * time.Second, 30 * time.Second
```

a rule targeting only `readTimeout` silently rewrites `writeTimeout` as well. The failure
is silent: the build succeeds and the instrumented binary just has the wrong value for a
variable no rule mentioned.

There is also an arity hazard specific to the replace path. For a tuple-valued
initializer:

```go
var alpha, beta = pair()   // 2 names, 1 initializer
```

`make([]dst.Expr, len(spec.Names))` produces 2 values from a spec that had 1, emitting
`var alpha, beta = expr, expr` — a structurally different declaration from the one the
user wrote.

### Environment

- OS: Linux / any
- Go Version: 1.25
- Version: main (efb163d)

### To Reproduce

Apply a decl rule with `kind: var`, `identifier: alpha`, `replace: "99"` to:

```go
var alpha, beta = 1, 2
```

Observed output: `var alpha, beta = 99, 99`

The wrap advice behaves the same way: wrapping `alpha` with `double({{ . }})` produces
`var alpha, beta = double(1), double(2)`.

### Expected behavior

Only the initializer belonging to the targeted name is rewritten:
`var alpha, beta = 99, 2`.

For the tuple-valued case, where no single initializer belongs to the targeted name,
the tool should report the situation rather than silently reshape the declaration.
items.author: darkraider01

items.title: fix(tool/internal/instrument): skip directive rule injection when no function matches
items.body:
## Description

`applyDirectiveRule` added the rule's `imports:` to the target file before it computed
`ast.FindFuncsByDirective`. When the directive comment exists in the file but is not a
leading comment on a top-level func, the match set is empty and nothing is injected — but
the import is already in the AST, and `instrument()` writes the file out regardless. The
result is an `"fmt" imported and not used` compile error in code the user did not write.

This reorders the function so the match is computed first and returns early when nothing is
annotated, which is the same guard `apply_call.go` (`if !appendModified && !replaceModified`)
and `apply_struct.go` / `apply_decl.go` (find target, return early) already have.

`applyDirectiveRule` now also reports whether it instrumented anything, so `applyOneRule`
no longer returns `true` unconditionally for `*rule.InstDirectiveRule`. Previously a
zero-match directive rule still made `instrument()` call `writeGlobals` and emit the
`HookContext` interface into the target package.

Two tests cover this:

- A golden fixture, `testdata/golden/directive-rule-no-match/`, applies a directive rule
  carrying `imports: {fmt: fmt}` to a file whose directive sits on an assignment inside a
  function body. Against the unfixed code the fixture fails to compile with
  `"fmt" imported and not used`; with the fix the output is byte-identical to the input.
- `TestApplyDirectiveRule_NoMatchingFuncs` calls `applyDirectiveRule` directly and asserts
  that no import spec was added and that the call reports "nothing instrumented". Note it
  counts import specs in `root.Decls` rather than checking `len(root.Imports)`:
  `imports.AddToFile` appends to `root.Decls` and never populates `root.Imports`, so an
  assertion on the latter would pass with or without this fix.
  `TestApplyDirectiveRule_MatchingFunc` covers the positive path, and
  `TestApplyDirectiveRule_TemplateErrors` covers the three template failure
  modes — an unterminated tag, an unknown tag, and a template that renders to
  invalid Go — each of which must be reported rather than silently skipped.

## Motivation

A directive rule that carries imports and matches nothing currently breaks the user's
build with an error that points at their own source file and gives no hint that a rule
caused it.

items.title: fix(tool/internal/instrument): rewrite only the targeted name of a multi-name declaration
items.body:
## Description

`ast.FindNamedDecl` returns the whole `*dst.ValueSpec` that contains a matched name and
discards which name matched, so `applyDeclRule` rewrote every name in the spec: the replace
path reassigned all of `spec.Values`, and `wrapDeclValues` wrapped all of them. A rule
targeting `alpha` in `var alpha, beta = 1, 2` produced `var alpha, beta = 99, 99`.

The fix locates the targeted name's position in `spec.Names` and rewrites only the
initializer at that index. `wrapDeclValues` becomes `wrapDeclValue` and the replace path
moves into `replaceDeclValue`, both taking that index.

### Arity handling — please weigh in

For a tuple-valued initializer such as `var alpha, beta = pair()` there are two names and
one initializer, so no single value belongs to the targeted name. The old code turned that
into `var alpha, beta = expr, expr`, a structurally different declaration. I chose to
**report an error** for both `replace` and `wrap` in that case rather than guess, since
producing correct code would mean splitting the declaration, and the alternatives all
change the user's declaration shape. I'd like reviewer input on whether erroring is the
behaviour you want, or whether a skip-with-warning would fit the tool better.

One existing behaviour is deliberately preserved: a **single** name with no initializer
still gains one on the replace path (`var X T` becomes `var X T = expr`). A *multi*-name
declaration with no initializer now errors instead of gaining one initializer per name.

### Tests

`TestDeclRuleDoesNotClobberSiblingNames` and `TestDeclRuleWrapDoesNotClobberSiblingNames`
render the rewritten file back to source and assert `var alpha, beta = 99, 2` and
`var alpha, beta = 1, double(2)`. Against the unfixed code they produce `99, 99` and
`double(1), double(2)`. `TestDeclRuleReplaceRejectsTupleValuedInitializer` and its wrap
companion cover the arity case and assert the declaration is left untouched. The existing
`wrapDeclValues` unit tests are renamed and `TestWrapDeclValue_MultipleValues` now asserts
the sibling is left alone rather than that both values are wrapped.

## Motivation

The failure is silent — the build succeeds and the instrumented binary just carries the
wrong value for a variable no rule mentioned. `var readTimeout, writeTimeout = ...` is a
realistic shape in the kind of library code this tool instruments.

Fixes #1044

## Verification

`make format` and `make test-unit` pass locally. The integration and e2e halves of
`make test` were verified through this PR's CI jobs — `Test (go …)`, the `Integration
Tests` shards on ubuntu/macOS/Windows and arm64, and `Coverage E2E Tests` — rather than a

`.github/workflows/lint-golang.yaml` pins — 0 issues. Worth flagging separately:
`.tools/go.mod` pins **v2.12.2**, so `make lint/go` locally builds a newer linter than CI
runs, and under v2.12.2 pristine `main` already reports 37 findings in files this PR does

items.title: bug(instrumentation/k8s.io/client-go): OnDelete forwards unwrapped object, stripping DeletedFinalStateUnknown from the user's handler
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`k8SOtelEventHandler.OnDelete` in `instrumentation/k8s.io/client-go/k8s_otel_handler.go` unwraps `cache.DeletedFinalStateUnknown` to extract object metadata for span attributes, but then forwards that same *unwrapped* value to the wrapped user handler instead of the original object:

```go
func (h k8SOtelEventHandler) OnDelete(obj any) {
	if o, ok := obj.(cache.DeletedFinalStateUnknown); ok {
		obj = o.Obj
	}

	objInfo := getObjectInfo(obj)
	...
	h.handler.OnDelete(obj)
}
```

`h.handler` is the application's real `cache.ResourceEventHandler` - confirmed via `beforeProcessDeltas` in `hook.go`, which fully replaces the informer's handler parameter with this wrapper (`ictx.SetParam(0, newK8SOtelEventHandler(handler, ctx))`). So every application using k8s client-go informers with `otelc` compile-time instrumentation loses the `DeletedFinalStateUnknown` wrapper on every delete event, regardless of whether it was actually a tombstone.

`DeletedFinalStateUnknown` signals that client-go's local cache lost track of the object (e.g. a missed watch event during a resync), so the delete is inferred rather than confirmed, and the wrapped object may be stale. Kubernetes controllers commonly type-assert on this to decide how to handle the delete (e.g. skip finalizer logic on a possibly-stale object). Stripping it silently changes application-observable behavior based on whether instrumentation is applied, not just what gets exported as telemetry.

### Environment

 - OS: Linux (not platform-specific)
 - Go Version: 1.25
 - Version: main (450a2b6)

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Instrument an app with `k8s.io/client-go` that registers an informer with an `OnDelete(obj any)` handler checking `if _, ok := obj.(cache.DeletedFinalStateUnknown); ok { ... }`.
2. Trigger a delete event that arrives as `DeletedFinalStateUnknown` (e.g. during a cache resync after a missed watch event).
3. The type assertion in the user's handler never succeeds under `otelc` instrumentation, even though it would without it.

### Expected behavior

The instrumentation should pass through the original `obj` (wrapped or not) to `h.handler.OnDelete`, using a separate variable only for the span-attribute extraction.

### Additional context

`TestOnDelete` in `k8s_otel_handler_test.go` only exercises a plain `*corev1.Pod`, never a `cache.DeletedFinalStateUnknown`-wrapped object, which is why this wasn't caught.

Relevant code:
https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/blob/450a2b6abdd37a46624a24f825e7027c219928fd/instrumentation/k8s.io/client-go/k8s_otel_handler.go#L59-L76
https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/blob/450a2b6abdd37a46624a24f825e7027c219928fd/instrumentation/k8s.io/client-go/hook.go#L50-L78

items.title: fix(instrumentation/net/http): http.ServeFile loses the sendfile fast path on instrumented servers
items.body:
## Description

`BeforeServeHTTP` swaps the handler's `http.ResponseWriter` for `writerWrapper` so the status code can be read back afterwards. net/http's own `*response` implements `io.ReaderFrom`, and that is the method `io.Copy` looks for on the destination — it's what ends up handing the body to the connection and reaching `sendfile(2)`.

`writerWrapper` didn't implement it. So once the wrapper is in place, `io.Copy` no longer finds a `ReaderFrom` and falls back to its generic 32KiB copy loop. `http.ServeFile` and `http.ServeContent` both end in `io.CopyN(w, sendContent, sendSize)`, so every file served by an instrumented server takes the slow path — not because of anything the application did, but because it's instrumented. The response is still correct, which is presumably why it went unnoticed.

This is the same shape as #795, which added `http.Pusher` to this wrapper: it shouldn't hide a capability of the writer it replaces.

## Fix

Implement `io.ReaderFrom` on `writerWrapper`. If the underlying writer has one (the real net/http case), delegate to it. If it doesn't, copy through `Write` behind a small `writeOnly` shim so `io.Copy` can't pick this method up again and recurse. Both paths record the implicit `200` first, the same as `Write` already does, so status capture doesn't change.

The second commit implements `io.StringWriter` for the same reason: net/http's `*response` implements it so `io.WriteString` can skip a `[]byte` conversion, and hiding it forces that conversion back on every string write. Same delegate-or-fall-back structure, same implicit-200 handling.

Both interfaces are added to the compile-time assertion block that already lists `Hijacker`, `Flusher` and `Pusher`.

## Performance

Measured on Linux (WSL), 1MB file over loopback, comparing against the pre-fix wrapper forced onto the copy loop:

| | latency | alloc/request |
|---|---|---|
| pre-fix wrapper (copy loop) | 24.7ms | 41KB |
| with this fix | 16.9ms | 10KB |
| unwrapped (no instrumentation) | 14.2ms | — |

The ~31KB allocation difference is the 32KiB buffer `io.Copy` allocated on every request while `ReadFrom` was hidden. The fix lands close to the unwrapped ceiling, so the remaining gap is wrapper overhead unrelated to the copy path.

These numbers come from a local benchmark comparing the copy loop against the fast path. Per review feedback the benchmark isn't part of the diff — it needed a duplicate of the old wrapper to measure against, which isn't worth carrying in the tree.

## Motivation

Instrumentation shouldn't make the application slower in ways the application can't see or control. No existing issue covers this — I found it reading the wrapper while looking at something else. Happy to open one if you'd rather it were tracked.

To be clear about the scope: this restores performance, it does not fix incorrect output. Responses were always byte-correct, and the improvement is zero for handlers that don't serve files or write strings.

## Notes on the tests

The ones that matter are `TestWriterWrapper_ReadFromUsesUnderlyingFastPath` and `TestWriterWrapper_WriteStringUsesUnderlyingFastPath`, which fail on `main` — I checked by stashing the fix and re-running.

One thing that caught me out and is worth knowing if you touch these tests: `io.Copy` prefers a `WriterTo` on the **source** over a `ReaderFrom` on the destination. My first version used `strings.NewReader` as the body and passed without the fix, because the copy never consulted the writer at all. The tests use an `*io.LimitedReader` instead — no `WriterTo`, and it's the exact shape `http.ServeContent` produces via `io.CopyN`. There's a comment on the helper so it doesn't get simplified back later.

A related trap, caught in review: `httptest.ResponseRecorder` **does** implement `io.StringWriter`. The `WriteString` fallback test can't be built on the recorder, because it would take the fast path and never exercise the fallback — it passed for the wrong reason, since both paths emit identical bytes. That test now uses a minimal writer implementing exactly `http.ResponseWriter`, asserts the fallback actually goes through `Write`, and guards the premise so it can't silently drift back onto the fast path. (`ResponseRecorder` has no `ReadFrom`, so the `ReadFrom` fallback test is unaffected.)

`tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz` is regenerated since `instrumentation/` changed.

items.title: bug(tool): blank receivers bypass collision-safe synthetic naming
items.body:
### Describe the bug

PR #1035 introduced collision-safe synthetic names for unnamed and blank parameters and return values. However, the blank receiver branch in `collectArguments` still uses the old `_ignoredParamN` naming scheme instead of `syntheticNamer`.

In `tool/internal/instrument/apply_func.go`, blank receivers are currently renamed using logic equivalent to:

```go
receiver = fmt.Sprintf("%s%d", ignoredParam, idx)
```

Unnamed receivers and blank parameters instead use:

```go
next(ignoredParam)
```

As a result, blank receivers can still collide with identifiers already declared in the function signature.

### Environment

- OS: any
- Go version: any supported version
- Version: current `main`, after #1035

### To Reproduce

Instrument a method with a blank receiver and a parameter using the legacy generated receiver name:

```go
package example

type T struct{}

func (_ T) Method(_ignoredParam0 int) {}
```

Apply a function rule targeting `Method`.

The blank receiver may be renamed to `_ignoredParam0`, producing a signature equivalent to:

```go
func (_ignoredParam0 T) Method(_ignoredParam0 int) {}
```

The generated source fails to compile because `_ignoredParam0` is redeclared in the same scope.

### Expected behavior

Blank receivers should use the same rule-identity-based, collision-safe synthetic name generator used for unnamed receivers, blank parameters, and return values.

### Proposed fix

Use `next(ignoredParam)` in the blank receiver branch of `collectArguments` and add regression coverage for a blank receiver whose legacy generated name collides with an existing parameter.
items.author: ADITYA-CODE-SOURCE

items.title: fix(tool): use collision-safe names for blank receivers
items.body:
## Description

Use `syntheticNamer` when remapping blank method receivers.

PR #1035 migrated generated parameter and return names to collision-safe, rule-identity-based names, but the blank-receiver branch retained the old counter-based implementation. Because the local counter was removed in the same migration, current `main` also fails to compile with `undefined: idx`.

This change routes blank receivers through the existing `next(ignoredParam)` generator.

## Motivation

Blank receivers should follow the same naming path as unnamed receivers and blank parameters. This prevents collisions with existing signature identifiers and restores compilation on current `main`.

Fixes #1054

items.body:
## Summary

Per [docs/testing.md](docs/testing.md), E2E tests spin up **multiple instrumented processes** and assert they form one coherent trace (shared trace ID).

`test/apps/grpcserverkafkaclient` is documented as a combined gRPC server + Kafka producer app **for e2e testing**, but today it is only exercised by an **integration** test:

- File: `test/integration/grpcserver_kafkaclient_test.go`
- The request is made with an in-test (uninstrumented) gRPC client via `grpc.NewClient`
- Asserts 1 trace with 2 spans: gRPC server → Kafka producer (in-process parent/child)
- Uses a Kafka testcontainer + `KAFKA_BROKERS`

That does **not** verify cross-process propagation from an instrumented gRPC client into the gRPC→Kafka chain.

Existing E2E coverage:

| E2E Test | File |
|---|---|
| HTTP client + server | `http_test.go` |
| gRPC client + server | `grpc_test.go` |
| Kafka producer + consumer | `kafka_test.go` |
| HTTP → SQL (multi-process) | `httpserver_dbclient_test.go` |
| gRPC → SQL (multi-process) | `grpcserver_dbclient_test.go` |
| HTTP → Kafka (multi-process) | `httpserver_kafkaclient_test.go` |

## Proposed work

Add `test/e2e/grpcserver_kafkaclient_test.go`, mirroring `test/e2e/httpserver_kafkaclient_test.go` and `test/e2e/grpcserver_dbclient_test.go`:

1. Skip on Windows / unhealthy Docker (same as existing Kafka e2e/integration)
2. Start a Kafka testcontainer and set `KAFKA_BROKERS` on the fixture
3. `BuildAndStart("grpcserverkafkaclient", "-front-port=<port>")` using `FreePort` + `WaitForTCP`
4. `BuildAndRun("grpcclient", "-addr", "127.0.0.1:<port>", "-name", "...")`
5. Wait for spans with `f.WaitForSpans(3)` (needed because `BuildAndRun` returns when the client exits while the server/producer spans may still be in flight)
6. Assert **one** distributed trace with **3** spans:
   - instrumented gRPC **client**
   - gRPC **server** (frontend)
   - Kafka **producer** (frontend → broker)
7. Assert shared trace ID and parent/child links across the chain
8. Keep assertions focused on propagation (semconv detail already covered by `grpc_test.go` / `kafka_test.go` / the integration test), while pinning a successful RPC outcome (`rpc.grpc.status_code=0`) so a failed request cannot silently pass

- Reuse (no new apps / no app tweaks expected): `test/apps/grpcclient`, `test/apps/grpcserverkafkaclient`
- Reuse Kafka testcontainer helper pattern from e2e (`startKafkaContainer`)

gRPC client, gRPC server, and Kafka producer instrumentation already exist.

`otelc pin` previously extracted the complete embedded source bundle only to discover which built-in instrumentation modules matched application dependencies. The generated manifest introduced by #999 contains that metadata directly, making extraction and the embedded archive unnecessary.

The temporary source-checkout bridge keeps built-in instrumentation builds functional while #983 is developed separately.

This takes down `make build`, so every PR that reaches the build step fails with something unrelated to its own diff. I hit it as `Overhead Threshold Check` failing at the `Build otelc` step on an unrelated PR of mine:

```
Building instrumentation tool...
# go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/tool/internal/instrument
tool/internal/instrument/apply_func.go:126:50: undefined: idx
/bin/bash: line 5: ./otelc: No such file or directory
make: *** [Makefile:142: build] Error 127
```

Bisected: `1bec7dc` builds, `2d6daf5` does not.

## How it happened

Two PRs landed the same day and collided without either one's CI seeing the other:

- **#799** (`450a2b6`) added the blank-receiver branch to `collectArguments`, naming the synthetic receiver with the package's `idx` counter.
- **#1035** (`2d6daf5`) replaced that counter with `syntheticNamer` / `next()`, converting every call site that existed *on its base* — which did not yet include the branch #799 had just added.

Both were green on their own base. Neither branch was rebased on the other, so the missed call site only exists once both are merged. Nothing is wrong with either PR in isolation.

This is the failure mode @dobbydobap described in #973 — a green check from a stale base is indistinguishable from a green check from current `main` in the PR list. Worth noting as a live example, since the discussion there was about whether to require branches to be up to date before merging.

## Fix

Point the blank-receiver branch at `next(ignoredParam)`, matching the three sibling branches in the same function. That also gives the blank receiver the hash-qualified name #1035 introduced, which is exactly the collision-avoidance that PR was about — so this is the naming #1035 would have applied had the branch been visible to it.

The `"underscore receiver"` case in `TestCollectArguments` still asserted the pre-#1035 literal `"_ignoredParam0"`. It now uses the `syntheticParam(0)` helper the neighbouring `"unnamed receiver"` case already uses. That assertion is the reason the fix is not purely a one-line change: the test encoded the old naming scheme too.

## Verification

- `go build ./...` — clean
- `go test ./tool/...` — all 13 packages pass, including `tool/internal/instrument`

Given this blocks builds on `main`, it may be worth merging ahead of the queue.

### Description
In `tool/internal/setup/pin.go`, `generatePinnedProjects` currently decompresses the entire `otelc-bundle.tgz` tarball to disk and walks filesystem directories to parse `otelc.yaml` rules via `loadMinimalRules` and `loadModuleRules`.

2. **Code Duplication**: `pin.go` defines its own `yamlRule` struct and `loadMinimalRules` / `loadModuleRules` functions, which duplicate the functionality in `tool/internal/manifest`.

1. Replace `loadMinimalRules` in `pin.go` with `manifest.Load()` from `tool/internal/manifest`.
2. Update `matchInstrumentationImports` to operate directly on `manifest.Manifest`.
3. Extract `otelc-bundle.tgz` only if matching instrumentations were found (`len(imports) > 0`) prior to running `syncDeps`.
4. Remove redundant `yamlRule`, `loadModuleRules`, and `loadMinimalRules` helpers.

items.title: bug(instrumentation/database/sql): Tx.Commit and Tx.Rollback spans start a new trace instead of joining the caller's
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`(*sql.Tx).Commit` and `(*sql.Tx).Rollback` spans are not attached to the trace that opened the transaction. They become the root of a separate trace.

In a request that does `BeginTx` → `ExecContext` → `Commit`, the exported result is two traces rather than one:

```
Trace f70242878d75e76c...: 3 spans   (GET /tx, START, INSERT)
Trace 119db8bac0d382ea...: 1 span    (COMMIT)
```

The COMMIT span carries the right attributes, so it looks correct in isolation. It is simply not connected to anything, and the request trace shows a transaction that is opened and written to but never committed.

### Cause

`Commit` and `Rollback` are the only instrumented `database/sql` calls that take no `context.Context`, so their hooks have no argument to start the span from. Both start from `context.Background()`:

https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/blob/main/instrumentation/database/sql/client.go#L515

```go
instrumentStart(ictx, context.Background(), "commit", "COMMIT", tx.Endpoint, tx.DriverName, tx.DSN, tx.DbName)
```

A background context has no span, so the SDK gives the span no parent and allocates a new trace ID.

I assumed at first that the goroutine-local fallback in `instrumentation/go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace` would cover this, since it rewrites `trace.SpanFromContext` to return the GLS span when the context has none. It does not: `runtime.GetSpanFromGLS()` returns `nil` at the point `Commit` runs. I confirmed that by logging it from `beforeTxCommitInstrumentation` in an instrumented build.

### Why CI does not catch it

The two existing db propagation tests both use `QueryContext`, which takes a context, so parentage falls out of the argument:

- `test/integration/httpserver_dbclient_test.go`
- `test/integration/grpcserver_dbclient_test.go`

`TestDbClient/Transaction` does exercise `Commit`, but `test/apps/dbclient/main.go` creates no enclosing span, so every span there is a root already and the test only asserts names and attributes.

So the one code path that cannot take a context from an argument is the one path never asserted to join a trace.

### Steps to reproduce

Add a handler to `test/apps/httpserverdbclient/main.go`:

```go
mux.HandleFunc("/tx", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	tx, err := db.BeginTx(r.Context(), nil)
	if err != nil {
		http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusInternalServerError)
		return
	}
	if _, err := tx.ExecContext(r.Context(),
		"INSERT INTO orders (user_id, amount) VALUES (?, ?)", 1, 99.99); err != nil {
		_ = tx.Rollback()
		http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusInternalServerError)
		return
	}
	if err := tx.Commit(); err != nil {
		http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusInternalServerError)
		return
	}
	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
	_, _ = w.Write([]byte("frontend committed transaction"))
})
```

and a test alongside `TestHTTPServerDBClient`:

```go
f.WaitForSpans(4)
f.RequireTraceCount(1)
f.RequireSpansPerTrace(4)

httpServerSpan := testutil.RequireSpan(t, f.Traces(), testutil.IsServer,
	func(s ptrace.Span) bool { return s.Name() == "GET /tx" })

for _, op := range []string{"START", "INSERT", "COMMIT"} {
	span := testutil.RequireSpan(t, f.Traces(), testutil.IsClient,
		testutil.HasAttribute("db.operation.name", op))
	require.Equal(t, httpServerSpan.TraceID(), span.TraceID(),
		"%s span must share the HTTP server's trace", op)
	require.Equal(t, httpServerSpan.SpanID(), span.ParentSpanID(),
		"%s span parent must be the HTTP server span", op)
}
```

`RequireTraceCount(1)` fails with `Expected 1 traces, got 2`. START and INSERT pass the parentage assertions; COMMIT is in the other trace.

### Expected behaviour

COMMIT and ROLLBACK spans should sit in the same trace as the transaction that produced them, as siblings of the START span under the caller's span.

### What I tried

I attempted the fix that matches the existing pattern here, recording the caller's context on the `Tx` in `afterTxInstrumentation` the way `Endpoint`, `DSN`, `DriverName` and `DbName` already are, by adding a field to the `add_new_field_tx` rule:

```yaml
- name: OtelCtx
  type: context.Context
```

That did not build. `add_struct_fields` appears to handle unqualified types (`string`, `map[string]string`) but not a qualified type like `context.Context`, and the build fails during setup rather than with a type error, so I could not tell quickly whether this is a real limitation or something I got wrong. I did not want to guess at tool changes, so I am reporting the bug rather than opening a half-finished PR.

If the rule can carry a qualified type, storing the context on the `Tx` looks like the smallest fix. If not, the alternatives seem to be making the GLS fallback reachable from these hooks, or having the tool pass the enclosing context to hooks on context-less methods.

Happy to do the work on whichever direction maintainers prefer.

### Environment

- otelc built from `66d4af3` (main)
- Go 1.26.2, windows/amd64
- Reproduced with the in-repo `testdb` driver, so no external database needed

items.title: bug(tool/setup): GOWORK=off tracks an unrelated go.work.sum
items.body:
### Describe the bug

When workspace mode is explicitly disabled with `GOWORK=off`, auto-pin still tracks a `go.work.sum` file from the current working directory.

`getBackupFiles` runs `go env GOWORK` and treats every non-empty result as a workspace path:

```go
goWorkPath := strings.TrimSpace(string(goWorkOutput))
if goWorkPath != "" {
    goWorkSumPath := filepath.Join(filepath.Dir(goWorkPath), "go.work.sum")
    files = append(files, goWorkSumPath)
}
```

However, `go env GOWORK` returns the literal value `off` when workspace mode is disabled. Because `filepath.Dir("off")` evaluates to `.`, the code adds `./go.work.sum` to the backup list even though no workspace is active.

`AutoPin` then passes this path to `StateManager.TrackAll`:

- If the file exists, it is unnecessarily snapshotted and later restored.
- If the file does not exist, it is recorded for removal if it appears before cleanup.

As a result, a concurrent edit could be overwritten, or a file created by another process in the same directory could be removed during cleanup.

The repository already handles the `off` sentinel correctly in `pkgload.ModuleAndWorkspace`:

```go
workspace := goWork != "" && goWork != "off"
```

### To reproduce

1. Create a temporary module containing a `go.mod`.
2. Set `GOWORK=off`.
3. Call `getBackupFiles` from that directory.
4. Observe that the returned backup list includes `./go.work.sum`.

### Expected behavior

No `go.work.sum` should be tracked when `GOWORK=off`, because workspace mode is explicitly disabled.

### Proposed fix

Exclude the documented `off` sentinel before constructing the workspace sum path:

```go
if goWorkPath != "" && goWorkPath != "off" {
    goWorkSumPath := filepath.Join(filepath.Dir(goWorkPath), "go.work.sum")
    files = append(files, goWorkSumPath)
}
```

A regression test in `TestGetBackupFiles` can set `GOWORK=off` and verify that the result contains the expected module files but no `go.work.sum`.
