items.title: bug(tool/internal/instrument): stripBuildIgnoreTag corrupts //go:build ignore text appearing anywhere in a file rule's source
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`stripBuildIgnoreTag` in `tool/internal/instrument/apply_file.go` strips the `//go:build ignore` constraint from a file rule's source before it is injected into the target package, using a whole-file substring replace:

```go
func stripBuildIgnoreTag(content string) string {
	return strings.ReplaceAll(content, "//go:build ignore", "")
}
```

`strings.ReplaceAll` has no notion of Go syntax, so it deletes that text from *everywhere* in the file — string literals, doc comments, any position — not just the leading build-constraint line it is meant to remove.

The corruption is silent: the result is still valid Go, so nothing fails to compile and nothing is logged. The injected file just carries different values than its source.

### Environment

 - OS: Linux (WSL2 / Ubuntu); not platform-specific — the function is pure string manipulation
 - Go Version: 1.25.7
 - Version: `1110621` (`main`)

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Add the following test to `tool/internal/instrument/`:

```go
func TestStripBuildIgnoreTagPreservesNonConstraintText(t *testing.T) {
	src := "//go:build ignore\n" +
		"\n" +
		"package hooks\n" +
		"\n" +
		"// Every file rule source must carry //go:build ignore at the top.\n" +
		"const marker = \"//go:build ignore\"\n"

	got := stripBuildIgnoreTag(src)

	if !strings.Contains(got, "const marker = \"//go:build ignore\"") {
		t.Errorf("string literal was corrupted:\n%s", got)
	}
	if !strings.Contains(got, "must carry //go:build ignore at the top") {
		t.Errorf("comment prose was corrupted:\n%s", got)
	}
	if strings.HasPrefix(strings.TrimLeft(got, "\n"), "//go:build ignore") {
		t.Errorf("leading build constraint was not stripped:\n%s", got)
	}
}
```

2. Run `go test -run TestStripBuildIgnoreTagPreservesNonConstraintText ./tool/internal/instrument/`
3. See the failure:

```text
=== RUN   TestStripBuildIgnoreTagPreservesNonConstraintText
    zz_repro_test.go:22: string literal was corrupted:

        package hooks

        // Every file rule source must carry  at the top.
        const marker = ""
    zz_repro_test.go:25: comment prose was corrupted:

        package hooks

        // Every file rule source must carry  at the top.
        const marker = ""
--- FAIL: TestStripBuildIgnoreTagPreservesNonConstraintText (0.00s)
```

`marker` becomes the empty string and the comment has a hole in it. The corrupted output still parses cleanly via `ast.NewAstParser().ParseSource`, so there is no error at any stage — the value is simply wrong at runtime.

### Expected behavior

Only genuine leading build-constraint lines are removed. Text inside string literals and comment prose is preserved verbatim.

### Additional context

**Current exposure.** The only in-tree file rule source today (`instrumentation/go.opentelemetry.io/otel/init/init_otelsdk.go`, referenced from `instrumentation/go.opentelemetry.io/otel/init/otelc.yaml`) does not contain the text outside its leading constraint, so nothing is broken right now. This is a latent trap for the next file rule whose source mentions the tag — plausible precisely because the convention requires every such file to carry it, making it a natural thing to document in a comment.

**Why existing tests do not catch it.** `TestStripBuildIgnoreTag` only supplies inputs where `//go:build ignore` appears as a standalone line (including a `multiple go:build ignore comments` case). Those pass under both the current implementation and a correct one, so they characterize current behavior rather than constrain it. No case places the text inside a string literal or mid-comment.

**Suggested fix.** Operate line-wise over the leading comment block preceding `package`, dropping only lines whose trimmed form is a build constraint, instead of substring-replacing over the whole file. Go's own `go/build` header parsing / `constraint.IsGoBuild` semantics are the reference: a `//go:build` line is only a constraint when it appears before the package clause.

items.title: fix(tool/internal/instrument): sort file keys in instrument() for deterministic error reporting
items.body:
## Description

`instrument()` iterates the file-to-rules map returned by `groupRules` directly with a bare
`range`. Go randomizes map iteration order per range statement, and the loop returns on the
first error it hits. When a package's rule set spans multiple files and more than one has a
failing rule, which failure gets reported — and the order the per-file `Info`/`Debug` log
lines are emitted in — varies between otherwise-identical runs of the same broken input.

The fix extracts a `sortedFiles` helper that returns `file2rules`'s keys via
`slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(...))` and has `instrument()` range over that instead of the map,
matching the pattern already used in #986 and #971 for the same class of ordering issue.

### Severity

Generated output is unaffected — I checked the three paths that could have made this
worse and confirmed none of them are:

- `ip.varDecls`, `ip.hookCtxDecl`, and `ip.hookCtxMethods` are reset and re-derived from the
  static embedded template on every `materializeTemplate()` call, so the globals file
  content is identical regardless of which file is processed last.
- `ip.appliedFuncIdentities` persists across files, but `InstFuncRule.Identity()` includes
  both `Func` and `Recv`, and `findFuncDecl` requires `!HasReceiver` when `recv` is empty.
  Go forbids duplicate `(Func, Recv)` pairs in one package, so two files can't produce a
  colliding identity and no file can be silently skipped.
- `groupRules`'s CGO remap (`resolveCgoFile`) is bijective (`foo.cgo1.go` → `foo.go`), so no
  two source files merge into one key with a nondeterministic rule order.

So this is about error and log reproducibility during a failing build, not correctness of a
successful one.

### Tests

`TestSortedFiles` builds a rule set with a deliberately unsorted file insertion order and
asserts `sortedFiles` returns them alphabetically, calling it 20 times against the same map
to pin that the result is stable. I verified the test actually catches the regression it's
meant to catch: temporarily reverting `sortedFiles` to a bare `for f := range m` loop made
the test fail with a real order mismatch, confirming it isn't just re-testing that
`slices.Sorted` returns sorted output.

## Motivation

Fixes #1070

## Verification

`make format` and `go test -shuffle=on -timeout=5m -count=1 ./tool/...` (what
`make test-unit/tool` runs) pass locally, including with shuffled test order — relevant
here since the fix itself is about ordering. The integration and e2e halves of `make test`
were verified through this PR's CI jobs rather than locally, since the testcontainers-based
suites had no usable Docker host here.

`make lint` was checked with golangci-lint **v2.11.3**, the version
`.github/workflows/lint-golang.yaml` pins — 0 issues on the changed files. As noted on
#1045/#1046: `.tools/go.mod` pins a newer local linter version, and pristine `main` already
reports pre-existing findings under it in files this PR does not touch.

---

## Checklist

- [x] PR title follows [conventional commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) format
- [x] Code formatted: `make format`
- [x] Linters pass: `make lint`
- [x] Tests pass: `make test`
- [x] Tests added for new functionality
- [x] Tests follow [testing guidelines](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/blob/main/docs/testing.md)
- [ ] Documentation updated (if applicable)
- [ ] OpenTelemetry Registry updated (if applicable, see [registry guide](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/blob/main/docs/instrument-guide.md#4-register-the-instrumentation))
- [ ] This PR has content that I did not fully write myself.
  - [ ] I used AI and I have read and followed the [Generative AI Contribution Policy](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md).
- [x] I have the experience and knowledge necessary to understand, review, and validate all content in this PR.[^I-know-my-stuff]

items.title: feat(instrumentation/kafka-go): add auto-instrumentation for (*kafka.Reader).FetchMessage
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Applications using `github.com/segmentio/kafka-go` with manual offset management consume messages via `(*kafka.Reader).FetchMessage(ctx context.Context) (kafka.Message, error)` instead of `ReadMessage`.

Currently, `instrumentation/github.com/segmentio/kafka-go/consumer/otelc.yaml` only targets `(*kafka.Reader).ReadMessage`. As a result, when an application calls `FetchMessage`:
1. No consumer `receive` spans are generated.
2. Trace context propagated in Kafka message headers is not extracted or attached to the trace tree, breaking distributed tracing for manual-commit Kafka workflows.

### Environment

 - OS: Linux / All
 - Go Version: 1.25 / 1.26
 - Version: v0.0.0 (main branch)

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Build an application compiled with `otelc` using `github.com/segmentio/kafka-go`.
2. Produce a message with `w.WriteMessages(ctx, msg)` (span created and trace context injected into headers).
3. Consume the message using `msg, err := r.FetchMessage(ctx)`.
4. Observe that no consumer span is emitted and trace propagation breaks.

### Expected behavior

`(*kafka.Reader).FetchMessage` should be instrumented symmetrically with `ReadMessage`, creating consumer `receive` spans and extracting trace context from message headers.

### Additional context

`FetchMessage` shares the exact parameter and return signature as `ReadMessage`:
`func (r *Reader) FetchMessage(ctx context.Context) (Message, error)`

**Proposed Implementation Plan**:
1. Add rule `kafka_reader_fetchmessage` to `instrumentation/github.com/segmentio/kafka-go/consumer/otelc.yaml` targeting `func: FetchMessage`, `recv: "*Reader"`.
2. Reuse `BeforeReadMessage` and `AfterReadMessage` (or alias them for clarity).
3. Add unit test coverage in `consumer_hook_test.go` and integration test coverage in `test/integration/httpserver_kafkaclient_test.go`.

items.title: New Instrumentation Request for github.com/segmentio/kafka-go (*kafka.Reader).FetchMessage
items.body:
**Package**

`github.com/segmentio/kafka-go`

**Version**

v0.4.x and later

**Environment**

Any Go application using compile-time instrumentation with `otelc`, deployed as a service consuming Kafka messages with manual offset management (i.e., calling `FetchMessage` + `CommitMessages` instead of `ReadMessage`).

**Use-case**

Applications that need fine-grained control over offset commits call `(*kafka.Reader).FetchMessage(ctx)` to receive a message without automatically committing the offset, then process it and call `CommitMessages` only on success. This is a common pattern for at-least-once processing guarantees.

Currently, the instrumentation in `instrumentation/github.com/segmentio/kafka-go/consumer/otelc.yaml` only hooks `ReadMessage`. When an application uses `FetchMessage` instead:

- No consumer `receive` spans are emitted.
- Trace context injected by the producer into message headers is never extracted, breaking distributed traces across the producer and consumer.

**Telemetry**

`FetchMessage` has the same signature as `ReadMessage` — `func (r *Reader) FetchMessage(ctx context.Context) (Message, error)` — so the same `BeforeReadMessage` / `AfterReadMessage` hooks can be reused. The expected telemetry is:

- A `<topic> receive` span with `SpanKindConsumer` on every `FetchMessage` call.
- Trace context extracted from message headers and linked to the producer span.
- Attributes matching the semantic conventions already applied for `ReadMessage`: `messaging.system`, `messaging.destination.name`, `messaging.operation`, `messaging.kafka.consumer.group`, `messaging.kafka.message.key`, `messaging.kafka.message.offset`, `messaging.kafka.destination.partition`.

**Anything else?**

The fix only requires adding a second rule entry in `otelc.yaml`:

```yaml
kafka_reader_fetchmessage:
  target: github.com/segmentio/kafka-go
  where:
    func: FetchMessage
    recv: "*Reader"
  do:
    - inject_hooks:
        before: BeforeReadMessage
        after: AfterReadMessage
        path: "go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/instrumentation/github.com/segmentio/kafka-go/consumer"
```

No changes to `consumer_hook.go` are needed since the function signatures are identical. A unit test case in `consumer_hook_test.go` and an integration test should accompany the change.

### Describe the bug

The orchestration tests introduced in PR #760 (`test(setup): cover Pin, pinLocked, AutoPin, prepareVendoredBuild`) are failing on the `windows-latest` unit test runner. 

The tests run successfully on Linux and macOS, but the Windows CI job times out or fails (e.g., `Unit Tests / Unit Tests (go windows-latest amd64) Failing after 6m`). The failure is highly likely due to path handling mismatches in `tool/internal/setup/pin_test.go`. The tests make extensive use of `filepath.Join()`, `filepath.Abs()`, and `filepath.Clean()`, which use backslashes (`\`) on Windows, causing them to fail when asserted against the internal state manager which might be standardizing on forward slashes (`/`).

### Environment

 - OS: Windows (`windows-latest` GitHub runner)
 - Go Version: 1.23
 - Version: `main` (commit 219f415+)

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Check out the latest `main` branch (commit `219f415` or newer).
2. Run `make test-unit/tool` on a Windows environment.
3. Observe the failures or hangs in `TestAutoPin_BacksUpGoMod` or similar tests inside `pin_test.go`.

### Expected behavior

The unit tests in `tool/internal/setup/pin_test.go` should pass cleanly across all supported operating systems, including Windows, without timing out or failing path assertions.

### Additional context

This is currently causing the `Unit Tests (go windows-latest amd64)` check to fail across all open PRs that sync with the latest `main`.

items.title: fix(instrumentation): map openai max_completion_tokens to gen_ai.request.max_tokens
items.body:
## Description

The OpenAI `chat/completions` request parameter `max_completion_tokens` was not mapped to the GenAI semantic convention attribute `gen_ai.request.max_tokens`, so spans for requests using the newer parameter (`gpt-4.1`, `gpt-5`, `o-series`, etc.) were missing the attribute entirely. The instrumentation only read the legacy `max_tokens` field.

Each version of the OpenAI middleware (v1, v2, v3) now reads both fields and maps whichever is set:

```go
if req.MaxCompletionTokens != nil {
    attrs = append(attrs, semconv.GenAIRequestMaxTokens(*req.MaxCompletionTokens))
} else if req.MaxTokens != nil {
    attrs = append(attrs, semconv.GenAIRequestMaxTokens(*req.MaxTokens))
}
```

`max_completion_tokens` takes precedence over `max_tokens` because OpenAI marks it as the preferred parameter for the newer models; `max_tokens` remains as a fallback for models that only support the legacy field.

## Motivation

`gen_ai.request.max_tokens` is part of the GenAI semantic conventions. Requests sent with `max_completion_tokens` (the parameter required by OpenAI's newer models) previously produced spans with no token-limit attribute, making it impossible to correlate the configured completion budget with telemetry.

Adds `TestParseChatRequest_MaxCompletionTokens` (unit) and `TestOtelMiddleware_ChatCompletion_MaxCompletionTokens` (integration) in each module asserting the mapping, including precedence when both fields are present.

Fixes #1007

items.title: bug(pkg/instrumentation/nethttp/server): writerWrapper breaks ResponseController deadlines, HTTP/2 Push, and sendfile fast-path
items.body:
## Description
The `writerWrapper` in `pkg/instrumentation/nethttp/server/response_writer.go` is substituted for the application's original `http.ResponseWriter` during `BeforeServeHTTP`. The wrapper previously lacked several standard Go HTTP server interface contracts, silently degrading application capabilities when HTTP server auto-instrumentation was active.

## Identified Defects
1. **Missing `Unwrap() http.ResponseWriter`**: Handlers using Go 1.20+ `http.ResponseController` (e.g. `rc.SetWriteDeadline()`, `rc.SetReadDeadline()`) received `http.ErrNotSupported` through the wrapper.
2. **Incorrect `http.Pusher` signature**: The wrapper defined a custom `Pusher() http.Pusher` method instead of implementing `Push(target string, opts *http.PushOptions) error`. Standard `w.(http.Pusher)` assertions evaluated to `false`, disabling HTTP/2 Server Push.
3. **Missing `io.ReaderFrom`**: `http.ServeFile` and `io.Copy` could not reach the underlying writer's `ReadFrom` method, losing the zero-copy `sendfile` fast path.
4. **Silent Flush Failures**: Lacked `FlushError() error`, causing `http.ResponseController.Flush()` to swallow underlying flush errors.

## Proposed Fix
- Added `Unwrap() http.ResponseWriter` to expose the underlying writer to `http.ResponseController`.
- Implemented standard `Push(string, *http.PushOptions) error`, `ReadFrom(io.Reader)`, and `FlushError() error` on `writerWrapper`.
- Standardized non-supported capability returns to the `http.ErrNotSupported` sentinel.
- Added compile-time interface assertions (`var _ http.Pusher = (*writerWrapper)(nil)`, etc.) to prevent regressions.

## Verification
- Added unit tests covering `ResponseController` deadline propagation, `ReadFrom` fast-path preservation, and `Push` interface satisfaction.
- Tested under `go test -race` in `pkg/instrumentation/nethttp/server`.
items.author: gyanranjanpanda

items.title: fix(instrumentation/net/http/server): support ResponseController, Pusher, ReaderFrom, and FlushError in writerWrapper
items.body:
Fixes #1084

## Problem
The `writerWrapper` substituted for `http.ResponseWriter` during `BeforeServeHTTP` lacked several standard Go HTTP server interface capabilities, leading to subtle behavioral bugs in instrumented HTTP servers:
1. **`io.ReaderFrom`**: `http.ServeFile` and `io.Copy` lost kernel-level `sendfile` zero-copy optimizations.
2. **`FlushError() error`**: `http.ResponseController.Flush()` swallowed underlying flush errors.
3. **`Hijack()` Sentinel Error**: `Hijack()` returned a generic formatted string error instead of `http.ErrNotSupported`.

## Solution
- Implemented `io.ReaderFrom` on `writerWrapper` to forward to the underlying writer when available, and fall back to copying into `w.ResponseWriter` to prevent recursive `ReadFrom` probing.
- Implemented `FlushError() error` for `http.ResponseController.Flush()` support.
- Standardized `Hijack()` non-support return to `http.ErrNotSupported`.
- Added compile-time interface assertions (`_ io.ReaderFrom`, `_ interface{ Unwrap() http.ResponseWriter }`).
- Expanded unit tests to verify `ReadFrom` fast-path retention, fallback, `FlushError`, and `Hijack` sentinel errors.

## Verification
- `go test -v -race ./...` in `instrumentation/net/http/server` passes completely.
- `make lint` clean (golangci-lint, yamlfmt, actionlint, checkmake, license headers).

items.title: feat(tool): package-level candidate schema for matched.json [1/6]
items.body:
## Parent

Part of #552 (Option B: move file-level rule matching to the toolexec phase).

This is step 1 of the breakdown posted on #552. Later steps (toolexec file match, stop writing source paths, cache/`isSetup`, internal setup) stay out of this issue.

## Problem

Setup today AST-matches rules against absolute source paths from `go build -a -x -n` and writes those paths into `matched.json` as `InstRuleSet` map keys (`addRule` requires `filepath.IsAbs`). Toolexec only compares compile `-p` to `ModulePath` and then applies the stored file keys.

That file-keyed artifact is what Option B wants to replace. We cannot move matching into toolexec until `matched.json` can describe **candidate rules per package** (target + version) without embedding user-source paths.

## Proposal

Define (and, if needed, dual-read) a `matched.json` shape that records:

- import path / module path
- resolved dependency version
- candidate rules for that package (not keyed by absolute user-source paths)
- hook `ResolvedPath` (setup still has module dirs; toolexec does not)
- CGO mapping only if we still need it for the current toolexec path

Keep current toolexec working: `load()` today assumes file-keyed maps. Either:

- keep writing the old shape and add the candidate fields alongside it, or
- version the artifact and teach `load()` to accept both

Do **not** change when AST matching runs in this PR. Setup should still produce a working instrumented build.

## Acceptance criteria

- Documented `matched.json` candidate fields (struct comments and/or a short note in `docs/configuration.md` / troubleshooting if that file is user-facing).
- Tests that marshal/unmarshal the new shape and that existing `load()` still instruments.
- No behavior change for `otelc go build` beyond extra/compatible fields.
- Absolute user-source paths may still be present until a later #552 step; this issue only **introduces** the package-level candidate schema.

## Out of scope

- Moving `runMatch` into toolexec
- Removing setup-time AST matching
- Changing `isSetup()` / coordinating with #1038
- Folding setup into `otelc go build`

## Related

- #552
- `tool/internal/rule/base.go` (`InstRuleSet`)
- `tool/internal/setup/store.go`
- `tool/internal/instrument/toolexec.go` (`load` / `match`)

items.title: feat(tool): extract shared file/AST rule matcher [2/6]
items.body:
## Parent

Part of #552 (Option B: move file-level rule matching to the toolexec phase).

Depends on the candidate-schema issue ([1/6]). This is a no-behavior-change extract so setup and toolexec can share the same matcher later.

## Problem

File-level matching lives in setup (`runMatch` in `tool/internal/setup/match.go`): `where` filters, func/struct/decl matching, test vs non-test (`isTestBuild`), call-rule fan-out, package name from sources.

Toolexec (`tool/internal/instrument/match.go`) only matches import path. If we copy `runMatch` into the instrument package later, the two copies will drift (CGO remap, `_test.go`, build tags).

## Proposal

Extract the file/AST matching used by `runMatch` into a package both setup and (later) toolexec can call, for example `tool/internal/rule` or a small `tool/internal/match` package.

The extracted API should take:

- a package import path
- a list of source files (absolute or compile-argv paths)
- candidate rules already filtered by target + version
- optional CGO map

and return an `InstRuleSet` keyed by those files (today’s shape).

Setup `matchDeps` should call this helper instead of inlining the walk. Toolexec should **not** call it yet.

## Acceptance criteria

- `runMatch` behavior is unchanged (existing `match_test.go` cases still pass: `where`, glob/`$root`, test builds, file rules with/without sources).
- Matcher has its own unit tests for the extracted helpers (not only through setup).
- No toolexec compile-path change in this PR.

- Matching compile argv in toolexec (step 3)

items.title: bug(instrumentation/openai): cached prompt tokens are never recorded
items.body:
The openai-go instrumentation never records cached prompt tokens, while the anthropic-sdk-go instrumentation does. Credit to @dobbydobap, who spotted this in the #709 discussion.

## The gap

OpenAI has automatic prompt caching and reports it on every chat/completion response as `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` (exposed by openai-go v1.12.0 as `CompletionUsagePromptTokensDetails.CachedTokens`). There are no cache references anywhere under `instrumentation/github.com/openai/`, and no cache key in any of the three OpenAI semconv packages, so that portion of prompt spend is invisible for OpenAI users but visible for Anthropic ones.

## It is also in the registry, not just the code

`schemas/otelc/groups/anthropic.yaml` declares `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens` with `id:` inside `registry.otelc.gen_ai.anthropic`, the provider-specific group, and the header comment states:

> The two prompt-cache attributes are Anthropic-specific and are declared locally with `id:` in the attribute group below.

Cache reads are not Anthropic-specific. Because the attribute is defined in a provider-scoped group, `openai.yaml` cannot declare it without referencing another provider's group, so the wrong assumption is encoded in the contract as well as in the middleware comment at `anthropic-sdk-go/middleware.go:264`.

`gen_ai.usage.cache_creation.input_tokens` is genuinely Anthropic-specific: OpenAI's cache is automatic with no separate cache-write step to report.

## The semantics differ, and that is the part worth getting right

The two providers count cached tokens differently:

- **Anthropic** excludes cache reads from `input_tokens`, so the instrumentation folds them back in (`middleware.go:248-251`) to report the full prompt per semconv.
- **OpenAI** already includes cached tokens in `prompt_tokens`.

So OpenAI must record the value as a breakdown only. Folding it in the way the Anthropic path does would double-count the cached portion of every cache-hit request.

## Suggested fix

1. Record `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens` from `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, only when greater than zero, matching the Anthropic instrumentation's conditional behaviour. Do not add it to `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`.
2. Move the `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens` declaration from `registry.otelc.gen_ai.anthropic` to the shared `registry.otelc.gen_ai` group, which is where `openai.yaml` already documents shared otelc-invented attributes as living. Leave `cache_creation` where it is.

Point 2 touches the group organisation that #728 lists as an open decision ("Registry files are per-library but attribute groups are per-domain"), so it is worth a maintainer opinion. Following the convention the two files already document seemed like the smallest step that does not pre-empt that decision.

Happy to send a PR.

items.title: fix(instrumentation/openai): record cached prompt tokens
items.body:
OpenAI has automatic prompt caching and reports it as `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, but the openai-go instrumentation never read that field, so cached prompt spend was invisible for OpenAI while the anthropic-sdk-go instrumentation has recorded it since #689. Credit to @dobbydobap, who spotted the asymmetry in the #709 discussion.

The two providers count cached tokens differently, and that difference is the reason this is not a copy of the Anthropic code. Anthropic excludes cache reads from `input_tokens`, so that instrumentation folds them back in to report the full prompt. OpenAI already includes them in `prompt_tokens`. So here the value is recorded as a breakdown of the input count and is never added to it, otherwise every cache-hit request would double-count the cached portion. There is a test pinning exactly that, since it is the easy thing to get wrong later.

Recorded only when greater than zero, so a request that did not hit the cache omits the attribute rather than reporting a zero, matching the Anthropic behaviour.

No `cache_creation` counterpart: OpenAI's cache is automatic and has no separate cache-write step to report.

On the registry side, `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens` was declared with `id:` inside `registry.otelc.gen_ai.anthropic`, the provider-specific group, with a header comment calling both prompt-cache attributes Anthropic-specific. Cache reads are not, and while the attribute lives in a provider-scoped group `openai.yaml` cannot declare it without referencing another provider's group. This moves that one declaration to the shared `registry.otelc.gen_ai` group, which is where both files already document shared otelc-invented attributes as living, and leaves `cache_creation` in the Anthropic group. `weaver registry check` passes.

That move touches group organisation that #728 lists as an open decision, so if you would rather resolve it there first I am happy to split the schema change out and land only the code fix.

Tested with unit tests covering a cache hit (asserting `input_tokens` is unchanged), a response with no `prompt_tokens_details`, and one with `cached_tokens: 0`. `make lint-schema`, `golangci-lint` and the module test suite all pass, and the bundle is regenerated.

Fixes #1089

items.title: Redis `db.query.text` includes AUTH/HELLO passwords
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Redis spans dump the raw command args into `db.query.text`, including the connection handshake.

If the client has `Password` set, first command triggers `HELLO … AUTH <password>` (or `AUTH` on fallback) through `ProcessHook`. I got:

```
db.query.text = "hello 3 auth default s3cret"
```

`getRedisV9Statement` just joins `cmd.Args()` with no masking.


### To Reproduce

1. Use a Redis client with a password:

```go
rdb := redis.NewClient(&redis.Options{
    Addr:     "localhost:6379",
    Password: "s3cret",
})
rdb.Ping(ctx)
```

2. Look at the client spans.
3. The `hello` (or `auth`) span has the password in `db.query.text`.

### Expected behavior

Keep the span, redact the secret. e.g. `HELLO 3 AUTH default s3cret` → `HELLO 3 AUTH ? ?`

items.title: fix(tool/internal/instrument): prevent nil pointer panic on bodyless functions in directive and raw rules
items.body:
### Describe the bug

In `applyDirectiveRule` (`tool/internal/instrument/apply_directive.go`) and `insertRaw` (`tool/internal/instrument/apply_raw.go`), statements are prepended to function bodies without checking whether the function has a body:

```go
funcDecl.Body.List = append(stmts, funcDecl.Body.List...)
```

In Go AST representations, external assembly routines and forward declarations (for example, `func asmRoutine()`) have `funcDecl.Body == nil`.

If a directive comment or a raw rule targets a bodyless function declaration, dereferencing `funcDecl.Body.List` causes a runtime nil pointer dereference (`SIGSEGV`), crashing the compiler during compilation.

### Expected behavior

A bodyless function should be detected and an informative error should be returned, for example:

```text
cannot apply directive ...: function ... has no body
```

The compiler should return the error instead of panicking.

### To Reproduce

1. Open `tool/internal/instrument/apply_directive.go` and look at `applyDirectiveRule`.
2. Add a directive to a bodyless assembly function or forward declaration, for example:

```go
//otelc:span
func asmFunc()
```

3. Run the compilation with:

```bash
otelc go build
```

4. The compiler panics with a runtime nil pointer dereference instead of returning a descriptive error.

### Environment

* Installation type: Any (source/dev build)
* otelc Version: Current `main`
* Relevant files:

  * `tool/internal/instrument/apply_directive.go`
  * `tool/internal/instrument/apply_raw.go`

### Are you able to fix this issue?

Yes. I will propose a PR.

### Additional Context

This does not appear to be a regression tied to a specific version. The current implementation assumes that function declarations always have non-nil bodies during AST transformations.

The fix is small: add `funcDecl.Body == nil` checks in both `applyDirectiveRule` and `insertRaw` and return a descriptive error when a bodyless function is targeted.

I have already implemented and verified the fix on the branch:

`fix/instrument-bodyless-func-nil-panic`

The fix also has 100% test coverage.

items.title: fix(net/http): end spans after instrumentation is disabled
items.body:
## Description

Fix the HTTP server instrumentation lifecycle so spans created before a
runtime instrumentation state change are always ended.

`AfterServeHTTP` previously re-checked the instrumentation enablement state before retrieving the span stored by `BeforeServeHTTP`. If instrumentation was disabled after the span was created but before the request completed, the after-hook returned early and skipped `span.End()`.

This change removes that redundant enablement check and relies on the presence of the span in the hook context to determine whether there is a span to end.

A regression test covers the enabled to disabled transition.

## Motivation

Instrumentation enablement can be evaluated dynamically between the
`BeforeServeHTTP` and `AfterServeHTTP` hooks.

Previously, this sequence could occur:

1. Instrumentation is enabled and `BeforeServeHTTP` creates a span.
2. The instrumentation is disabled while the request is in flight.
3. `AfterServeHTTP` observes the disabled state and returns early.
4. The span created by `BeforeServeHTTP` is never ended.

The regression test reproduces this behavior against the previous
implementation and verifies that the span is ended after the fix.

The existing test expectation was also updated to reflect the corrected
span lifecycle when a span is already present in the hook context.

## Testing

- `go test ./instrumentation/net/http/server/...`
- `go test ./...`

items.title: fix(tool/internal/instrument): strip build-ignore tag per line, not by substring
items.body:
## Description

`stripBuildIgnoreTag` strips the `//go:build ignore` constraint from a file rule's source
before it gets spliced into the target package, using a whole-file substring replace:

```go
func stripBuildIgnoreTag(content string) string {
	return strings.ReplaceAll(content, "//go:build ignore", "")
}
```

`strings.ReplaceAll` has no notion of Go syntax, so it deletes that text from anywhere in
the file — a string literal, a doc comment describing the convention, anywhere the text
happens to appear — not just the leading build-constraint line. The corruption is silent:
the result still parses as valid Go, so nothing fails to compile.

The fix uses the standard library's `go/build/constraint.IsGoBuild`, applied per line
instead of as a whole-file substring match:

```go
func stripBuildIgnoreTag(content string) string {
	lines := strings.Split(content, "\n")
	for i, line := range lines {
		if constraint.IsGoBuild(line) {
			lines[i] = ""
		}
	}
	return strings.Join(lines, "\n")
}
```

A line only gets blanked if it *is* a build-constraint line (matching the same syntax the
Go toolchain itself recognizes), not merely if it contains that text somewhere within a
larger line.

### Known limitation — not fixed, flagging for visibility

This checks every line in the file, not just the leading comment block before `package`
that real Go build-constraint semantics restrict `//go:build` to. So a standalone line that
trims to exactly `//go:build ignore` — with nothing else on that physical line — occurring
later in the file (e.g. as one line inside a multi-line raw string literal) would still be
incorrectly blanked, since this is a textual line scan, not an AST-aware one that tracks
whether a line falls inside a string or comment token.

I considered restricting the scan to the leading block, which is what I originally proposed
in #1069 and what would close this gap entirely. I didn't do that here because it changes
existing, unrelated test behavior: `TestStripBuildIgnoreTag`'s `multiple go:build ignore
comments` case has a second `//go:build ignore` line positioned *after* `package main`, and
restricting to the leading block would stop that second occurrence from being stripped —
a real behavior change beyond what this issue reported, not something I wanted to decide
unilaterally. Happy to make that change too if you'd rather have it closed now.

### Tests

Added a case to the existing `TestStripBuildIgnoreTag` table: a source with the tag text
inside both a comment and a string literal, asserting both survive. I verified the test
actually catches the regression it's meant to catch — reverting the fix to the old
`strings.ReplaceAll` implementation makes it fail with the exact corruption described in
the issue (`marker` becomes `""`, the comment gets a hole in it). All four pre-existing
cases pass unchanged, byte-for-byte, including the mid-file second occurrence in
`multiple go:build ignore comments`.

## Motivation

Fixes #1069

## Verification

`make format` and `go test -shuffle=on -timeout=15m -count=1 ./tool/...` pass locally. The
integration and e2e halves of `make test` were verified through this PR's CI jobs rather
than locally, since the testcontainers-based suites had no usable Docker host here.

`make lint` was checked with golangci-lint **v2.11.3**, the version
`.github/workflows/lint-golang.yaml` pins — 0 issues. As noted on prior PRs in this
series: `.tools/go.mod` pins a newer local linter version, and pristine `main` already
reports pre-existing findings under it in files this PR does not touch.

items.title: bug(setup): findModVersion cannot parse +incompatible versions in module cache paths
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Version-gated instrumentation rules are silently skipped when a dependency is resolved from the Go module cache with a `+incompatible` version suffix.

`findModVersion` in `tool/internal/setup/find.go` derives a dependency's version by regex-parsing the compile source path for a module cache segment (`...@vX.Y.Z/...`):

```go
var versionRegexp = regexp.MustCompile(`@v\d+\.\d+\.\d+(-.*?)?/`)

func findModVersion(path string) string {
    version := versionRegexp.FindString(filepath.ToSlash(path))
    if version == "" {
        return ""
    }
    return version[1 : len(version)-1]
}
```

For legacy pre-module repositories (v2+ tagged without a `go.mod`), the Go module cache stores the `+incompatible` suffix in the path directory name. Because `versionRegexp` only matches hyphenated suffixes (`-`), `findModVersion` fails:

| Source Path | `findModVersion()` Result | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `/go/pkg/mod/github.com/foo/bar@v1.2.3/pkg/foo.go` | `v1.2.3` | `v1.2.3` |
| `/go/pkg/mod/github.com/foo/bar@v1.2.3-rc.1/pkg/foo.go` | `v1.2.3-rc.1` | `v1.2.3-rc.1` |
| `/go/pkg/mod/github.com/foo/bar@v1.2.3+incompatible/pkg/foo.go` | `""` | `v1.2.3+incompatible` |
| `/go/pkg/mod/github.com/foo/bar@v0.0.0-20210101120000-abcdef/pkg/foo.go` | `v0.0.0-20210101120000-abcdef` | `v0.0.0-20210101120000-abcdef` |

An empty `Dependency.Version` causes `VersionInRange("", range)` to evaluate to `false`, causing the rule to be dropped during both the setup phase (`tool/internal/setup/match.go`) and the pin phase (`tool/internal/setup/pin.go`).

### Environment

 - OS: Linux / macOS / Windows
 - Go Version: 1.23+
 - Version: `main` branch

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Target a dependency resolved from the Go module cache with a `+incompatible` tag (e.g. `...@v1.2.3+incompatible/...`).
2. Define a version-gated instrumentation rule targeting this dependency.
3. Run setup / pin with `otelc`.
4. See error/warning: The rule does not match because the dependency version is extracted as `""`, emitting a warning that the version is unresolved even though it is present in the path.

### Expected behavior

`findModVersion` should extract `v1.2.3+incompatible` from `/go/pkg/mod/github.com/foo/bar@v1.2.3+incompatible/pkg/foo.go` so version-gated rules function properly for `+incompatible` dependencies.

### Additional context

Fixing `versionRegexp` to accept `[-+]` (e.g. `@v\d+\.\d+\.\d+([-+][^/]*)?/`) covers both `+incompatible` and build metadata (`+build`) alongside existing pre-release tags (`-rc.1`).

<sub>**Tip**: [React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

items.title: fix(redis): instrument ring shards created before the hook runs
items.body:
## Description

`NewRing` builds a shard for every entry in `RingOptions.Addrs` during construction. `afterNewRingClientV9` runs after that and calls `OnNewNode`, which only invokes its callback for shards created after it is registered. The hook therefore never reached any shard the caller configured up front.

The fix keeps the `OnNewNode` registration, which still matters for shards added later through `SetAddrs`, and adds a pass over the shards that already exist.

`client_hook.go` had no coverage on any of its six hook functions, so this also adds tests for all of them. Each builds a client against a port nothing listens on and asserts the command produced a client span carrying the expected endpoint. The hook opens its span before handing off to the next hook in the chain, so a failed dial still exercises the full path and the tests need no Redis server.

`TestAfterNewRingClientV9_AttachesHookToEachNode` fails on main and passes with the change, so it pins the behaviour rather than describing it. Package coverage goes from 89.2% to 96.9%.

## Motivation

Configuring shards up front is how a ring is normally set up, so in practice Redis Ring clients were producing no telemetry at all. The failure is silent: no error, no warning, just an absence of spans. Nothing tested those six functions, which is why it went unnoticed.

## Compatibility / behavioral change

This changes the telemetry contract for existing `redis.Ring` users, so it is worth calling out in the release notes:

- **Pre-configured ring shards are now instrumented.** Shards configured up front via `RingOptions.Addrs` (the common case) produced zero spans before this change and now emit per-command client spans. To a telemetry pipeline this can look like a traffic spike: new time series, higher storage cost, and potentially false alerts on first rollout.
- **Manual workarounds now double-count.** Anyone who worked around the bug by attaching `otelRedisHook` to ring shards themselves (their own `ForEachShard` + `AddHook`) will get two hook entries in the chain and two identical spans per command. Those workarounds should be removed once this ships.

The code fix itself is unaffected by the above; these are operational notes for upgraders.

items.body:
## Description

Redis spans were putting the connection password into `db.query.text`.

`getRedisV9Statement` joins every command argument, and go-redis sends the handshake before any of your own commands run, so with `Options.Password` set you get:

```
db.query.text = "hello 3 auth default s3cret"
```

This redacts the credential arguments to `?` and keeps the span, so the handshake is still visible and timed:

```
hello 3 auth default s3cret   ->   hello 3 auth ? ?
```

It covers `AUTH password`, the ACL form `AUTH username password`, and the optional `AUTH` section inside `HELLO`. The AUTH section of `HELLO` is optional and comes after the protocol version, so I look for the `auth` token rather than assuming an index. A trailing `SETNAME clientname` stays visible since only the two arguments after `auth` are hidden, and only `args[0]` is matched so a key that happens to be named `auth` is untouched.

## Motivation

It affects any app that sets a Redis password, not only ones that call `AUTH` themselves, and the value gets exported to whatever tracing backend is configured.

Out of scope here: `CONFIG SET requirepass` also carries a secret. Happy to do that separately if you want it.

Fixes #1091

items.title: fix(tool/internal/instrument): prevent nil pointer panic on bodyless functions in directive and raw rules
items.body:
## Description

Fixes #1093

In `applyDirectiveRule` (`tool/internal/instrument/apply_directive.go`) and `insertRaw` (`tool/internal/instrument/apply_raw.go`), statements are prepended to function bodies without checking whether the function declaration has a body (`funcDecl.Body == nil`).

In Go AST representations (`go/ast` and `dst`), assembly stubs and forward declarations have `funcDecl.Body == nil`. Directly accessing `funcDecl.Body.List` caused an unhandled runtime nil pointer dereference panic at compile time.

### Changes
1. Added `if funcDecl.Body == nil` check in `applyDirectiveRule` returning an informative error (`cannot apply directive %q: function %s has no body`).
2. Added `if decl.Body == nil` check in `insertRaw` returning `cannot instrument bodyless function %s`.
3. Added unit tests in `tool/internal/instrument/apply_directive_test.go` covering bodyless functions, valid directive application, invalid template syntax, and syntax error handling.
4. Added `TestInsertRawBodylessFunction` in `tool/internal/instrument/apply_raw_test.go`.

### Verification
- `golangci-lint`: **0 issues**
- Statement coverage on `apply_directive.go`: **95.2%**
- All unit and integration test suites pass cleanly.

items.title: fix(grpc): ensure span.End() is invoked for non-recording / non-sampled spans
items.body:
## Description

In both gRPC server (`server_hook.go`) and client (`client_hook.go`) stats handlers, `span.End()` was placed inside the `if span.IsRecording()` condition in the `*stats.End` event handler. For non-recording or non-sampled spans, `span.IsRecording()` returns `false`, causing `span.End()` to be skipped.

This PR moves `span.End()` outside of the `if span.IsRecording()` condition so that all spans properly end regardless of sampling state, adhering to OpenTelemetry span lifecycle semantics. Unit tests have been added to verify that `span.End()` is invoked for non-recording spans.

Fixes #1104

items.title: chore(test): add multi-process e2e for HTTP→OpenAI GenAI client propagation
items.body:
## Summary

Per [docs/testing.md](docs/testing.md), E2E tests spin up **multiple instrumented processes** and assert they form one coherent trace (shared trace ID).

OpenAI GenAI client instrumentation is covered by **integration** tests only today:

- Apps: `test/apps/openaiclient`, `test/apps/openaiclientv2`
- File: `test/integration/openai_client_test.go`
- The app is a single process calling a mock OpenAI HTTP server
- Asserts `gen_ai.*` on the GenAI client span (via `RequireGenAIClientSemconv`)

That does **not** verify that a GenAI client span stays correctly parented under an upstream instrumented HTTP server when the request arrives from a separate instrumented HTTP client (cross-process propagation into an HTTP→OpenAI chain).

There is also **no** combined HTTP server + OpenAI client app under `test/apps/` (unlike `httpserverdbclient` / `httpserverkafkaclient`).

Existing E2E coverage:

| E2E Test | File |
|---|---|
| HTTP client + server | `http_test.go` |
| gRPC client + server | `grpc_test.go` |
| Kafka producer + consumer | `kafka_test.go` |
| HTTP → SQL (multi-process) | `httpserver_dbclient_test.go` |
| gRPC → SQL (multi-process) | `grpcserver_dbclient_test.go` |
| HTTP → Kafka (multi-process) | `httpserver_kafkaclient_test.go` |
| gRPC → Kafka (multi-process) | `grpcserver_kafkaclient_test.go` (in progress) |

No GenAI / OpenAI e2e coverage yet.

## Proposed work

Add a combo app + e2e test, mirroring `test/e2e/httpserver_dbclient_test.go`:

1. Add `test/apps/httpserveropenaiclient` — HTTP server that handles `/hello` and issues one OpenAI chat completion (same SDK pattern as `openaiclient`), with flags for front port + OpenAI base URL / API key / model
2. Reuse the mock OpenAI server pattern from `test/integration/openai_client_test.go`
3. `BuildAndStart("httpserveropenaiclient", "-front-port=<port>", "-addr=<mock>/v1", ...)` using `FreePort` + `WaitForTCP`
4. `BuildAndRun("httpclient", "-addr", "http://127.0.0.1:<port>", "-name", "...")`
5. Wait for spans with `f.WaitForSpans(3)` (same reason as other multi-process e2e: client exits before server/GenAI spans fully flush)
6. Assert **one** distributed trace with **3** spans:
   - instrumented HTTP **client**
   - HTTP **server** (frontend)
   - GenAI **client** (`gen_ai.*` / OpenAI chat) — not a duplicate `http.client` span (OpenAI instrumentation suppresses HTTP client instrumentation)
7. Assert shared trace ID and parent/child links across the chain
8. Keep assertions focused on propagation; pin a successful HTTP outcome (`http.response.status_code=200`) and a basic GenAI identity check (e.g. `gen_ai.provider.name` / `gen_ai.operation.name`) so a failed or mis-wired request cannot silently pass. Full `gen_ai.*` semconv detail stays in the existing integration test.

### Files
- Add: `test/apps/httpserveropenaiclient/` (new combo app)
- Add: `test/e2e/httpserver_openaiclient_test.go`
- Reuse: `test/apps/httpclient`, mock OpenAI helper pattern from `test/integration/openai_client_test.go`

### No new instrumentation needed
HTTP client, HTTP server, and OpenAI (`openai-go`) GenAI instrumentation already exist.

### Out of scope
- Anthropic twin e2e (can be a follow-up)
- Shared GenAI adapter work / new providers (orthogonal)

- [ ] Multi-process E2E: instrumented `httpclient` → `httpserveropenaiclient` (+ mock OpenAI)
- [ ] `RequireTraceCount(1)` and 3 spans (HTTP client, HTTP server, GenAI client)
- [ ] Assert shared trace ID + parent/child relationships
- [ ] Use `FreePort`, `WaitForTCP`, and `f.WaitForSpans(3)`
- [ ] `make test-e2e` / `make all` passes

items.title: bug(instrumentation/database/sql): sql.OpenDB is uninstrumented, causing missing telemetry attributes on connector-based DB connections
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Applications using Go's `database/sql` with connector-based initialization (such as `sql.OpenDB(c driver.Connector)`) do not have telemetry metadata (`db.Endpoint`, `db.DriverName`, `db.DSN`, `db.DbName`) populated on the returned `*sql.DB` instance.

Currently, `instrumentation/database/sql/otelc.yaml` only hooks `sql.Open(driverName, dataSourceName)`. When an application initializes database connections using `sql.OpenDB` (common in `pgx`, `go-sql-driver/mysql` `NewConnector`, `sqlite3`, and custom connection poolers):
1. `sql.OpenDB` executes without triggering any `afterOpen` hook.
2. `db.Endpoint`, `db.DriverName`, `db.DSN`, and `db.DbName` remain empty on `*sql.DB`.
3. All subsequent queries (`QueryContext`, `ExecContext`, `PingContext`, `BeginTx`) emit spans where `server.address` is set to `"unknown"` and `db.system.name` / `db.namespace` are incomplete or omitted.

### Environment

 - OS: Linux / All
 - Go Version: 1.25 / 1.26
 - Version: v0.0.0 (main branch)

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create a `driver.Connector` (e.g. `connector, err := mysql.NewConnector(cfg)` or `stdlib.GetConnector(cfg)`).
2. Open a database handle using `db := sql.OpenDB(connector)`.
3. Execute a query with `db.QueryContext(ctx, "SELECT 1")`.
4. Observe emitted span: `server.address` is `"unknown"`, and `db.DriverName` / `db.Endpoint` attributes are missing on the span.

### Expected behavior

`sql.OpenDB` should be instrumented symmetrically with `sql.Open`. The connector metadata (or connector type/driver info) should be extracted so `*sql.DB` receives `Endpoint`, `DriverName`, and `DbName` fields, resulting in complete database span attributes.

### Additional context

**Root Cause**:
- `instrumentation/database/sql/otelc.yaml` lacks a `hook_opendb` rule targeting `func: OpenDB`.
- `client.go` only contains `beforeOpenInstrumentation` / `afterOpenInstrumentation` for `sql.Open`.

**Proposed High-Level Fix**:
1. Add `hook_opendb` rule to `instrumentation/database/sql/otelc.yaml` targeting `sql.OpenDB`.
2. Add `beforeOpenDBInstrumentation` and `afterOpenDBInstrumentation` in `client.go` to inspect the `driver.Connector` (e.g. via `c.Driver()` or DSN interface inspection).
3. Add unit test coverage in `client_test.go` and integration test coverage in `test/integration/db_client_test.go`.

<sub>**Tip**: [React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

items.title: feat(instrumentation/database/sql): instrument sql.OpenDB connector-based initialization
items.body:
## Description

Add compile-time instrumentation for `sql.OpenDB(c driver.Connector)`, the connector-based initialization entry point in Go's standard library `database/sql`.

- **`otelc.yaml`**: Add `hook_opendb` rule targeting `func: OpenDB` in package `database/sql`.
- **`client.go`**: Add `beforeOpenDBInstrumentation` and `afterOpenDBInstrumentation` hooks to extract driver type information from `c.Driver()` and DSN metadata (via `DSN()` or `DataSourceName()` interfaces when provided by custom connectors).
- **`otelc-bundle.tgz`**: Updated with the regenerated instrumentation binary.

## Motivation

Many modern Go database drivers and connection pools (such as `pgx/v5/stdlib`, `go-sql-driver/mysql` `NewConnector`, `sqlite3.NewConnector`) initialize database connections using `sql.OpenDB` rather than `sql.Open`. Before this change, `sql.OpenDB` was uninstrumented, meaning `db.Endpoint`, `db.DriverName`, `db.DSN`, and `db.DbName` were never populated on `*sql.DB`. Consequently, all subsequent query/exec/ping spans emitted `server.address: "unknown"` and missed driver metadata.

Fixes #1108

items.title: test(instrument): cover trampoline jump point discovery
items.body:
## Description

Adds tests for `findJumpPoint`, which decides where a new trampoline jump gets spliced when several func rules apply to the same function. It had no tests and sat at 57.1%, with both interesting branches unreached: the recursive descent into an existing chain, and the nil return for an `if` that is not a trampoline jump.

Five cases:

- an unlabelled `if` yields no insertion point
- a lone jump yields its own else block
- a two-jump chain yields the inner block, not the outer one
- a three-jump chain descends the whole way rather than stopping one level in
- a chain whose tail is unlabelled yields nothing rather than guessing

`findJumpPoint` goes from 57.1% to 100%, and the package from 92.7% to 93.0%.

## Motivation

The nil case matters more than the percentage suggests. `insertToFunc` hands `findJumpPoint` the first statement of a function body, which is frequently an ordinary `if` belonging to the author. Returning a block there would splice a trampoline into unrelated user code, so the label check is load-bearing rather than an optimisation, and nothing was pinning it.

The fixtures are built the way `buildTJump` and `insertToFunc` build them, so the recursion is exercised the way it happens during a real build rather than through a structure invented for the test.

items.title: fix(instrumentation/database/sql): join Tx.Commit and Tx.Rollback spans to caller trace
items.body:
## Description
`(*sql.Tx).Commit` and `(*sql.Tx).Rollback` spans were starting a separate trace because `Commit` and `Rollback` do not take a `context.Context` parameter, causing instrumentation hooks to fall back to `context.Background()`.

This PR fixes the issue by:
1. **Tool AST Parser Fix**: Fixed `AddStructField` in `tool/internal/ast` to properly parse qualified package types (like `context.Context`) into valid AST selector expressions instead of invalid identifier strings.
2. **Tx Field Injection**: Updated `add_new_field_tx` rule in `database/sql/otelc.yaml` to inject `Ctx context.Context` into `sql.Tx` and import `context`.
3. **Context Propagation**: Updated `database/sql/client.go` to record the transaction's caller context on `tx.Ctx` during `BeginTx`, and use `tx.Ctx` when creating `Commit` and `Rollback` spans.
4. **Integration Test**: Added `TransactionCommit` subtest in `test/integration/httpserver_dbclient_test.go` asserting that `START`, `INSERT`, and `COMMIT` spans share the caller's HTTP request trace.

Fixes #1064.

items.title: bug(pkg/runtime): instrumentation identifiers use two naming schemes, so some disable settings silently do nothing
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Instrumentation identifiers follow two different naming schemes, and two of the resulting mismatches are user visible. Setting `OTEL_GO_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS` to the obvious name either does nothing, or disables only half of what the user meant, with nothing logged either way.

Running `runtime.Instrumented` directly against the keys currently declared in the tree:

```
DISABLED="redis"        Instrumented("REDIS")        = false
DISABLED="REDIS"        Instrumented("REDIS")        = false

DISABLED="logrus"       Instrumented("logs/logrus")  = true     <- ignored
DISABLED="LOGRUS"       Instrumented("logs/logrus")  = true     <- ignored
DISABLED="logs/logrus"  Instrumented("logs/logrus")  = false

DISABLED="mongodb"      Instrumented("MONGODB")      = false
DISABLED="mongodb"      Instrumented("MONGODB_V2")   = true     <- half disabled

DISABLED="openai"       Instrumented("OPENAI")       = false    <- covers v1, v2 and v3
```

### Expected behavior

A user who disables an instrumentation by its obvious name gets it disabled, or is told the name was not recognised.

### The two schemes in use

Most instrumentations use a flat uppercase key:

`DATABASE`, `NETHTTP`, `GRPC`, `MONGODB`, `MONGODB_V2`, `K8S_CLIENT_GO`, `ANTHROPIC`, `GIN`, `REDIS`, `LINODEGO`, `KAFKA`, `AWS_SDK_V2`, `OPENAI`

The three logging ones use a slash namespaced lowercase key:

`logs/log`, `logs/slog`, `logs/logrus`

Versioning is inconsistent too. `MONGODB` and `MONGODB_V2` are separate keys, so disabling mongo requires knowing there are two, while `OPENAI` is shared across the v1, v2 and v3 modules and `LINODEGO` covers a v2 module without saying so. `AWS_SDK_V2` carries its version, `LINODEGO` does not.

The doc comment on `Instrumented` says the name "should be lowercase (e.g. `nethttp`, `grpc`)", which matches neither scheme as declared.

### Why it is worth settling now

Two of these are already bugs rather than untidiness. `logrus` is a silent no-op, which is the same complaint as #839 where the setting was ignored with nothing logged. `mongodb` leaving the v2 driver instrumented is worse, because it looks like it worked.

Beyond that, #705 proposes mapping declarative configuration onto per-instrumentation settings. That needs a stable identifier per instrumentation to key on, and a slash inside a key is awkward in a nested YAML node. Whatever shape that work takes, it inherits whatever these keys are, so it seems better to agree the convention before it becomes an API surface rather than after.

### Possible directions

No strong opinion on which, and this is a maintainer call:

- pick one scheme and migrate the outliers, keeping the old spelling accepted as an alias for a release
- decide whether a key identifies a library or a library major version, and apply it consistently to mongo, openai, aws and linodego
- log once at startup when a name in `OTEL_GO_ENABLED/DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS` matches nothing, which would have surfaced the logrus case immediately regardless of the naming decision

Happy to do the work on any of these if it is useful, including the unmatched name warning on its own, since that one is small and independent of the naming decision.

### Steps to reproduce

Call `runtime.Instrumented` with the keys above while setting `OTEL_GO_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS`, or set `OTEL_GO_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS=logrus` on a build using the logrus instrumentation and observe that hooks still run.

items.title: Trampoline generation drops type constraints for generic method receivers
items.body:
When generating trampoline functions for methods with generic receivers (e.g. `func (s Set[T comparable]) Add(v T)`), the extracted type parameter's constraint is currently discarded and replaced with `any`.

## Where this happens

`extractReceiverTypeParams` in `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go:747-780` parses the receiver expression (`*dst.IndexExpr` for a single type param, `*dst.IndexListExpr` for multiple) and carries over only the type parameter name. Both branches hardcode the constraint field to `Type: ast.Ident("any")` (lines 760, 771). This widened signature is then used directly to build the trampoline's type parameters via `findTargetGenericType` (trampoline.go:480-504, 511, 516).

This is deliberate today, not accidental — `TestExtractReceiverTypeParamsConstraint` in `trampoline_receiver_test.go` (added in #1099) explicitly asserts the widened "any" behavior. But it isn't documented as a known limitation anywhere outside that test, and there's no tracking issue for fixing it.

## Why it matters

If a generated trampoline body ever needs to invoke an operation on the receiver's type parameter that depends on the original constraint (e.g. calling `<` on a value expected to satisfy `comparable`/`Ordered`), widening to `any` produces invalid generated Go code — it won't compile.

## Proposed fix

- Locate the original generic type declaration (e.g. `type Set[T comparable] struct{...}`) corresponding to the receiver and recover its constraint, rather than defaulting to `any`.
- Handle named and package-qualified constraints (e.g. `constraints.Ordered`), including resolving and adding any necessary imports to the generated file.
- Add test coverage for constrained receivers (built-in constraints like `comparable`, plus a custom/package-qualified interface constraint) to `trampoline_receiver_test.go`, alongside the existing unconstrained cases.

Note: no existing `go/types`-based mechanism in `tool/` resolves constraints from a type declaration today (`grep -rn "go/types" tool/` and `grep -rn "comparable" tool/` both come up empty), so this needs new logic rather than reuse of something existing.
items.author: om7057

items.title: fix(tool/instrument): recover generic receiver constraints in trampoline generation
items.body:
## Description

`extractReceiverTypeParams` in `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go` widened every extracted receiver type parameter's constraint to `any`, discarding the original constraint declared on the type (e.g. `type Set[T comparable] struct{...}`). If a generated trampoline body ever needed to operate on the parameter under its real constraint, the widened signature would produce generated Go that doesn't compile.

## Changes

- `findGenericTypeDecl` locates the receiver's own generic type declaration in the target file, if present.
- `receiverConstraintAt` recovers the constraint at a given position from that declaration, walking fields positionally so a multi-name field (e.g. `[T, U comparable]`) resolves correctly, and falls back to `any` when no matching declaration is found.
- Type parameters are matched **positionally**, not by name, since a method receiver is free to rename them relative to the declaration (`type Set[T comparable] struct{}` but `func (s Set[U]) Add(v U)` is valid Go; `U` is still constrained by `comparable`).
- `extractReceiverTypeParams` and `findTargetGenericType` now take the source `*dst.File` so the lookup has somewhere to search; all 4 call sites in `trampoline.go` are within `*InstrumentPhase` methods, so `ip.target` was already available at each.
- Package-qualified constraints (e.g. `constraints.Ordered`) resolve for free: since the lookup only searches the receiver's own file, any import the constraint needs is already present there (the file wouldn't compile otherwise), so no new import-resolution logic was needed for that case.

## Known limitation

If the receiver's generic type is declared in a *different* file of the same package, this doesn't resolve it and still falls back to `any` (same as before this change). Solving that would need a whole-package view (e.g. `go/types`/`go/packages`), which nothing in `tool/` currently has (see the linked issue). Left as a follow-up rather than pulled into this PR's scope.

## Testing

- `trampoline_receiver_test.go`: added `TestExtractReceiverTypeParamsConstraint_Recovered` (built-in constraint, renamed type parameter, package-qualified constraint) and `TestExtractReceiverTypeParamsConstraint_MultipleParams` (mixed constraints across multiple type parameters). Renamed the old `TestExtractReceiverTypeParamsConstraint` to `TestExtractReceiverTypeParamsConstraint_NoMatchingDecl` since it now documents the fallback path specifically, not universal behavior.
- `go test ./tool/internal/instrument/...` passes.
- `gofmt`, `golangci-lint run` clean on both changed files.

Fixes #1121

```go
// .tools/bundle/main.go
func shouldExclude(name string) bool {

}
```

So any untracked junk sitting under `pkg/` or `instrumentation/` is archived, including files listed in `.gitignore`. `.DS_Store` is the one that bites, because macOS Finder creates it as soon as a directory is browsed, and `.gitignore` line 11 already hides it from every diff and every `git status`.

The result on a macOS machine is a bundle containing an entry that CI, running on Linux, will never produce. Verify Bundle then fails permanently, and the advice it prints does not help:

```
Binary files a/tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz and b/tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz differ
archive verification failed.
To fix: rebase your branch on main, run "make package", and commit the updated archive.
```

Rebasing does nothing, and re-running `make package` re-adds the file every time, because it is still on disk. Nothing in git, the diff, or the job output points at the cause.

### Steps to reproduce

On clean `main`:

```
make package && tar tzf tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz | wc -l      # 298
touch instrumentation/github.com/redis/go-redis/v9/.DS_Store
make package && tar tzf tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz | wc -l      # 299
tar tzf tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz | grep DS_Store              # instrumentation/.../.DS_Store
```

### Seen in the wild

#1074 is currently stuck on exactly this. Its committed archive carries `instrumentation_temp/.DS_Store`, 299 entries against 298 from a fresh build, and the author has pushed twice trying to clear it.

It may also explain #737 and the archive discussions around #585, where the suspicion was that some bundles had been "generated wrongly" without a cause being identified.

### Expected behavior

The archive should depend only on tracked source, so that the same commit produces the same bundle on any machine.

### Suggested fix

Widening `shouldExclude` to cover `.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db` and similar would fix the immediate case. Excluding anything git ignores, or packaging from the git index rather than the filesystem, would close the class rather than the instance, since the next stray file will behave the same way.

Happy to send a patch if that is useful, though I appreciate the review queue is long at the moment, so equally happy for someone else to pick it up.

items.title: otelc generates uncompilable trampolines for constrained generic receivers
items.body:
## Description

`otelc` can generate uncompilable Go code when instrumenting a method whose
receiver is a generic type with a constraint narrower than `any`.

### Reproduction

Given this valid Go source:

```go
type Set[T comparable] struct{}

func (s *Set[T]) Add(v T) {}

nd an inject_hooks rule matching Add:

AddHook:
  target: main
  where:
    func: Add
    recv: "*Set[T]"
  do:
    - inject_hooks:
        before: HBefore
        path: main

the current instrumentation generates a trampoline whose receiver type
parameter is widened to any, equivalent to:

func AddHook[T any](s *Set[T], v T) {
    // ...
}

The generated code then fails to compile with:

T does not satisfy comparable

This was reproduced using the actual otelc instrumentation pipeline.

Why this happens

extractReceiverTypeParams reconstructs receiver type parameters from the
receiver expression:

*Set[T]

The receiver expression contains the type argument T, but not the constraint
declared on Set.

The current implementation therefore creates the receiver type parameter with
any, while the original constraint is declared separately on the generic
type.

Existing design context

I understand that widening receiver type parameters to any is intentional
and is covered by #1099.

The issue is the interaction between that behavior and constrained generic
receivers. Widening is valid for an unconstrained type such as:

type Set[T any] struct{}

but can produce invalid generated Go when the underlying type requires T to
satisfy a narrower constraint.

Expected behavior

Instrumentation of valid Go code should not result in generated code that
fails type checking.

For a constrained receiver such as:

type Set[T comparable] struct{}

the generated trampoline should remain type-correct.

Question

Are constrained generic receivers expected to be supported?

If so, what is the intended behavior for preserving type correctness while
retaining the receiver parameter widening behavior established by #1099?

items.title: bug(tool/internal/instrument): generic composite parameters produce non-assignable hook arguments
items.body:
## Description

When instrumenting a generic function with a composite parameter such as `[]T`, `otelc` can generate a hook declaration whose parameter type is incompatible with the value passed by the generated trampoline.

For example:

```go
func F[T any](v []T) {}

func main() {}
```

The generated trampoline still receives `[]T`, while the generated hook declaration uses `[]interface{}`.

### Reproduction

With an `inject_hooks` rule targeting `F`, the generated code is effectively:

```go
func FHook_trampoline[T any](param0 *[]T) {
    HBefore(*param0)
}

func HBefore(hookContext HookContext, param0 []interface{}) {
}
```

This fails to compile with:

```text
cannot use *param0 (variable of type []T) as []interface{} value in argument to HBefore
```

The issue comes from `replaceTypeParamsWithAny` in `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go`, which currently rewrites composite types containing type parameters. For example:

```text
[]T -> []interface{}
```

The existing unit test also expects this transformation.

### Expected behavior

The generated hook declaration should remain type compatible with the value passed by the generated trampoline, so that valid generic source code does not result in uncompilable generated code.

This also applies to other composite types containing type parameters, such as pointers, maps, channels, and function types.

This is separate from the constrained generic receiver issue in #1121.
items.author: SSOHEB

items.title: fix(tool): preserve assignability for generic parameters
items.body:
## Description

Fixes an issue where generic function parameters containing type parameters inside composite types, such as `[]T`, can result in incompatible generated hook signatures.

The generated trampoline may continue to pass `[]T` while the generated hook declaration expects `[]interface{}`, causing the generated code to fail compilation.

This change detects type parameters within composite type expressions and widens the complete parameter to `interface{}` at the generated hook boundary. It also adjusts variadic handling for generic parameters.

## Motivation

Generic composite parameter types must remain assignable across the generated trampoline and hook boundary. Replacing only the inner type parameter is not sufficient because Go does not treat composite types such as `[]T` and `[]interface{}` as assignable.

This change ensures the generated hook signature remains compatible with the value passed by the trampoline.

Fixes #1126

items.title: bug(tool/internal/instrument): checkHookDecl permits incompatible parameter types due to over-stripping in baseTypeName
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`checkHookDecl` in `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go` is responsible for verifying that hook functions defined in instrumentation packages have matching parameter and return types against the target function before generating trampolines.

However, `baseTypeName` (the helper used by `checkHookDecl` to normalize types) overly strips composite type information and defaults unhandled types to empty strings:
1. `*dst.ArrayType` and `*dst.Ellipsis` recursively resolve to `baseTypeName(t.Elt)`. As a result, a scalar type (e.g. `string`) produces `"string"`, which falsely matches a slice `[]string`, `[][]string`, or variadic `...string`.
2. `*dst.MapType`, `*dst.ChanType`, `*dst.StructType`, and `*dst.FuncType` hit the `default:` branch and return `""`. In `checkHookDecl`, comparing `trampBase` and `hookBase` results in `"" == ""` evaluating to `true`. This causes any map to falsely match any channel, struct, or func type (e.g. `map[string]int` falsely matches `chan bool`).

When a mismatched hook is configured, `checkHookDecl` silently passes instead of returning a descriptive signature mismatch error. The instrumenter then generates invalid trampoline code that fails downstream with cryptic Go compiler errors during the `toolexec` build phase.

### Environment

 - OS: All
 - Go Version: All supported (1.25, 1.26)
 - Version: main (v0.0.0)

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce:
1. Target a function with signature `func Target(msg string)`
2. Define a before hook with mismatched slice signature `func BeforeTarget(ctx hook.HookContext, msg []string)`
3. Run `checkHookDecl` during instrumentation phase.
4. `baseTypeName(*string)` returns `"string"` and `baseTypeName([]string)` returns `"string"`.
5. `checkHookDecl` returns `nil` (no error), claiming signatures match.

Similarly:
- Target function parameter: `map[string]int` (tramp param: `*map[string]int`)
- Hook function parameter: `chan bool`
- `baseTypeName(*map[string]int)` -> `""`, `baseTypeName(chan bool)` -> `""`.
- `checkHookDecl` returns `nil`.

### Expected behavior

`checkHookDecl` should reject type mismatches between target parameters and hook parameters with a clear error:
`hook func param 1 type mismatch, expected string, got []string`

It should preserve slice/array (`[]`), variadic (`...`), and composite type structure (e.g. `map`, `chan`) while only stripping package qualifiers and the outermost trampoline pointer indirection.

### Additional context

**Root Cause**:
In `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go`:
```go
func baseTypeName(expr dst.Expr) string {
	switch t := expr.(type) {
	case *dst.Ident:
		return t.Name
	case *dst.StarExpr:
		return baseTypeName(t.X)
	case *dst.SelectorExpr:
		return t.Sel.Name
	case *dst.ArrayType:
		return baseTypeName(t.Elt)
	case *dst.Ellipsis:
		return baseTypeName(t.Elt)
	case *dst.InterfaceType:
		return trampolineInterfaceType
	default:
		return ""
	}
}
```

**Proposed Fix**:
1. Refactor type normalization in `trampoline.go` so that slice (`[]`), variadic (`...`), map (`map[...]...`), and channel constructors are preserved in the normalized type representation, while package qualifiers and trampoline pointer wrappers (`*`) are stripped.
2. Ensure `checkHookDecl` correctly catches scalar vs slice, variadic vs non-variadic, and mismatched composite types.
3. Add regression tests in `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline_test.go` covering slices, variadics, maps, and channels.

Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

items.title: fix(tool/internal/instrument): normalize composite types in checkHookDecl
items.body:
## Description

This PR improves type normalization and signature verification in `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go`:
- Updates `baseTypeName()` to preserve composite type constructors, including slices (`[]T`), multi-dimensional slices (`[][]T`), variadics (`...T`), maps (`map[K]V`), channels (`chan T`, `<-chan T`, `chan<- T`), structs (`struct{}`), function types (`func(...) ...`), and generic indexing while stripping package qualifiers and outermost pointer indirections.
- Introduces `hookTypeMatches()` to validate compatibility between trampoline parameters and hook function parameters, properly handling exact normalized matches, `any` / `interface{}` wildcards, and variadic-to-slice (`...T` vs `[]T`) parameter passing.
- Adds comprehensive unit test cases in `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline_test.go` covering `baseTypeName` normalization on composite types and `checkHookDecl` validation against valid and invalid hook declarations (including scalar vs slice mismatches, slice element mismatches, and map vs channel mismatches).

## Motivation

In `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go`, `baseTypeName()` previously stripped `*dst.ArrayType` and `*dst.Ellipsis` down to `baseTypeName(t.Elt)` (e.g. `[]string` returned `"string"`) and defaulted unhandled composite types (`*dst.MapType`, `*dst.ChanType`, etc.) to `""`. Because `checkHookDecl` compared `trampBase != hookBase`, scalar parameters falsely matched slice/variadic parameters (e.g. `string` matched `[]string`), and unhandled composite types compared `"" == ""` and falsely matched each other (e.g. `map[string]int` matched `chan bool`).

This prevented `checkHookDecl` from rejecting incompatible hook signatures at compile-time validation, leading to invalid AST injection and cryptic downstream compiler errors during `toolexec`.

Fixes #1129

items.title: fix(database/sql): parse non-parenthesized MySQL Unix-socket DSNs
items.body:
## Problem

The MySQL DSN parser incorrectly handles non-parenthesized Unix-socket DSNs.

For example:

```text
unix:/tmp/mysql.sock/db
```

This should produce:

```text
server.address = /tmp/mysql.sock
server.port = ""
db.namespace = db
```

The current parser instead splits at the first `/`, which is part of the absolute socket path, and returns incorrect address and database values.

This gap was documented as a follow-up in #785 and was confirmed with @NameHaibinZhang.

## Root Cause

In the non-parenthesized branch of `parseMySQLDSN`, the parser uses the first `/` as the separator between the address and database name.

For a Unix-socket DSN, the address itself begins with `/`, so the first slash cannot be used as that separator.

## Proposed Fix

For a recognized non-parenthesized `unix:` DSN whose remaining address starts with `/`, split at the final `/` instead.

Preserve the current behavior for TCP, parenthesized Unix-socket DSNs, unknown protocols, and other DSN forms.

## Tests

Add focused coverage for:

- `unix:/tmp/mysql.sock/db`
- `user:pass@unix:/tmp/mysql.sock/mydb`
- `unix:/tmp/mysql.sock/`
- Existing parenthesized form: `unix(/tmp/mysql.sock)/db`
- Regression coverage for TCP and other existing address forms

The no-database form `unix:/tmp/mysql.sock` is structurally ambiguous when the final slash is also used as the database separator. Its expected behavior should be confirmed before encoding it in the parser.

## References

- #785
@NameHaibinZhang
