items.title: refactor(instrumentation/net/http): hooks allocate a map and build debug log arguments on every request
items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

The net/http client and server hooks do two things on every request that cost
allocations without doing useful work in the default configuration.

First, the Before hooks pass state to the After hooks with
`ictx.SetData(map[string]interface{}{...})`. That allocates a map and hashes
string keys per request just to carry a span and a start time. Two of the stored
entries are never read at all: `"ctx"` on both sides, and `"req"` on the client
side.

Second, the hooks call `logger.Debug(...)` with computed arguments such as
`r.URL.String()`. slog evaluates arguments before it checks the level, so at the
default INFO level every request serializes the full URL and boxes attributes
that are then discarded. The disabled path logs per request too.

Benchmarking the Before+After pair (mock hook context, SDK tracer, no exporter)
on go1.25.0 linux/amd64 shows 27 allocs/op on the server side and 29 on the
client side. Six and nine of those respectively come from the two items above.
For a project whose pitch is low runtime overhead, that seemed worth raising.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Replace the map with a small typed struct holding just the span and start time,
and gate the argument-taking `Debug` calls behind a level check so the URL
serialization and attribute boxing only happen when debug logging is on. Also
stop logging on the disabled path, which is the principle the gin hook already
documents ("Keep the disabled path free of logging", `context_hook.go`) but
net/http never picked up.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Keeping the map but dropping only the unread `"ctx"` / `"req"` entries. Saves
  the least and leaves the map allocation and key hashing in place.
- `sync.Pool` for the carried state. More machinery than a two-field struct
  needs, and the struct is a single small allocation anyway  a pool is more machinery than two fields justify.
- Converting the Debug calls to `slog` `LogAttrs` instead of gating them. That
  removes the boxing but not the `r.URL.String()` call, which is the larger
  cost.
- Leaving the disabled path logging as-is. Reasonable if it's deliberate for
  troubleshooting, which is why I'd rather ask than assume.

**Additional context**

I have this implemented and benchmarked with benchstat (10 runs per side,
`-benchtime=2s`, all comparisons p=0.000) and can open a PR. Happy to hear first
if either of these is intentional, or if you'd prefer the two changes split into
separate PRs.

items.title: refactor(tool/internal/setup): every build reruns go mod tidy even when the pin changed nothing
items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

For a project with a committed `otel.instrumentation.go`, every `otelc go build`
goes through `updateToolFile()` in `tool/internal/setup/pin.go`, which
unconditionally rewrites the tool file — even when the rendered result is
byte-identical to what's already on disk — and then runs `go mod tidy`.

`go mod tidy` loads the whole module graph and can take seconds, and may touch
the network on a cold cache. In the steady state, where setup was done once and
the files are committed, that work repeats on every build and cannot produce a
different result. It's the difference between a build that shells out to the Go
toolchain and one that doesn't.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Skip both when this run provably changed nothing. The signal already exists:
`ensureOtelcRequire()` returns a `modified` bool reporting whether it touched
go.mod, and `updateToolFile` has been discarding it since the pin command landed
in #655. Rendering the updated AST to bytes first and comparing against the file
on disk gives the same signal for the tool file. Tidy then runs only when the
tool file changed, go.mod changed, or go.sum is missing.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- The broader `isSetup()` TODO in #161. This is adjacent in spirit but much
  narrower: it doesn't try to detect "already set up" globally, only whether
  this particular run changed anything tidy could react to. The narrow version
  seemed safer to land first.
- A timestamp or mtime check on the tool file. Fragile across checkouts and
  clean builds; a byte comparison of the rendered output is exact.
- Caching a content hash of the inputs in a stamp file. Closes one more edge
  case (a stale-but-present go.sum from a tidy that died mid-run) but adds state
  to manage. I left it out and can add it if reviewers want that case fully
  covered.

**Additional context**

Rough size of the effect: in the test suite, `TestUpdateToolFile` — which
reaches the real tidy — takes ~16s on a cold module cache and ~1s warm  while the steady-state call skips the Go toolchain entirely, and cold caches or network-touching tidies widen the gap.
cache, while a second `updateToolFile` call in the steady state completes
without invoking the Go toolchain at all. Cold caches or network-touching tidies
widen that, not narrow it.

I have this implemented with tests covering both the skip and the deleted-go.sum
re-tidy, and can open a PR.

items.body:
## Summary

Per [docs/testing.md](docs/testing.md), E2E tests spin up **multiple instrumented processes** and assert they form one coherent trace (shared trace ID).

HTTP→OpenAI is now covered by a multi-process e2e (#1107 / #1120):

Anthropic GenAI client instrumentation is still **integration-only**:

- File: `test/integration/anthropic_client_test.go`
- Single process calling a mock Anthropic HTTP server

That does **not** verify that an Anthropic GenAI span stays parented under an upstream instrumented HTTP server when the request arrives from a separate instrumented HTTP client.

There is also **no** combined HTTP server + Anthropic client app under `test/apps/` (unlike `httpserveropenaiclient` / `httpserverdbclient`).

Existing multi-process E2E coverage:

| E2E Test | File |
|---|---|
| HTTP → SQL | `httpserver_dbclient_test.go` |

| HTTP → Kafka | `httpserver_kafkaclient_test.go` |
| HTTP → OpenAI | `httpserver_openaiclient_test.go` |

No Anthropic e2e coverage yet. This was listed as an explicit follow-up / out of scope on #1107.

## Proposed work

Mirror `test/e2e/httpserver_openaiclient_test.go`:

1. Add `test/apps/httpserveranthropicclient` — HTTP server that handles `/hello` and issues one Anthropic `Messages.New` call (same SDK pattern as `anthropicclient`), with flags for front port + Anthropic base URL / API key / model

5. Wait for spans with `f.WaitForSpans(3)`
6. Assert **one** distributed trace with **3** spans:
   - instrumented HTTP **client**
   - HTTP **server** (frontend)
   - GenAI **client** (`gen_ai.system=anthropic`) — not a duplicate `http.client` span (Anthropic instrumentation suppresses HTTP client instrumentation)
7. Assert shared trace ID and parent/child links across the chain
8. Keep assertions focused on propagation; pin `http.response.status_code=200` and a basic GenAI identity check (`gen_ai.system=anthropic`). Full `gen_ai.*` semconv detail stays in the existing integration test.

items.title: fix(instrumentation/net/http): cut per-request allocations in client
items.body:
## Description

Two code changes, both in the hook files.

**Typed struct instead of a map for Before→After state.** The
`map[string]interface{}` becomes a small `hookData` struct holding the span and
the start time. One small allocation instead of a map, no key hashing, and the
never-read `"ctx"` / `"req"` entries are gone. This data is written and read by
the same hook pair within these files, so it isn't part of any exported
contract.

**Level check before building debug arguments.** The `Debug` calls that take
computed arguments are gated behind a level check, so `r.URL.String()` and
attribute boxing only run when debug logging is actually enabled. The disabled
path no longer logs per request, matching the principle the gin hook documents.

The diff also updates the hook unit tests and `tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz`. The
bundle embeds these hook sources and the Verify Bundle check requires it to be
in sync; since the regenerate bot can't push to fork PRs, it's regenerated here
with `make package`.

### Benchmarks

Added in this PR. Environment: go1.25.0 linux/amd64, 13th Gen Intel Core
i7-13620H (16 threads), WSL2. Each side:

    OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=warn go test -bench=. -benchmem -run '^$' -count=10 -benchtime=2s

compared with benchstat.

    goos: linux
    goarch: amd64
    cpu: 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-13620H
                      │    main     │             this PR                 │
                      │   sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base                │
    ServeHTTPHooks-16   9.609µ ± 7%   7.816µ ± 7%  -18.66% (p=0.000 n=10)
    RoundTripHooks-16   8.088µ ± 3%   6.441µ ± 3%  -20.36% (p=0.000 n=10)

                      │     B/op     │     B/op      vs base               │
    ServeHTTPHooks-16   4.312Ki ± 0%   3.930Ki ± 0%   -8.88% (p=0.000 n=10)
    RoundTripHooks-16   3.312Ki ± 0%   2.867Ki ± 0%  -13.44% (p=0.000 n=10)

                      │  allocs/op  │ allocs/op   vs base                │
    ServeHTTPHooks-16    27.00 ± 0%   21.00 ± 0%  -22.22% (p=0.000 n=10)
    RoundTripHooks-16    29.00 ± 0%   20.00 ± 0%  -31.03% (p=0.000 n=10)

All six comparisons are p=0.000 at n=10; allocation and byte counts are exact.

Two notes for anyone reproducing this. `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=warn` is only there
because the one-time init INFO log interleaves with the benchmark output and
breaks benchstat's parsing; it doesn't tilt the comparison, since the
Debug-argument cost this PR removes is paid on main at every log level. And
`-benchtime=2s` matters — at 1s the client sec/op result wasn't claimable
(p=0.052, ±22% spread) and only stabilized at 2s. The allocation numbers were
stable either way.

The benchmark includes the mock context and SDK span start/end, so the hook-only
relative improvement is larger than the headline percentages.

### Behavior

No telemetry change: same spans, same attributes, same status handling.

Debug logging changes slightly at `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=debug`. The informative lines
(`BeforeServeHTTP called`, `AfterRoundTrip called`, and so on) are unchanged.
The redundant trailing `... completed` lines and the per-request
`instrumentation disabled` lines are gone.

## Motivation

These hooks run on every request of every instrumented HTTP app; fixed
per-request overhead is the project's whole cost story.

Fixes #1133

items.title: bug(tool/internal/setup): rule load order is nondeterministic, producing different instrumented output between identical builds
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`parseRuleFromYaml` in `tool/internal/setup/match.go` iterates the unmarshalled YAML rule map directly and appends to the returned slice in that order:

```go
func parseRuleFromYaml(content []byte) ([]rule.InstRule, error) {
	var h map[string]map[string]any
	err := yaml.Unmarshal(content, &h)
	...
	rules := make([]rule.InstRule, 0)
	for name, fields := range h {   // <- randomized map iteration
		...
		rules = append(rules, r)
	}
	return rules, nil
}
```

Go randomizes map iteration order, so the returned rule order differs between runs of the same input. Nothing sorts it afterwards: both call sites (`loadRulesFromToolFiles`, and the `-rules` path) append it straight into the rule set, and `instrument()` applies rules to a file in slice order.

The `-rules` path adds a second layer of the same problem at `match.go:480`:

```go
return slices.Concat(slices.Collect(maps.Values(ruleSet))...), nil
```

Because rule application order is semantically meaningful — multiple func rules on one function nest their trampoline-jump-ifs in application order — **the instrumented output is not reproducible**. Two identical builds of the same project with the same rule files can produce different generated code.

### Environment

 - OS: Linux (WSL2 / Ubuntu); not platform-specific — this is map iteration order
 - Go Version: 1.25.7
 - Version: `d95997a` (`main`)

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

**1. Show the parse order itself varies.** Add this to `tool/internal/setup/`:

```go
func TestParseRuleFromYamlOrder(t *testing.T) {
	names := []string{"aaa", "bbb", "ccc", "ddd", "eee", "fff", "ggg", "hhh"}
	yamlSrc := ""
	for _, n := range names {
		yamlSrc += fmt.Sprintf(
			"rule_%s:\n  target: main\n  where:\n    func: Func1\n  do:\n    - inject_hooks:\n        before: %sBefore\n        path: p\n",
			n, n)
	}

	seen := map[string]int{}
	for range 40 {
		rules, err := parseRuleFromYaml([]byte(yamlSrc))
		if err != nil {
			t.Fatalf("parse failed: %v", err)
		}
		order := ""
		for _, r := range rules {
			order += r.GetName() + " "
		}
		seen[order]++
	}
	if len(seen) > 1 {
		t.Errorf("identical input produced %d different rule orders", len(seen))
	}
}
```

Result — 40 parses of byte-identical YAML:

```text
distinct rule orders over 40 parses of the SAME yaml input: 8
   order: rule_fff rule_ggg rule_hhh rule_aaa rule_bbb rule_ccc rule_ddd rule_eee
   order: rule_ddd rule_eee rule_fff rule_ggg rule_hhh rule_aaa rule_bbb rule_ccc
   order: rule_aaa rule_bbb rule_ccc rule_ddd rule_eee rule_fff rule_ggg rule_hhh
```

**2. Show it reaches generated code.** The golden harness hides this, because `instrument_test.go:186` sorts rule names before building the rule set — with the comment *"Sort rule names to ensure deterministic order in tests"*. Production has no such sort.

Remove that one line so the harness matches production, then run the existing `multiple-func-rules` fixture (two rules, `hook_func_1` and `hook_func_2`, both targeting `Func1`) repeatedly:

```
go test -count=1 -run 'TestInstrumentation_Integration/multiple-func-rules' ./tool/internal/instrument/
```

Over 12 runs: **11 passed, 1 failed**. The failure is a swap of the two trampolines:

```text
-	if hookContext3592294264, _ := OtelBeforeTrampoline_Func13592294264(&p1, &p2); false {
+	if hookContext1830170046, _ := OtelBeforeTrampoline_Func11830170046(&p1, &p2); false {
-		if hookContext1830170046, _ := OtelBeforeTrampoline_Func11830170046(&p1, &p2); false {
+		if hookContext3592294264, _ := OtelBeforeTrampoline_Func13592294264(&p1, &p2); false {
```

The nesting order of the trampoline-jump-ifs inverts, and the declaration order in the generated globals file inverts with it. Same source, same rules, different output.

### Expected behavior

Rules load in a stable order, so a given set of rule files always produces byte-identical instrumented output.

### Additional context

**Why this has gone unnoticed.** The golden suite sorts rule names in its own harness, so CI is deterministic by construction and can never surface this. The intermittency in step 2 (1 failure in 12) is also characteristic: for a two-key map Go's randomization does not flip the order on every run, so a naive repeat-run check usually passes.

**Severity.** This is the same class the project has already fixed twice — #986 (sorting `moduleDirs` in `generatePinnedProjects`/`getBackupFiles`) and #971 (sorting `moduleDirs` in `resolveRulePaths`) — and more recently #1070 for `instrument()`'s file iteration. Unlike #1070, which only changed which error message surfaced, this one changes the generated code, so it affects build reproducibility and any downstream artifact hashing or caching that assumes identical inputs give identical output.

**Suggested fix.** Sort the rule names in `parseRuleFromYaml` before building the slice (`slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(h))`), and give `match.go:480` a deterministic order rather than `maps.Values`. Once production is deterministic, the sort in `instrument_test.go` can stay as a belt-and-braces measure or be dropped — but it should no longer be the only thing providing the guarantee.

**Related, not filed separately.** `StateManager.Revert()` (`tool/internal/setup/state.go`) iterates `s.files` unsorted while `Commit()` in the same file explicitly sorts "for deterministic behavior". That one only affects the ordering of joined error messages on a partially-failed revert, so it is far less serious, but it is the same inconsistency and could be swept up by the same PR.

items.title: chore(tool): unexport internal identifiers with no cross-package use
items.body:
## Description

First slice of #1143, covering the packages with only a handful of affected symbols so the
approach can be reviewed cheaply before the larger ones (`ast`, `setup`, `rule`) follow.

Unexported:

- `util.IsUnix` → `isUnix`
- `pkgload.ResolveModuleDir` → `resolveModuleDir`
- `manifest.Load` → `load`
- `profile.CPU` / `Heap` / `Trace` → `typeCPU` / `typeHeap` / `typeTrace`

The profile constants get a `type` prefix rather than plain `cpu`/`heap`/`trace` because
`profile.go` imports `runtime/trace`; a bare `trace` constant would shadow the package
within that file.

### How the list was produced

Rather than work from a hand-written list, I wrote a `go/packages` analyzer (full type
info, `Tests: true`) that collapses a package with its internal test variant
(`p [p.test]`) and its external test package (`p_test`) into one logical package — an
external `_test` package is not a real API consumer, since it can be converted to an
internal test instead. It then reports exported package-scope identifiers with zero
references from any other logical package.

I sanity-checked it against ground truth before trusting it: `cmd/otelc` references

items.title: grpc: HandleRPC ends and overwrites caller span on skipped OTLP export calls
items.body:
### Description

When `TagRPC` opts out of instrumenting OTLP export RPCs via `grpcsemconv.IsOTELExporterPath(info.FullMethodName)`, it returns the caller's `context.Context` unmodified without attaching `gRPCContext` or creating a gRPC span.

However, gRPC's stats handler lifecycle still executes `HandleRPC(ctx, rs)`. In `HandleRPC`:
1. `span := trace.SpanFromContext(ctx)` retrieves the caller's active span.
2. `*stats.OutHeader` and `*stats.End` inspect `if span.IsRecording()` without checking `gctx != nil`.
3. As a result, the caller's span is stamped with `rpc.grpc.status_code` / server address attributes and ended prematurely via `span.End()`.

### Common Reproduction Scenario

This occurs during standard graceful shutdown or flush flows:
```go
ctx, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "shutdown-task")
defer span.End()

tp.ForceFlush(ctx) // OTLP exporter gRPC call executes HandleRPC with ctx and ends 'shutdown-task'

This was flagged and approved on the issue before I started: `filter_test.go` was an external black-box test package referencing `setup.Filter`/`FuncFilter`/`AllOf`/`Not`/etc — exactly the types being unexported here. Converted it to an internal test file, dropped the self-import, and stripped all 111 `setup.` prefixes. **Self-referencing locals.** `state.go` had `toolFileCanonical := filepath.Join(moduleDir, ToolFileCanonical)` — renaming the constant would have made this `toolFileCanonical := filepath.Join(moduleDir, toolFileCanonical)`, undefined on the right-hand side since the left-hand side isn't in scope yet. Renamed the two locals to `canonical`/`alias`, matching a pattern the same package already uses in `config.go`.

**Field access on a different package's identically-named fields.** `rule.WhereDef` and `rule.FilterDef` (a separate package) have their own fields literally named `AllOf`, `OneOf`, `Not`. items.title: fix(grpc): HandleRPC must not touch caller span on skipped RPCs
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes #1147 `HandleRPC` in the gRPC client and server stats handlers was silently
corrupting and prematurely ending the caller's active span whenever
`TagRPC` opted out of instrumenting an OTLP export RPC.

## Root cause

`TagRPC` signals "I skipped this RPC" by returning the caller's
`context.Context` unchanged — no `gRPCContext` is attached. The metric
branches in `HandleRPC` (`OutPayload`, `InPayload`, and the `End`
metrics block) already respected this contract with `if gctx != nil`
guards. The span branches (`OutHeader` and the span portion of `End`)
did not: they only checked `span.IsRecording()`.

Because `trace.SpanFromContext(ctx)` was called before the `gctx`
check, on the skipped path it resolved to **the caller's active span**.
Any caller span that happened to be recording would:

- Have `rpc.grpc.status_code` and peer address attributes written onto it.
- Be ended via `span.End()` during the OTLP export RPC.

This is silently destructive: no error, no log — the span simply
reports the wrong duration, wrong attributes, and is exported at the
wrong time.

## Reproduction

The standard graceful-shutdown pattern triggers this:

```go
ctx, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "graceful-shutdown")
defer span.End()
tp.ForceFlush(ctx)  // → OTLP export gRPC call → HandleRPC ends "graceful-shutdown" here
```

`tp.ForceFlush(ctx)` → `bsp.exportSpans(ctx)` → `UploadTraces(ctx)` →
gRPC Export. The context carries the caller span through because
`exportContext` derives from the caller's `ctx`. The OTLP exporter uses
the instrumented gRPC connection, so our `HandleRPC` fires with a
context that still has the caller's recording span on it.

## Fix

Add an early return at the top of `HandleRPC` when `gctx == nil`:

```go
gctx, _ := ctx.Value(gRPCContextKey{}).(*gRPCContext)
if gctx == nil {
    return
}
span := trace.SpanFromContext(ctx)
```

This makes all branches consistent with the existing metric guards and
ensures the caller's span is never reachable on the skipped path.
The `span` lookup is hoisted below the guard so it cannot be resolved
against a caller-owned span.

The redundant per-branch `if gctx != nil` guards on `OutPayload` and
`InPayload` are removed since `gctx` is guaranteed non-nil past the
early return.

## Note on #1104

Issue #1104 proposes decoupling `span.End()` from the
`span.IsRecording()` guard. If that change is made without the `gctx`
guard established here, the skipped path would unconditionally call
`span.End()` on the caller's span. The early return makes that safe.

## Tests

Two regression tests are added — one per package:

- `TestClientStatsHandler_SkippedRPC_DoesNotTouchCallerSpan`
- `TestServerStatsHandler_SkippedRPC_DoesNotTouchCallerSpan`

Each test:
1. Starts a real recording caller span (`"graceful-shutdown"`).
2. Calls `TagRPC` with an OTLP export method name (skip path).
3. Drives all five `HandleRPC` event types through the skipped context.
4. Asserts the caller span is **still recording** (not ended).
5. Ends the span explicitly and asserts only 1 span is exported with
   the correct name and no `rpc.grpc.status_code` attribute.

items.title: feat(instrumentation/genai): add compile-time instrumentation for google.golang.org/genai
items.body:
## Description

Adds compile-time instrumentation for the Google Gen AI Go SDK (`google.golang.org/genai`), so applications using Gemini get GenAI client spans without any code changes.

The SDK is the single Go client for both of Google's generative AI surfaces, the Gemini Developer API and Vertex AI. Both route `GenerateContent` through the same `generateContent` HTTP method, so one instrumentation covers both. `client.Chats` sessions are covered too, since they issue the same requests underneath.

What is included:

- Rule (`otelc.yaml`) matching `genai.NewClient`, with an after hook.
- Hook and tracing `http.RoundTripper` under `instrumentation/google.golang.org/genai/`.
- Unit tests for the hook and the transport.
- Integration test in `test/integration/` that builds an instrumented binary against a mock endpoint and asserts the emitted span.
- Telemetry contract in `schemas/otelc/groups/gemini.yaml`.
- Docs and supported-library table updates.

### Why an after hook rather than a before hook

`NewClient` fills in a nil `ClientConfig.HTTPClient` itself, and for Vertex AI without explicit credentials the client it builds carries application default credentials. A before hook that substituted its own client would break that authentication. Hooking the return value means the instrumentation decorates whatever client the SDK settled on, so authentication is left alone.

`Client.ClientConfig()` returns a copy of the config, but `HTTPClient` is a pointer that the copy shares with the internal API client, so replacing its transport takes effect for every subsequent call. Clients sharing one `*http.Client` are wrapped once, not once per client.

### Provider detection

`gen_ai.provider.name` and `gen_ai.system` are read from the backend the client was configured for rather than guessed from the request host, so the Gemini Developer API reports `gcp.gemini` / `gemini` and Vertex AI reports `gcp.vertex_ai` / `vertex_ai`. This avoids the host-matching problem that #824 fixed for the other providers.

### Token accounting

Two Gemini specific details are normalised so the span means the same thing it does for the other GenAI instrumentations:

- `thoughtsTokenCount` is generated and billed as output but reported separately from `candidatesTokenCount`, so the two are summed into `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`.
- `promptTokenCount` already covers cached content, so it maps onto `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` unchanged. This is unlike Anthropic's `input_tokens`, which excludes cache reads and has to be folded back together.

`gen_ai.usage.total_tokens` uses the API's `totalTokenCount` when present and is otherwise derived.

### Not included

- Streaming (`streamGenerateContent`) passes through without a span. Usage totals only arrive in the final server sent event and this does not accumulate SSE yet. Same gap as #679 left for Anthropic, and #970 tracks the wider SSE work.
- `countTokens`, `embedContent`, image and video generation, and the remaining model RPCs are not instrumented.
- Spans only, no metrics.
- Prompt and response content is never captured. The semantic conventions gate that behind `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT`, which is not implemented here, so metadata only is the only behaviour.

`error.type` uses the numeric status code, following #976 rather than the older full status string that the Anthropic middleware still uses.

## Motivation

Gemini is one of the three major model providers, and otelc already instruments the other two (`openai-go` and `anthropic-sdk-go`). Go services calling Gemini currently get either nothing or a bare `net/http` client span with no model, token usage, or finish reason on it, which leaves a visible hole when a service calls more than one provider and you want to compare cost and latency across them.

This fills that hole using the same shape as the existing GenAI instrumentations, so the three providers emit comparable spans.

items.body:
<!--
Thank you for contributing to OpenTelemetry Go Compile Instrumentation!

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Fill in the description and motivation sections below
2. Complete the checklist before submitting
3. Ensure PR title follows conventional commits format (enforced by CI)

PR TITLE FORMAT (required):

BEFORE SUBMITTING:

  make lint    # Run all linters
  make test    # Run all tests (unit + integration + e2e)

If your PR adds a new user-facing instrumentation, please also submit a corresponding OpenTelemetry Registry PR:
https://opentelemetry.io/ecosystem/registry/adding/

For detailed contribution guidelines, see CONTRIBUTING.md
For available make targets, run: make help
-->

## Description

`parseRuleFromYaml` iterates over a Go map (`for name, fields := range h`) which has nondeterministic iteration order. This causes rule application order to vary across runs, leading to non-reproducible instrumentation behavior. Similarly, `loadCustomRules` collects rule values via `slices.Concat(slices.Collect(maps.Values(ruleSet))...)` which also depends on map iteration order.

Both functions now iterate over map keys in sorted (lexicographic) order using `slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(...))`.

## Motivation

Reproducible builds and deterministic instrumentation output are important for debugging and correctness. With nondeterministic map iteration, the same YAML rule file can produce different instrumentation results across runs.

Fixes #1144

items.title: fix(database/sql): parse non-parenthesized MySQL Unix-socket DSNs
items.body:
## Description

`parseMySQLDSN` splits the address from the database name at the first `/`. That works for tcp/host addresses since they never contain a `/`, but not for a unix socket, where the address itself is an absolute path.

For `unix:/tmp/mysql.sock/db`, the first `/` is the one right after `unix:`, so the parser split it into address `unix:` and db `/tmp/mysql.sock/db`. `mysqlStripProtocol` then saw an empty address after the protocol and returned an empty host, and the db name came out as `tmp/mysql.sock/db` instead of `db`.

## Fix

Added `isMySQLUnixAddr`, which checks the non-parenthesized address for an exact `unix:` prefix. When it matches, the address/database separator is the last `/` in the DSN instead of the first, since the socket path itself owns every `/` before that one. Every other non-parenthesized form (tcp, bare host, bare port) has no `/` in the address at all, so first and last agree there and nothing changes for them.

The parenthesized form (`unix(/tmp/mysql.sock)/db`) was already correct and is untouched.

## Tests

Added `TestParseDSN_MySQLUnixSocketNonParenthesized`, covering:
- `unix:/tmp/mysql.sock/db`
- `user:pass@unix:/tmp/mysql.sock/mydb`
- `unix:/tmp/mysql.sock/` (trailing slash, empty db)
- a socket path nested under multiple directories
- the parenthesized form, as a regression check
- a protocol name that starts with "unix" but isn't it (`unixish`), so the match stays exact
- tcp and bare host forms, to confirm they still use the first `/`

Also ran the existing `FuzzParseDSN` for 600k+ executions after the change, no crashes.

One thing I left alone on purpose: `unix:/tmp/mysql.sock` with no trailing slash at all is ambiguous, the last `/` would land inside the socket path itself instead of at a real separator. The issue flagged this as needing confirmation before encoding, so I didn't add a test or a rule for it. Behavior there is unchanged from before this fix.

Fixes #1131

items.title: fix(instrumentation/mongo): stop injected CommandMonitor from overriding a user's Monitor
items.body:
## Description

`BeforeConnect`/`BeforeNewClient` in both the v1 and v2 mongo-driver instrumentation injected the OTel `CommandMonitor` by checking each `*options.ClientOptions` struct's own `Monitor` field in isolation:

```go
for _, opt := range opts {
    if opt == nil {
        continue
    }
    if opt.Monitor == nil {
        opt.SetMonitor(monitor)
    }
}
```

`mongo.NewClient`/`mongo.Connect` don't resolve `opts` in isolation, though — they call `options.MergeClientOptions(opts...)`, which folds the whole slice into one struct by keeping the **last non-nil** value of each field, in slice order. If a caller's own `CommandMonitor` was set on a struct that wasn't last in `opts`, this loop would inject the OTel monitor into a later, still-nil struct, and the merge would pick the injected monitor over the user's — silently dropping it.

## Root cause

The hook decided whether to inject per-struct (`opt.Monitor == nil`), but the driver decides the *effective* value across the whole slice with last-non-nil-wins semantics. These two rules disagree whenever the user's `Monitor` isn't on the last struct in `opts`.

I verified this against the real `mongo-driver` `MergeClientOptions` source and with a standalone reproduction before writing the fix — details in #1148.

## Fix

Instead of mutating individual structs, `injectMonitor` now checks the *effective* merged `Monitor` once. If it's already non-nil (a user monitor is present anywhere in `opts`), nothing changes. Otherwise it appends a new trailing `*options.ClientOptions` carrying the OTel monitor. Being last, `MergeClientOptions`'s last-non-nil-wins rule guarantees it always applies when needed, and — since a fresh `options.Client()` leaves every other field `nil` — it can never override, or be overridden by, anything the caller already passed in.

Applied identically to both `instrumentation/go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver/mongo` and `instrumentation/go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver/v2/mongo`, which had the same logic.

## Testing

- Updated existing unit tests for the new "append a trailing struct" behavior (previously asserted injection into every struct, which is exactly what caused the bug).
- Added a regression test for the reported scenario: a user monitor on an earlier `ClientOptions` struct, with a later struct left at its zero value — asserts the *merged* result still keeps the user's monitor.
- `go test ./...` passes for both `instrumentation/go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver/mongo` and `instrumentation/go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver/v2/mongo`.
- `golangci-lint run` on both packages reports only pre-existing issues (globals, local `replace` directives, existing function signatures) that are unchanged by this diff — verified by comparing against the pre-fix code.

## Impact

Without this fix, a user with their own `CommandMonitor` (e.g. existing APM/logging) silently loses it the moment `otelc` instruments their `mongo.Connect`/`mongo.NewClient` call, with no error or log — a correctness regression for a tool whose whole value proposition is being a safe, additive drop-in.

Fixes #1148

items.title: fix(tool): exclude OS junk files from otelc bundle archive
items.body:
Fixes #1123

`make package` walks the filesystem, so any untracked file sitting under `pkg/` or `instrumentation/` gets archived even though it's not part of the source. `.DS_Store` is the common case since macOS Finder writes it as soon as a directory is opened, and it's already in `.gitignore` so nothing about it shows up in git status or diffs. The result is a bundle that depends on what happened to be on the machine that ran `make package`, and Verify Bundle fails with no clue why.

This widens `shouldExclude` to also drop `.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`, and `desktop.ini` by exact filename, alongside the existing `.log` suffix check. Added a test for `shouldExclude` and one that reproduces the bug report's repro steps directly (archive a dir with a `.DS_Store` in it, check it's not in the output).

## Test plan
- [x] `go test ./...` in `.tools/bundle`
- [x] `make package` still produces a valid archive

items.title: fix(instrumentation/logrus): lazily init hook maps to survive go:linkname init-order
items.body:
Fixes #1028

Any app with `github.com/sirupsen/logrus` in its dependency graph, even without calling into logrus directly, prints this on every startup once instrumented:

```
failed to exec After hook AfterLogrusNew
assignment to entry in nil map
```

`AfterLogrusNew` is wired to `logrus.New()` via `//go:linkname`, which doesn't create a normal Go import edge. So when logrus's own `var std = New()` fires during logrus's package init, there's no guarantee this hook package's own `var hookInitMap = make(...)` has run yet. The hook can fire against a still-nil map and panic on the write.

Fix: stop initializing `hookInitMap` and `fieldInitMap` at var-declaration time, and lazily create them under `hookInitMu` inside `AfterLogrusNew` / `AfterLogrusWithField` instead. That's safe no matter which order the two packages' inits run in. `formatterInit` is a plain bool so its zero value was never a problem.

Added two tests that set both maps to nil right before calling the hooks (simulating the pre-init state) and assert no panic, alongside the existing coverage.

items.title: bug(tool/internal/instrument): recovered generic constraint keeps declaration's param names, breaks on renamed receiver with inter-parameter constraint
items.body:
### Describe the bug

#1122 recovers a generic receiver's real type-parameter constraints instead of widening them to `any`, which is a genuine improvement. But it clones each constraint verbatim from the type declaration without remapping the type-parameter names, so when a method receiver renames the type parameters and a constraint references another parameter, the generated trampoline references a name that is not in scope and fails to compile.

### Where

`extractReceiverTypeParams` / `receiverConstraintAt` in `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go`. `receiverConstraintAt` returns `dst.Clone(field.Type)` from the type declaration, keeping the declaration's parameter names, while the surrounding field uses the receiver's (possibly renamed) parameter names.

### Reproduction

Valid Go, where the receiver renames the type parameters (`K -> A`, `V -> B`) and `V`'s constraint references `K`:

```go
type M[K any, V ~[]K] struct {
	k K
	v V
}

func (m M[A, B]) Method() {}
```

Running the receiver through the current code produces:

```
param[0] name=A constraint=any
param[1] name=B constraint=~[]K     <-- references K, but the params are A and B
```

The generated trampoline is therefore equivalent to:

```go
func otel_trampoline[A any, B ~[]K](recv *M[A, B]) { /* ... */ }
```

which does not compile:

```
undefined: K
B does not satisfy ~[]A
```

The correct output re-scopes the constraint to the receiver's names, `B ~[]A`, which compiles.

### Steps to reproduce

Parse the source above, call `extractReceiverTypeParams(file, receiverType)`, and inspect the second field: its name is `B` but its constraint is `~[]K`. Building `func f[A any, B ~[]K]() {}` directly gives `undefined: K` on Go 1.24.

### Scope

This needs both a receiver that renames the type parameters and a constraint that references another parameter (an inter-parameter constraint such as `~[]K` or `map[K]V`). Both are valid but uncommon, so the common case #1122 targets is unaffected and its tests pass. It is the same class of failure #1122 set out to remove (uncompilable generated code), for an input its tests do not cover.

### Suggested fix

When cloning a constraint in `receiverConstraintAt`, substitute the type declaration's parameter names with the receiver's names before use. A small `dst` walk that rewrites `*dst.Ident` nodes matching a declaration parameter name to the corresponding receiver name would cover `~[]K`, `map[K]V`, and any other inter-parameter constraint. A regression test with a renamed receiver over an inter-parameter constraint would lock it down, since the current tests use matching names only.

I verified the recovered constraint and the compile failure directly; happy to send the fix if it is useful.

items.title: fix(tool): re-scope recovered generic constraints to receiver names
items.body:
## Description

`extractReceiverTypeParams` recovers a generic type parameter constraint from the receiver's own type declaration and attaches it to the receiver's parameter name. When the receiver renames a parameter, an inter-parameter constraint kept the declaration's name instead of the receiver's.

Concretely, for:

```go
type M[K any, V ~[]K] struct{ /* ... */ }

func (m M[A, B]) InstrumentedMethod() { /* ... */ }
```

the recovered type parameter list came out as `[A any, B ~[]K]`. The `~[]K` refers to `K`, which the generated trampoline never declares (it declares `A` and `B`), so the emitted code fails to compile with `undefined: K`.

The fix maps the declaration's parameter names to the receiver's names positionally (`K -> A`, `V -> B`), then rewrites the identifiers inside each recovered constraint, so `~[]K` becomes `~[]A` and every reference stays in scope. Constraints with no rename are returned untouched, so the common case allocates nothing extra.

## Motivation

A receiver is free to rename a generic type's parameters, and constraints that reference a sibling parameter (`~[]K`, `map[K]V`, and similar) are common on container types. Without this, instrumenting a method on such a type emits code that does not build, which fails the whole compile-time rewrite for that package.

New unit test `TestExtractReceiverTypeParamsConstraint_RenamedInterParam` covers the renamed receiver with an inter-parameter constraint and asserts the recovered constraint reads `~[]A`.

Fixes #1169

items.title: bug(tool/internal/instrument): generic receiver constraint recovery doesn't search other files of the same package, falls back to `any`
items.body:
> **Note:** this is a known, self-flagged gap, not a new discovery. PR #1122 (fixes #1121) explicitly documented it in a "Known limitation" section and referenced "the linked issue" for the follow-up — but no such issue was ever filed, as far as I can find (searched `findGenericTypeDecl`, "cross-file", "different file", "sibling file", "whole-package", "go/packages" as both issue and PR terms, and #1121's full cross-reference timeline, which only shows #1122 and #1126). Filing it now so it's tracked.

### Problem

When instrumenting a method with a generic receiver, the tool tries to recover the receiver's real type constraint (e.g. `comparable`) so the generated trampoline's own type-parameter declaration matches the source, rather than widening it to `any`. This recovery only searches the single already-parsed file containing the instrumented method. If the generic type is declared in a *different* file of the same package — an ordinary Go layout — the lookup misses it and the constraint silently falls back to `any`, with no error or warning.

### Why it happens

`findGenericTypeDecl` (`tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go:809-826`) only receives the single `*dst.File` being instrumented (`ip.target`), which `parseFile` sets from a strictly one-file-at-a-time processing loop (`instrument.go`'s per-file loop calling `parseFile`, `apply_func.go:370-376`). No code path combines a package's files into one AST before this lookup runs, so a type declared in a sibling file is structurally invisible to it.

```go
// findGenericTypeDecl searches file's top-level declarations for a generic type
// declaration named typeName ... The declaration may live in a different file
// of the same package; that case is not resolved today, so it falls through
// to the caller's any fallback.
func findGenericTypeDecl(file *dst.File, typeName string) *dst.FieldList {
	if file == nil || typeName == "" {
		return nil
	}
	for _, decl := range file.Decls {
		...
	}
	return nil
}
```

When it returns `nil`, `receiverConstraintAt` (`trampoline.go:833-848`) skips its positional-match loop and returns `ast.Ident("any")` at line 847.

### Minimal reproducer

```go
// file_a.go
package pkg

type Box[T comparable] struct { value T }

// file_b.go — same package, different file
package pkg

func (b *Box[T]) Get() T { return b.value }
```

Instrument `Get` with a func rule. `findGenericTypeDecl` receives only `file_b.go`'s AST, finds no `type Box[...]` there, and returns `nil`.

### Current behavior

The generated trampoline's type-parameter declaration is emitted as `[T any]`, silently, purely because of file layout.

### Expected behavior

The generated trampoline's type-parameter declaration should be `[T comparable]`, matching what already happens correctly when the type declaration and the method are in the same file (covered by `trampoline_receiver_test.go`).

### Relevant code path / file locations

- `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go`
  - `findGenericTypeDecl` (809-826) — the single-file-scoped lookup
  - `extractReceiverTypeParams` (758-791) — calls it, only production call sites
  - `receiverConstraintAt` (833-848) — the `any` fallback, line 847
  - `findTargetGenericType` (480-504) — combines receiver + method-own type params
  - `buildTrampSignature` (506-531, calls at 511 and 516) — the only place the result is consumed for codegen; this is what actually changes the emitted trampoline signature
- `tool/internal/instrument/apply_func.go:370-376` (`parseFile`) and `tool/internal/instrument/instrument.go` (per-file loop) — confirm files are parsed and processed one at a time, never as a combined multi-file AST

### Why this matters

This is a real, deterministic gap triggered by ordinary Go file layout (splitting a generic type's declaration from its methods across files), not a hypothetical edge case. The degradation is silent — nothing indicates to the author that their instrumentation is running with a weaker constraint than the source declares. Whether this manifests as a generated-code compile failure (as #1125 showed for the same-file case before #1122 fixed it) depends on whether a given trampoline body path exercises the constraint; I haven't audited every `impl.tmpl` path for that, so I'm not asserting compile failure as a certainty — only that the constraint information is genuinely lost, which is the exact class of problem #1121/#1122 were filed to fix, just for the file layout #1122 explicitly left unhandled.

### Suggested test cases

- A two-file unit test: parse the type declaration and the method into two separate `*dst.File` values, run `extractReceiverTypeParams` against the method's file only, and assert today's actual (degraded) fallback as a baseline.
- Same setup, asserting the constraint is correctly recovered once fixed.
- A golden end-to-end test with the split-file layout, compared against the existing same-file golden case's precision.
- A regression test confirming the genuine "no declaration exists anywhere in the package" case still correctly falls back to `any` rather than erroring.

### Possible direction 

`findGenericTypeDecl` would need visibility into the rest of the package's files, not just the one being instrumented. Since the pipeline currently parses and instruments one file at a time, this likely means threading some form of package-level type-declaration index into the instrument phase — a structural change to a currently file-scoped step, not a one-line fix.

items.title: chore(tool/internal/instrument): leftover panicking HookContextImpl methods after After-hook removal in optimizeTJumps
items.body:
### Problem

When a generic function or generic-receiver method is instrumented with only a Before hook (no After), `optimizeTJumps` deletes the generated After trampoline function — but leaves the four always-panicking `HookContextImpl{suffix}` methods (`GetParam`, `SetParam`, `GetReturnVal`, `SetReturnVal`, installed by `rewriteHookContextMethods` for any generic target) declared in the output. They're genuinely unreachable by any tool-generated code path in this scenario, but still get compiled into the binary.

This is the exact gap the code's own TODO already names — see `optimize.go:367`. Related but independent finding while investigating this: #1174 — same neighborhood of code, different symptom (a runtime panic risk, not dead code), no shared fix.

### Why it happens

`optimizeTJumps` (`tool/internal/instrument/optimize.go:356-411`) branches on `rule.After == ""` (line 370):

```go
// No After hook present? Remove generated calls to After trampoline.
// Why we don't remove the whole else block of trampoline-jump-if? Well,
// because there might be more than one trampoline-jump-if in the same
// function, they are nested in the else block. See findJumpPoint for
// more details.
// TODO: Remove corresponding HookContextImpl methods
removedOnExit := false
rule := tjump.rule
if rule.After == "" {
	err := removeAfterTrampolineCall(tjump)
	...
	err = removeAfterTrampolineDecl(ip.target, tjump)
	...
}
```

`removeAfterTrampolineCall` strips the call sites; `removeAfterTrampolineDecl` deletes the After trampoline's `*dst.FuncDecl` entirely. Neither touches the `HookContextImpl{suffix}` struct or its methods — those were already declared earlier, during `createTrampoline` (`trampoline.go:1077-1112`), via `materializeTemplate`/`implementHookContext`/`rewriteHookContextMethods`, which run once per rule regardless of whether Before/After are both present. `optimizeTJumps` runs later and has no code path that walks back to remove now-unreachable `HookContextImpl` methods.

### Current behavior

For a generic target with only a Before hook, the compiled output retains four dead `panic(...)`-bodied methods on `HookContextImpl{suffix}` that nothing in the generated code ever calls.

### Expected behavior

Either the panicking methods are removed when they're provably unreachable (After absent + generic target), or — if removing them is judged not worth the complexity — the TODO should be resolved one way or the other rather than left open indefinitely (introduced in #119, never revisited since).

### Relevant code path / file locations

- `tool/internal/instrument/optimize.go:356-411` (`optimizeTJumps`, the TODO at line 367)
- `tool/internal/instrument/optimize.go:93-117` (`removeAfterTrampolineCall`) and `:188-199` (`removeAfterTrampolineDecl`) — what's already removed
- `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go:895-938` (`rewriteHookContextMethods`) and `:940-951` (`makeMethodPanic`) — where the panic methods are installed
- `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go:1077-1112` (`createTrampoline`) — confirms `HookContextImpl` declaration happens before `optimizeTJumps` runs, in a separate pass

### Why this matters

Purely a code-quality / generated-binary-size concern, not a correctness bug — confirmed by tracing `populateHookContext`, `callBeforeHook`, and `callAfterHook`, none of which ever call these four methods on the tool's own generated `HookContextImpl` (they only assign directly to the struct's `Params`/`ReturnVals` fields). Low severity, but it's a five-year-old-in-repo-years TODO the maintainers wrote themselves, with no test currently distinguishing "After absent + generic" from any other case.

### Suggested test cases

- A golden test combining a generic target with a Before-only hook rule (no existing testdata dir covers this combination — `testdata/golden/generic-functions/rules.yml` currently declares both Before and After for its cases).
- An assertion (golden-diff or AST inspection) on whether the four `HookContextImpl` methods are present or removed in that specific output.

### Possible direction (not a proposed implementation)

Two legitimate paths, not preferring either without more context: (a) extend `optimizeTJumps`'s After-absent branch to also strip the four methods from the `HookContextImpl{suffix}` type when the target is generic, or (b) if removal is judged too fragile/low-value relative to the complexity, resolve the TODO explicitly (a comment explaining why it's intentionally left, plus closing/superseding the open TODO) so it stops reading as an unaddressed gap.

items.title: docs(tool): HookContextImpl.GetParam/SetParam/GetReturnVal/SetReturnVal panic for any generic target, undocumented and undiscoverable until runtime
items.body:
### Problem

For any generic function or generic-receiver method target, the generated `HookContextImpl{suffix}`'s `GetParam`, `SetParam`, `GetReturnVal`, and `SetReturnVal` methods are replaced with unconditional `panic(...)` bodies. A hook author who writes `ctx.GetParam(0)` (or any of the other three) inside their own Before/After hook function for a generic target gets a runtime panic — with no compile-time warning, no lint, and nothing in the tool's documentation or golden examples flagging that these specific methods are unsafe to call for generic targets. The same `hook.HookContext` interface is handed to hook authors regardless of whether the underlying function is generic, so there's no type-level signal that these four methods have silently become unsafe.

Related but independent finding from the same investigation: #1173 — same neighborhood of code (`rewriteHookContextMethods`), different symptom (dead code, not a runtime panic risk), no shared fix.

### Why it happens

`rewriteHookContextMethods` (`tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go:895-938`) checks whether the target is generic:

```go
if findTargetGenericType(ip.target, ip.targetFunc) != nil {
	makeMethodPanic(methodGetParam, "GetParam is unsupported for generic functions")
	makeMethodPanic(methodGetRetVal, "GetReturnVal is unsupported for generic functions")
	makeMethodPanic(methodSetParam, "SetParam is unsupported for generic functions")
	makeMethodPanic(methodSetRetVal, "SetReturnVal is unsupported for generic functions")
	return
}
```

`makeMethodPanic` (`trampoline.go:940-951`) replaces the method body wholesale with a single `panic("...")` statement. This is gated purely on genericity — it applies identically whether or not an After hook is present, and regardless of how the hook author intends to use the accessor methods.

### Current behavior

Confirmed by tracing `populateHookContext`, `callBeforeHook`, and `callAfterHook`: the tool's own generated code never calls these four methods — it only ever writes directly to the `HookContextImpl`'s `Params`/`ReturnVals` fields, and passes the raw parameter values as separate positional arguments to the hook function (e.g. `GenericFuncBefore(ctx, p1, p2)`), which is presumably why the repo's own golden testdata hook examples never call `ctx.GetParam(...)` and so never trip this path. The panic is real, but only reachable through hand-written hook code that a user could plausibly write, especially since nothing distinguishes a generic-target `HookContext` from a non-generic one at the type level — both satisfy the same `hook.HookContext` interface.

### Minimal reproducer

```go
// target
func GenericFunc[T any](p1 T, p2 int) (T, error) { return p1, nil }
```

```go
// hook.go — a plausible, not-unreasonable hook author mistake
func GenericFuncBefore(ctx hook.HookContext, p1 interface{}, p2 int) {
	v := ctx.GetParam(0) // panics at runtime: "GetParam is unsupported for generic functions"
	_ = v
}
```

Nothing in the rule file, the hook function's own signature, or any build-time check stops this from compiling; the panic only fires when the instrumented `GenericFunc` is actually called at runtime.

### Expected behavior

At minimum, this should be documented clearly wherever hook-authoring is explained, so it isn't discovered only via a production panic. Ideally there's also some earlier signal — e.g. instrumentation-time validation that flags a hook function calling these methods when the target is generic, though this may be difficult given hook bodies aren't fully analyzed today.

### Relevant code path / file locations

- `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go:895-938` (`rewriteHookContextMethods`) — the genericity gate
- `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go:940-951` (`makeMethodPanic`) — the panic-body installer
- `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go:604-644` (`populateHookContext`) — confirms tool-generated code never calls these methods itself
- `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go:306-356` (`callBeforeHook`/`callAfterHook`) — confirms hook functions are called with positional args, not required to go through `ctx.GetParam`
- `tool/internal/instrument/testdata/golden/generic-functions/hook.go` — existing example hooks that happen to avoid this path, which is likely why it hasn't surfaced before

### Why this matters

This is a real, if narrow, correctness/DX gap: valid-looking hook code compiles cleanly and only fails at runtime, for a reason that isn't discoverable without already knowing this specific implementation detail. It's distinct from the already-tracked `HookContext` panic bugs (#916, #903 — both about `KeyData` type-assertion panics — and #726, about `SetParam(idx, nil)` silently dropping writes) — none of those concern the generic-target accessor-panic behavior.

### Suggested test cases

- A test confirming the current panic behavior is intentional and stable (i.e., a regression guard, not a "fix" test) — calling each of the four methods on a generic-target `HookContextImpl` and asserting the panic message.
- If documentation is added: no code test needed, but the golden testdata could include a comment noting why the example hooks avoid `ctx.GetParam`/etc.

### Possible direction (not a proposed implementation)

Not proposing a specific fix — supporting the accessor methods properly for generics would need real design work (the tool has no `go/types`-based mechanism today, per the earlier constraint-recovery investigation). The lower-cost option is documentation: state plainly, wherever hook-authoring conventions are documented, that these four methods panic for generic targets and hook authors should use the positional parameters instead.

items.title: bug(instrumentation/kafka-go): producer spans always end as Ok with meaningless duration when Writer.Async is true
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`AfterWriteMessages` in the kafka-go producer instrumentation ends every span created by `BeforeWriteMessages` using the error returned directly from `(*kafka.Writer).WriteMessages`. This assumes `WriteMessages` only returns after the write has actually completed (or failed) against the broker. That assumption is false whenever the writer is configured with `Async: true`.

In `github.com/segmentio/kafka-go` (`writer.go`), `WriteMessages` batches the messages and then:

```go
batches := w.batchMessages(msgs, assignments)
if w.Async {
    return nil
}
```

With `Async: true`, the call returns `nil` immediately after handing the messages to per-partition batch queues — the actual produce-to-broker happens later on background goroutines (`partitionWriter.writeBatch`). Any resulting error is only ever reported through the user-supplied `Writer.Completion` callback:

```go
// writer.go
Completion func(messages []Message, err error)
...
if ptw.w.Completion != nil {
    ptw.w.Completion(batch.msgs, err)
}
```

The instrumentation's `AfterWriteMessages` never hooks `Completion`, so for an async writer it always sees `err == nil` and ends every span as `codes.Ok`, essentially instantly.

### Environment

- Go Version: 1.23+
- kafka-go Version: v0.4.51 (instrumentation/github.com/segmentio/kafka-go/go.mod)

### To Reproduce

1. Configure a `kafka.Writer` with `Async: true` and a `Completion` callback.
2. Call `w.WriteMessages(ctx, msg)` in a project built with `otelc`.
3. `BeforeWriteMessages` starts a producer span for `msg`.
4. `WriteMessages` returns `nil` immediately (per `writer.go:667-669`, before the message is actually sent).
5. `AfterWriteMessages` is invoked with `err == nil` and ends the span as `codes.Ok` — before the message has even been dispatched to the broker, let alone acknowledged.
6. If the write subsequently fails (broker unreachable, leader not available, etc.), that failure is reported only via `Completion`, which the instrumentation never observes — the already-closed, already-Ok span has no way to reflect it.

This can be shown directly from the kafka-go source without needing a live broker: any test that instruments `WriteMessages` on an `Async: true` writer and asserts `AfterWriteMessages` fires before `Completion` (or before any injected transport delay/error resolves) demonstrates the gap, since `WriteMessages` unconditionally returns at line 668 without waiting on `batch.done`.

### Expected behavior

For an async writer, spans should not be finalized with a success status based on `WriteMessages`'s immediate (and essentially meaningless) return value. Either:
- the span shouldn't be ended until the actual produce result is known (via `Completion`), or
- at minimum, spans for async writes should be marked in a way that distinguishes "enqueued, delivery unknown" from "confirmed delivered", so consumers of the trace data don't read span duration/status as delivery latency/success.

### Additional context

Impact: for any application using kafka-go's `Async: true` mode — the standard configuration recommended by kafka-go itself for high-throughput producers — every producer span otelc emits is silently wrong: duration measures only local enqueue time (microseconds) rather than the actual Kafka round-trip, and status is always OK regardless of whether the broker write actually succeeds. This makes latency dashboards and error-rate alerting built on these spans meaningless for async producers, and is a correctness bug in a fairly common configuration, not an edge case.

Affected component: `instrumentation/github.com/segmentio/kafka-go/producer/producer_hook.go` (`BeforeWriteMessages`/`AfterWriteMessages`).

Suggested direction: when `w.Async` is true, wrap `w.Completion` (preserving any user-supplied callback) to end the pending spans there instead of in `AfterWriteMessages`, matching messages back to spans (e.g. by tracking span-per-message alongside a correlation key, since `Completion` receives the batch of `[]kafka.Message`). If matching messages back to spans reliably isn't feasible for all cases, an acceptable fallback is to at least avoid asserting `codes.Ok` for async writes and to annotate the span (e.g. an event or attribute) noting delivery confirmation is unavailable.
items.author: bhuvan-somisetty

items.title: fix(instrumentation/kafka-go): mark async producer spans and log otherwise-invisible async failures
items.body:
## Description

`kafka.Writer.WriteMessages` returns as soon as messages are enqueued when `Async` is true — before the broker write happens. `AfterWriteMessages` (in `instrumentation/github.com/segmentio/kafka-go/producer/producer_hook.go`) ends the producer spans created by `BeforeWriteMessages` using that immediate return value, so:

- Span duration only ever reflects local enqueue time (microseconds), never the actual Kafka round-trip.
- Any real delivery failure is reported later, solely through `Writer.Completion` — which this instrumentation never hooked — so such failures were invisible everywhere: not on the span, not in any log.

Verified against the real `kafka-go` v0.4.51 source: `WriteMessages` unconditionally returns `nil` at the `if w.Async { return nil }` early-return in `writer.go`, before any batch is awaited, and `Completion func(messages []Message, err error)` is the only place a delivery result for an async write surfaces.

## Root cause

The instrumentation assumed `WriteMessages`'s return value always reflects the outcome of the broker write. That's true for the default synchronous writer, but not for `Async: true`, which is kafka-go's documented high-throughput mode.

## Solution

- Added a `messaging.kafka.async` span attribute (`instrumentation/github.com/segmentio/kafka-go/semconv`), set on producer-send spans when the writer is async, so consumers of the trace data know duration and status here reflect hand-off, not confirmed delivery — never emitted for the sync path or for consumer spans.
- Wrapped `Writer.Completion` (`ensureAsyncFailureLogging`), installed once per `*kafka.Writer` and chaining any callback the caller already configured, so an async write failure is at least logged instead of silently disappearing.

I deliberately did **not** attempt full per-message span correlation through `Completion`. I considered it, but both realistic approaches have real problems:
- Correlating via the propagated trace context in message headers silently finds nothing when no `propagation.TextMapPropagator` is configured — which is the OTel SDK default.
- Adding a dedicated correlation header would work, but that header gets sent to the broker as part of the message and is then visible to every real Kafka consumer reading the topic, for the lifetime of that message — a bigger footprint than is justified here.

Given that, logging the failure (with the caller's own `Completion` still firing normally) is the honest, dependency-free improvement over the previous behavior, where these failures were entirely invisible.

## Testing

- `instrumentation/github.com/segmentio/kafka-go/producer`: added `TestBeforeWriteMessages_AsyncWriterMarksSpans`, `TestBeforeWriteMessages_SyncWriterOmitsAsyncAttr`, `TestEnsureAsyncFailureLogging_LogsFailureAndChainsOriginalCompletion` (asserts the failure is logged *and* the caller's own `Completion` still receives the real error), and `TestEnsureAsyncFailureLogging_WrapsOnce` (asserts a writer reused across multiple `WriteMessages` calls only gets one logging wrapper, not a new layer per call).
- `instrumentation/github.com/segmentio/kafka-go/semconv`: added `TestKafkaRequestTraceAttrs_ProducerAsync`, `TestKafkaRequestTraceAttrs_ProducerSyncOmitsAsync`, `TestKafkaRequestTraceAttrs_ConsumerIgnoresAsync`.
- `go test ./...` passes for both packages.

## Description

In `tool/internal/instrument/apply_raw.go`, `insertRaw()` parses and applies raw instrumentation rules to target functions. When a raw rule specifies a statement-matching regex pattern (`r.Pattern`), `insertRaw()` compiled the regular expression using `regexp.MustCompile(r.Pattern)`. This PR replaces `regexp.MustCompile(r.Pattern)` with `regexp.Compile(r.Pattern)` and returns a wrapped error if compilation fails. Unit tests have also been added in `apply_raw_test.go` to verify this error handling.

items.title: fix(ci): required done jobs pass when change detection fails
items.body:
### Describe

Several required workflow aggregate jobs treat skipped downstream jobs as success without first checking whether their `Detect Changes` job succeeded.

If `actions/checkout` or `dorny/paths-filter` fails in the `changes` job, the filtered downstream job is skipped because the filter output is missing. The final required `done` job then accepts that `skipped` result and exits successfully, so the required check can go green even though change detection failed.

Affected workflows:

- `.github/workflows/lint-golang.yaml`
- `.github/workflows/check-license-headers.yaml`
- `.github/workflows/verify-bundle.yaml`
- `.github/workflows/test-latestlibbuild.yaml`
- `.github/workflows/check-consistency.yaml`

### Expected behavior

The final required `done` job should:

- fail if `needs.changes.result != "success"`
- pass if change detection succeeds and the relevant filter output is explicitly `false`
- fail if the filter output is missing or unexpected
- require the downstream jobs to succeed when the filter output is `true`

This is already the pattern used by:

- `.github/workflows/test-unit.yaml`
- `.github/workflows/test-integration.yaml`
- `.github/workflows/test-e2e.yaml`

### Why this matters

These are required workflows. A change-detection infrastructure failure should not be hidden as an intentional path-filter skip.

### Reproduction

Using the current logic:

1. Make the `changes` job fail, for example by temporarily adding a failing step after checkout.
2. The filtered downstream job is skipped because the path-filter output is unavailable.
3. The final `done` job sees the downstream result as `skipped`.
4. The final job exits successfully.

This means the required check can pass even though change detection failed.

### Suggested fix

Update the five affected `done` jobs to follow the existing `test-unit`, `test-integration`, and `test-e2e` pattern:

- capture `needs.changes.result`
- capture the relevant `needs.changes.outputs.*` value
- fail when change detection failed
- pass only for an explicit `false` filter output
- fail on missing or unexpected filter output
- require all downstream jobs to succeed when the filter output is `true`

For `check-consistency.yaml`, require all four consistency jobs to succeed when `code == true`.

items.title: bug: k8s.informer span duration does not reflect actual handler execution time
items.body: ### Describe the bug The `k8s.informer..add` / `.update` / `.delete` spans created by the k8s.io/client-go instrumentation do not reflect the actual execution time of the registered event handler. The span wraps a call into the informer's own dispatch code, which only enqueues the notification onto each listener's channel. The real handler runs later, in a separate goroutine, outside the span entirely. I confirmed this by giving a handler a deliberate 500ms delay and the span duration did not change. ### Environment - OS: Ubuntu 22.04 (Jammy), x86_64 - Go Version: 1.26.0 - Version: built from main, commit 128eb42 (run `./otelc version` for the exact string if needed) ### To Reproduce Steps to reproduce the behavior: Small app using `k8s.io/client-go`'s fake clientset, a shared informer for Pods, and two `ResourceEventHandler`s registered with `AddEventHandler`: cat /tmp/k8s-repro/baseline/main.go 1. Build the app with otelc and run it, triggering a single Pod Add through the fake clientset: ```bash OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=console otelc go build -o app . OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=console ./app ``` Baseline run, no artificial delay: 2. Note the StartTime/EndTime on the printed k8s.informer.pod.add span. 3. Add a time.Sleep(500 * time.Millisecond) inside one handler before it does its real work: 4. Rebuild and run again: 5. Compare the span duration between the two runs. It does not change. I have a small repro app I can share if useful. Expected behavior If a registered handler takes real time to run, the span created for that event should reflect that. In this case the span duration stayed at roughly 12 microseconds in both runs, with and without the 500ms delay, so it is not measuring the handler's actual execution. Additional context This surfaced while discussing whether the k8s instrumentation should move from hooking internal processDeltas/processDeltasInBatch to hooking the public AddEventHandler API instead, since the internal functions have already broken across client-go versions once (see #875). While looking into that I also checked whether multiple registered handlers cause duplicate spans, since that came up as a concern from an earlier attempt at this. With two handlers registered on the same informer, I only see one k8s.informer.objects.process span and one k8s.informer.pod.add span per delta, so that specific problem does not reproduce against current main. It may have been specific to whatever that earlier attempt did differently.

### Description

The manifest generator accepts malformed `rule.version` ranges that are rejected during normal rule loading.

For example:

```yaml
rule:
  target: example.com/target
  version: v1.0.0,
```

Running:

```bash
go run ./tool/cmd/gen-manifest
```

successfully generates the manifest and writes:

```json
"versionRange": "v1.0.0,"
```

However, normal rule loading validates version ranges and rejects this malformed value.

### Expected behavior

Manifest generation should validate `rule.version` using the same validation logic as normal rule loading and return an error for malformed version ranges.

### Actual behavior

Manifest generation accepts malformed version ranges and includes them in `instrumentation-manifest.json`.

### Proposed fix

Validate `rule.version` while loading manifest entries, preferably by reusing the existing version-range validation helper.

Add regression tests covering:

* Rejection of malformed version ranges
* Acceptance of valid version ranges
* Propagation of a clear validation error

### Scope

I plan to keep the PR focused on:

* Validating manifest-side `rule.version` values
* Returning an error for malformed ranges
* Adding regression tests for valid and invalid version ranges

## Description
When instrumenting a method on a generic struct whose `type` definition is located in a different file of the same package (rather than in the same file as the method), `otelc` previously failed to resolve the type parameter constraints. This caused trampoline generation to either fall back to `any` or fail compilation when constraints referenced imported packages that were not present in the target file.
This PR introduces the following changes:
1. **Package File Discovery & Caching (`tool/internal/instrument/package_files.go`):**
   - Added `packageGoFiles()` to retrieve package `.go` files from `ip.compileArgs`.
   - Added `loadSiblingASTs()` to lazily parse and cache sibling package ASTs with `ast.ParseFileFast`.
   - Ensured deterministic sibling traversal by sorting map keys.
2. **Cross-file Constraint Recovery & Import Injection (`tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go`, `tool/internal/instrument/imports.go`):**
   - Added `resolveGenericTypeDecl()` to look up generic struct declarations across package sibling files when not found in the target file.
   - Added `injectConstraintImports()` to inspect constraint expressions, resolve their import paths via `imports.ResolveAlias()`, and inject missing imports into the target file AST and `importcfg` via `addRuleImports()`.
   - Refactored `findTargetGenericType()` to run once per rule at the top of `createTrampoline()` and propagate errors cleanly.
3. **Import Alias Helper (`tool/internal/imports/imports.go`):**
   - Added `ResolveAlias()` to look up the import path for a given alias or inferred package name within an AST file.
4. **Testing:**
   - Added unit tests in `package_files_test.go`, `trampoline_test.go`, and `imports_test.go`.
   - Added end-to-end golden test under `tool/internal/instrument/testdata/golden/generic-receiver-cross-file/`.
## Motivation
Fixes #1171
Generic receiver methods whose type declarations reside in sibling files could not recover constraints (e.g. `[T fmt.Stringer]`), leading to missing type parameters in trampoline functions or compilation failures when constraints required package imports in the target file.

items.title: [database/sql] Transaction Commit and Rollback spans are detached from distributed traces
items.body:
### Describe the bug

In `instrumentation/database/sql/client.go`, the instrumentation hooks for `Tx.Commit()` and `Tx.Rollback()` create new spans using `context.Background()` instead of the original transaction's context. Because they use an empty background context, the `commit` and `rollback` spans will not be linked to the parent trace, resulting in orphaned spans and broken distributed traces for database transactions.

### Environment

 - OS: All
 - Go Version: All
 - Version: `main` branch

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Instrument an application using `go.opentelemetry.io/otelc/instrumentation/database/sql`.
2. Begin a transaction using `db.BeginTx(ctx, nil)`.
3. Perform a query (`tx.ExecContext(ctx, ...)`).
4. Commit the transaction (`tx.Commit()`).
5. Observe the generated traces in your tracing backend (e.g. Jaeger).
6. **See error:** You will notice that the `COMMIT` span is not a child of the original trace context. It appears as an isolated, single-span trace.

**Code Pointers:**
In `instrumentation/database/sql/client.go`, the `beforeTxCommitInstrumentation` and `beforeTxRollbackInstrumentation` hooks hardcode `context.Background()`:
```go
// Line 515
func beforeTxCommitInstrumentation(ictx hook.HookContext, tx *sql.Tx) {
	// ...
	instrumentStart(ictx, context.Background(), "commit", "COMMIT", tx.Endpoint, tx.DriverName, tx.DSN, tx.DbName)
}

// Line 532
func beforeTxRollbackInstrumentation(ictx hook.HookContext, tx *sql.Tx) {
	// ...
	instrumentStart(ictx, context.Background(), "rollback", "ROLLBACK", tx.Endpoint, tx.DriverName, tx.DSN, tx.DbName)
}
```

### Expected behavior

The `COMMIT` and `ROLLBACK` spans should be correctly linked as children of the trace context in which the transaction was initiated (`BeginTx`), providing end-to-end visibility into the transaction's lifecycle.

### Additional context

**Impact:**
Any application relying on compile-time instrumentation for distributed tracing will have broken, detached spans for transaction finalization. This pollutes trace backends with orphaned traces and deprives developers of complete transaction latency visibility.

**Proposed Solution:**
1. In `instrumentation/database/sql/otelc.yaml`, update the `add_new_field_tx` directive to inject a new context field (e.g., `OtelCtx context.Context`) into the `Tx` struct.
2. In `client.go`, modify `beforeTxInstrumentation` (which hooks `BeginTx` and receives the transaction's context) to store the original `ctx` in `ictx`.
3. In `afterTxInstrumentation`, retrieve the context from `ictx` and assign it to the newly injected `tx.OtelCtx`.
4. In `beforeTxCommitInstrumentation` and `beforeTxRollbackInstrumentation`, use `tx.OtelCtx` instead of `context.Background()` to start the span (falling back to `context.Background()` only if `tx.OtelCtx` is nil).

items.title: fix(pkg): preserve trace context in database/sql transactions
items.body:
## Description
This PR fixes an issue where database spans generated during a transaction (such as `START TRANSACTION`, `INSERT`, `COMMIT`, or `ROLLBACK`) were orphaned and disconnected from their parent HTTP server trace.

The root cause was that `tx.Commit()` and `tx.Rollback()` in `database/sql` do not take a `context.Context` parameter, causing the `otelc` tracing hooks to fallback to `context.Background()`. 

To fix this, we've utilized `otelc`'s code injection capabilities to extend the `sql.Tx` struct:
- Added an `OtelCtx context.Context` field to `database/sql.Tx` via `instrumentation/database/sql/otelc.yaml`.
- Modified `beforeTxInstrumentation` to save the parent context inside the hook data map.
- Modified `afterTxInstrumentation` to inject the parent context into the newly initialized `*sql.Tx` instance.
- Modified `beforeTxCommitInstrumentation` and `beforeTxRollbackInstrumentation` to use `tx.OtelCtx` as the active context instead of falling back to `context.Background()`.

An E2E test `TestHTTPServerDBClient_Transaction` has been added to verify that trace IDs remain consistent across the transaction boundaries and span parenting correctly follows the HTTP server root span.

## Motivation

Database transaction spans were incorrectly creating disjointed traces instead of being grouped under the active parent HTTP trace. Preserving the context in the `sql.Tx` struct allows end-to-end trace correlation and correctly associates subsequent queries and commits to the original caller.

Fixes #1187
