items.title: bug(tool/internal/setup): quoted -mod=readonly in GOFLAGS is overridden by forceModMod
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`forceModMod()` in `tool/internal/setup/vendor.go` parses `GOFLAGS` with `strings.Fields()` before checking whether a `-mod` flag is already present.

Go accepts quoted `GOFLAGS` tokens, including a value such as:

```text
'-mod=readonly'
```

However, `strings.Fields()` leaves the quote characters attached to the token. As a result, `forceModMod()` does not recognize `'-mod=readonly'` as a `-mod` token and concludes that no module-mode flag was supplied.

It then appends `-mod=mod`, producing:

```text
'-mod=readonly' -mod=mod
```

Because repeated Go flags are last-value-wins, this changes the effective setting from `readonly` to `mod`.

This also conflicts with the function's documented behavior: `-mod=readonly` is intentionally supposed to be preserved because it already disables automatic vendoring while respecting the user's module-mode choice.

### Environment

- OS: Linux 7.1.9-arch1-2 x86_64 GNU/Linux
- Go Version: go1.27.0 linux/amd64
- Version: current `main` at 790631ccc042ba719239f3d0f89a2f3efb2ea6ef

### To Reproduce

1. Confirm that the Go command accepts the quoted token:

```bash
GOFLAGS="'-mod=readonly'" go list ./...
```

2. Add this temporary regression test in package `setup`:

```go
func TestQuotedReadonlyGoflagsRepro(t *testing.T) {
    assert.Equal(
        t,
        "'-mod=readonly'",
        forceModMod("'-mod=readonly'"),
    )
}
```

3. Run:

```bash
go test ./tool/internal/setup -run TestQuotedReadonlyGoflagsRepro -count=1 -v
```

4. The test fails because the current result is:

```text
'-mod=readonly' -mod=mod
```

instead of:

```text
'-mod=readonly'
```

### Expected behavior

Quoted `GOFLAGS` tokens should be interpreted using the same tokenization semantics as the Go command.

A quoted `-mod=readonly` token should be detected as an existing module-mode flag and left unchanged, just like an unquoted `-mod=readonly` token.

Similarly, quoted forms of supported `-mod` values should behave consistently with their unquoted forms.

### Additional context

The repository already contains quote-aware `GOFLAGS` tokenization in `tool/util/go.go` (`splitGoflags`), used by `StripToolexecFromGoflags`.

A possible direction would be to factor out or reuse the quote-aware tokenization and matching outer-quote removal already used by StripToolexecFromGoflags, instead of using strings.Fields() in forceModMod(), with regression tests for quoted -mod tokens.

I searched the repository's existing issues and pull requests for this quoted `GOFLAGS` / `forceModMod` behavior and did not find a matching report.

items.title: bug(tool): make package depends on host execute bits, so Verify Bundle differs between /mnt/c and ext4
items.body:
## Description:

On latest `main`, `make package` produces different `tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz` bytes depending on whether the repository is built from a `/mnt/c` checkout or a native Linux/ext4 checkout.

Under `/mnt/c`, DrvFS reports regular source files as executable (`0777`), so the bundle tool writes many archive entries as `0755`. The same commit built from ext4 writes those same files as `0644`. The tracked source content is identical, but the archive differs, so `Verify Bundle` fails.

## Steps to Reproduce:

1. Check out `main` at `790631ccc`.
2. From PowerShell in the repository root, run:
   ```powershell
   $repo = (wsl wslpath -a ((Get-Location).Path -replace '\', '/')).Trim()

   $script = @"
   set -euo pipefail

   cd '$repo'
   make package >/dev/null
   echo 'drvfs hash:'
   sha256sum tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz
   echo 'drvfs sample:'
   tar tvzf tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz | sed -n '1,4p'

   rm -rf /tmp/otelci-bundle-mode-repro
   git clone https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation /tmp/otelci-bundle-mode-repro >/dev/null 2>&1
   cd /tmp/otelci-bundle-mode-repro
   git checkout 790631ccc >/dev/null 2>&1
   make package >/dev/null
   echo 'ext4 hash:'
   sha256sum tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz
   echo 'ext4 sample:'
   tar tvzf tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz | sed -n '1,4p'

   echo 'source mode on drvfs:'
   stat -c '%a %n' '$repo/pkg/runtime/otel_setup.go'
   echo 'source mode on ext4:'
   stat -c '%a %n' /tmp/otelci-bundle-mode-repro/pkg/runtime/otel_setup.go
   "@

   wsl bash -lc $script
   ```

## Actual Behavior:

The repro prints different bundle hashes and different file modes for the same tracked file content.

Example output:
```text
drvfs hash:
240fdf34f9f90eb19e80e5160dad7a139e82f936c892a71dcf19efd6b98e3cd2  tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz
drvfs sample:
drwxr-xr-x 0/0               0 1970-01-01 00:00 instrumentation_temp/
drwxr-xr-x 0/0               0 1970-01-01 00:00 instrumentation_temp/database/
drwxr-xr-x 0/0               0 1970-01-01 00:00 instrumentation_temp/database/sql/
-rwxr-xr-x 0/0           17703 1970-01-01 00:00 instrumentation_temp/database/sql/client.go

ext4 hash:
3a47482852281260c0425e216cb47f85f5cf490d598c196eeed4a0812a99f18d  tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz
ext4 sample:
drwxr-xr-x 0/0               0 1970-01-01 00:00 instrumentation_temp/
drwxr-xr-x 0/0               0 1970-01-01 00:00 instrumentation_temp/database/
drwxr-xr-x 0/0               0 1970-01-01 00:00 instrumentation_temp/database/sql/
-rw-r--r-- 0/0           17703 1970-01-01 00:00 instrumentation_temp/database/sql/client.go

source mode on drvfs:
777 /mnt/c/.../pkg/runtime/otel_setup.go
source mode on ext4:
644 /tmp/otelci-bundle-mode-repro/pkg/runtime/otel_setup.go
```

So the bundle depends on the checkout filesystem’s execute-bit behavior, not just on the tracked source.

## Expected Behavior:

`make package` should produce the same `tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz` bytes for the same commit regardless of whether the checkout is on `/mnt/c` or on native Linux/ext4.

A Windows-mounted DrvFS checkout should not cause ordinary source files to be archived as `0755` when the same files from ext4 are archived as `0644`.

## Notes:

- `.tools/bundle/main.go` currently normalizes regular-file mode based on `hdr.Mode&0o111`.
- On `/mnt/c`, `tar.FileInfoHeader(...)` sees many regular source files as executable because DrvFS exposes them as `0777`.
- That causes `normalizeHeader` to write `0755` into the archive for ordinary `.go`, `go.mod`, `go.sum`, `yaml`, and `md` files.
- This makes `Verify Bundle` fail for contributors who regenerate `tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz` from a `/mnt/c` checkout, even when source content is otherwise correct.
- This is separate from #1123, which was about untracked junk files like `.DS_Store` entering the archive.

items.title: feat(tool): support minimum otelc version in rule files
items.body:
## Description

Adds support for declaring the minimum required `otelc` version in each rule file using a reserved top-level key:

```yaml
version: "v1.0.0"
```

This PR:

* Adds a shared parser for separating file-level version metadata from rule entries.
* Validates that minimum versions are released semantic versions.
* Rejects rule files that require a newer released `otelc` version.
* Skips compatibility checks for development and pseudo-version compiler builds.
* Treats unversioned rule files as requiring `v1.0.0` and emits a warning.
* Applies version handling to runtime rule loading, automatic pinning, manifest generation, and test utilities.
* Updates existing rule files to declare `version: "v1.0.0"`.
* Updates the documentation and embedded instrumentation bundle.
* Adds tests covering explicit versions, legacy files, malformed requirements, unsupported versions, and development builds.

## Motivation

Rule files can evolve to use features that older `otelc` releases do not understand. Without an explicit compatibility requirement, an older compiler may attempt to process a newer rule file and fail with an unclear parsing error or unexpected behavior.

A per-file minimum version provides users with an early, actionable compatibility error while keeping rule files self-contained. It also preserves compatibility with existing unversioned files through the `v1.0.0` fallback.

Fixes #1261

items.title: bug(tool/ast): handle import alias collisions gracefully and enforce strict import matching in `typename.go`
items.body:
### Problem Description

In `tool/internal/ast/typename.go`, package import resolution and AST type matching exhibit two edge-case issues:

1. **Import Alias Collisions:** `ImportAliasMap` maps default package aliases to import paths. When a source file contains multiple unaliased imports that share a default alias (such as `import "text/template"` and `import "html/template"`), `aliases[alias] = path` silently overwrites earlier entries with whichever import appears last. Consequently, calls to `MatchesTypeName` for types in the overwritten package fail or match against the wrong import path.
2. **Fallback Matching under Import Context:** In `parsedTypeName.matches` (`*dst.SelectorExpr`), when `imports` context is provided (`imports != nil`), failing to find `ident.Name` in `imports` falls through to path-tail matching (`defaultImportAlias(t.importPath) == ident.Name`). When explicit import context is available, missing a key in `imports` indicates that `ident.Name` is not that imported package, so falling back to tail matching can cause false-positive matches on unimported packages or local variables.

### Proposed Fix / Solution

- **Disambiguate Collisions in `ImportAliasMap`:** Track whether an import alias is explicitly set (`imp.Name != nil`). If multiple unaliased imports collide on a default alias, remove the ambiguous default alias from `aliases` so unaliased references do not resolve to an arbitrary import. Explicit aliases take precedence.
- **Strict Import Context Checking:** In `parsedTypeName.matches`, if `imports != nil` and `ident.Name` is not present in `imports`, return `false` immediately. Preserve path-tail fallback only when `imports == nil` (for synthetic/test AST nodes).

### Reproducer / Unit Tests

We have implemented and verified tests in `tool/internal/ast/typename_test.go`:
- `TestImportAliasMap_CollidingDefaultAliases`
- `TestTypeNameMatches_StrictImportContext`

items.body:
## Description

Fixes #1271.

This PR addresses two edge-case issues in `tool/internal/ast/typename.go`:

1. **Import Alias Collisions:** `ImportAliasMap` previously mapped default package aliases to import paths without checking for collisions. When a source file contained multiple unaliased imports sharing a default alias (e.g. `import "text/template"` and `import "html/template"`), `aliases[alias] = path` silently overwrote earlier entries. We now track explicit vs default aliases and exclude ambiguous default aliases from the map so unaliased references do not resolve to an arbitrary import.
2. **Strict Import Context Matching:** In `parsedTypeName.matches` (`*dst.SelectorExpr`), when `imports` context is provided (`imports != nil`), failing to locate `ident.Name` in `imports` now returns `false` immediately instead of falling through to path-tail matching on unimported packages or local variables.

## Verification / Unit Tests

- `TestImportAliasMap_CollidingDefaultAliases`

All tool package tests pass cleanly (`go test ./tool/...`).

items.title: fix(tool/ast): ensure file handle closure on panic in ast.WriteFile and importcfg.WriteFile
items.body:
### Problem Description

In `tool/internal/ast/parser.go` (`ast.writeFile`) and `tool/internal/imports/importcfg.go` (`ImportConfig.writeFile`), file writing functions invoke `w.Close()` after completing write operations without using `defer`.

If an unhandled panic occurs during writing (for instance, if an injected AST node is malformed or an internal formatting failure occurs), execution escapes before `w.Close()` is reached. This leaves open file descriptors on the operating system until garbage collection runs.

### Proposed Fix / Solution

Refactor both `ast.writeFile` and `ImportConfig.writeFile` to defer `w.Close()`:
- Use `defer` immediately upon entry so `w.Close()` is guaranteed to execute under all circumstances (normal return, error return, or panic).
- Capture close errors on successful writes and preserve original write errors when both fail.

### Reproducer / Unit Tests

Added panic-safety unit tests in `parser_test.go` and `importcfg_test.go` (`TestWriteFile_PanicSafety`) using mock writers that panic on `Write`, confirming `Close()` is executed under panic conditions.

items.title: bug(tool): preserve import context in call and raw template helpers
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`FuncArgumentOfType` and `FuncReturnOfType` do not reliably resolve types in call-rule and raw-rule templates when the target file uses aliased imports or when multiple packages share the same default package name.

The issue is caused by import context being dropped when creating `funcTemplateData`.

In `compileExpression`, the enclosing function is passed with `nil` imports:

```go
data.enclosing = newFuncTemplateData(enclosing, nil, nil, "")
```

Although `applyCallReplace` already has the target file's `importAliases`, they are not passed into `compileExpression`.

The same issue exists in `renderRawCode`, which also creates `funcTemplateData` with `nil` imports.

This differs from directive rules, which correctly pass `ast.ImportAliasMap(root)` into `newFuncTemplateData`.

As a result, `FuncArgumentOfType` / `FuncReturnOfType` may produce incorrect matches because `ast.MatchesTypeName` cannot resolve import aliases or distinguish packages with the same default package name.

For example:

```go
import althttp "net/http"

func Handler(r *althttp.Request) {
    http.Get("url")
}
```

With a call-rule template using:

```text
{{ .FuncArgumentOfType "*net/http.Request" }}
```

the expected result is `r`, but the current call-rule path can return an empty result because the `althttp` import alias is not available to the template data.

The same problem can cause incorrect matches when packages have the same final path component, such as `text/template` and `html/template`.

### Environment

* OS: Any
* Go Version: Any supported version
* OpenTelemetry Go compile-time instrumentation version: `release/main` (current development tree)

### To Reproduce

1. Create a target Go file that uses an aliased import:

```go
package main

import althttp "net/http"

func Handler(r *althttp.Request) {
    http.Get("url")
}
```

2. Create a call-rule with a `replace` template that uses `FuncArgumentOfType`:

```yaml
replace: 'traced({{ .FuncArgumentOfType "*net/http.Request" }}, {{ . }})'
```

3. Apply the instrumentation to the target file.

4. Observe that `FuncArgumentOfType` does not resolve `*net/http.Request` to the `r` parameter as expected.

The same behavior can be reproduced with `FuncReturnOfType` and with raw rules using these template helpers.

### Expected behavior

`FuncArgumentOfType` and `FuncReturnOfType` should resolve types using the import map of the target Go file, regardless of whether they are used through directive, call, or raw rules.

For the example above:

```text
{{ .FuncArgumentOfType "*net/http.Request" }}
```

should resolve to:

```text
r
```

Aliased imports should be resolved to their actual package paths, and packages with identical default names should be correctly distinguished.

### Additional context

The underlying type-matching logic already supports import resolution. Existing tests for `funcTemplateData` verify that aliased imports are handled correctly when the import map is provided.

The problem is in the wiring of the call-rule and raw-rule paths:

* `applyCallReplace` already has `importAliases`, but `compileExpression` does not receive them.
* `compileExpression` creates `funcTemplateData` with `nil` imports.
* `renderRawCode` also creates `funcTemplateData` with `nil` imports.
* Directive rules already pass the target file's import map correctly.

This suggests the fix should be localized to passing the target file's import context through the call/raw template paths.

Integration tests should cover at least:

* aliased imports such as `althttp "net/http"`
* packages with the same default package name, such as `text/template` vs `html/template`
* both `FuncArgumentOfType` and `FuncReturnOfType`
* call-rule and raw-rule template paths

items.title: fix(pkg/runtime): treat a parses-to-empty OTEL_GO_ENABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS as no allowlist
items.body:
## Description

`Instrumented` gated the enabled-list check on the raw environment string being non-empty, then compared the target instrumentation against the parsed names:

```go
enabledList := os.Getenv("OTEL_GO_ENABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS")
if enabledList != "" {
    enabled := parseInstrumentationList(enabledList)
    if !slices.Contains(enabled, name) {
        return false
    }
}
```

A value that is non-empty but parses to nothing, for example `","`, `",,"`, or `"  "`, makes `enabledList != ""` true while `parseInstrumentationList` returns an empty slice (it drops empty and whitespace-only items). `slices.Contains(nil, name)` is then false for every instrumentation, so the function returns false and disables all instrumentation.

The fix gates on the parsed list length instead of the raw string, so an allowlist only restricts when it actually names something. A malformed-but-nonempty value is treated the same as an unset one, and instrumentation stays enabled.

```go
enabled := parseInstrumentationList(os.Getenv("OTEL_GO_ENABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS"))
if len(enabled) > 0 && !slices.Contains(enabled, name) {
    return false
}
```

The disabled-list path already behaves correctly for the same input (an empty parsed list means `slices.Contains` is false, so nothing is disabled), so it is unchanged.

## Tests

`TestInstrumented` gains two cases: a comma-only value and a whitespace-only value both keep instrumentation enabled. I verified they fail against current `main` and pass with this change.

Fixes #1254

items.title: fix(tool): close the output file via defer in ast and importcfg writeFile
items.body:
## Description

`ast.writeFile` (`tool/internal/ast/parser.go`) and `ImportConfig.writeFile` (`tool/internal/imports/importcfg.go`) called `Close()` only after the write finished:

```go
func writeFile(w writeCloser, ...) error {
    if err := <write>(w, ...); err != nil {
        _ = w.Close()
        return ex.Wrapf(err, "failed to write ...")
    }
    if err := w.Close(); err != nil {
        return ex.Wrapf(err, "failed to close ...")
    }
    return nil
}
```

If the write panics (a malformed injected AST node, an internal formatting failure), execution escapes before either `Close()` runs, leaking the file descriptor until GC.

Both functions now close via `defer` with a named return, so the descriptor is released on a normal return, an error return, or a panic. A close error is reported only when the write itself succeeded, so the original write error is preserved. Behavior is unchanged on the normal, write-error, and close-error paths.

## Tests

Each package gains `TestWriteFile_PanicSafety`, using the existing `mockWriteCloser` extended to panic on `Write` and record whether `Close` ran. The test asserts the file is closed even when writing panics. I verified both fail against current `main` and pass with this change.

This is tool-only; no bundle regeneration is required.

Fixes #1275

items.title: fix(tool/internal/setup): recognize quoted -mod tokens in GOFLAGS
items.body:
## Description

`forceModMod` in `tool/internal/setup/vendor.go` split `GOFLAGS` with `strings.Fields` and matched the raw tokens. The go command accepts quoted `GOFLAGS` tokens such as `'-mod=readonly'`, and the surrounding quotes stayed attached to the token, so `isModToken` did not recognize it as a `-mod` flag.

`forceModMod` then concluded no module-mode flag was present and appended `-mod=mod`, producing:

```text
'-mod=readonly' -mod=mod
```

Because Go applies last-value-wins for a repeated flag, the effective mode flipped from `readonly` to `mod`, overriding the user's choice and defeating the function's own documented intent to preserve `-mod=readonly` (which already disables vendoring).

The fix matches on the unquoted form of each token, via a small `unquoteGoflagsToken` helper that strips one pair of surrounding matching quotes the way the go command does, while keeping the original token in the output. A quoted `-mod` flag is now recognized and preserved verbatim, and a quoted `-mod=vendor` is still rewritten to `-mod=mod`.

## Tests

`TestForceModMod` gains cases for single- and double-quoted `-mod=readonly` (preserved), a quoted `-mod` among other flags (preserved), and a quoted `-mod=vendor` (still overridden). I verified they fail against current `main` and pass with this change. This is tool-only; no bundle regeneration is required.

Fixes #1267

items.title: bug(tool/internal/instrument): ctx.GetParam/GetReturnVal panics when the target function is generic
items.body:
### Describe the bug

If you write a rule that hooks a generic function (one with a type parameter, like `func Query[T any](...)`), calling `ctx.GetParam()`, `ctx.SetParam()`, `ctx.GetReturnVal()`, or `ctx.SetReturnVal()` inside your hook panics at runtime, no matter what index you pass. These four methods seem to be hardcoded to panic for any generic target instead of actually doing anything.

### Environment

- OS: Windows 11
- Version: current `main` branch

### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Add a generic function to instrument:
```go
func Query[T any](ctx context.Context, query string) (T, error) {
    var zero T
    return zero, nil
}
```
2. Add a hook rule targeting it:
```yaml
query_hook:
  target: mypkg
  where:
    func: Query
  do:
    - inject_hooks:
        after: AfterQuery
        path: "myinstrumentation"
```
3. In the hook, try to read the return value the normal way:
```go
func AfterQuery(ctx hook.HookContext, ret error) {
    err, _ := ctx.GetReturnVal(1).(error)
    if err != nil {
        // record error on span
    }
}
```
4. Build and run the app, and call `Query`.

### Expected behavior

Expected `GetReturnVal`/`GetParam` to just work and give me the value, same as it does for non-generic functions.

### Additional context

Actual output:
```
panic: GetReturnVal is unsupported for generic functions
```

There's a workaround: skip `GetReturnVal`/`GetParam` and just add the value as a plain parameter on the hook function itself (it comes through as `interface{}`). That works, but it's not how any other hook in this repo is written, they all use `GetParam`/`GetReturnVal`, so this is easy to trip over.

Looks like this comes from `tool/internal/instrument/trampoline.go`, in `rewriteHookContextMethods` , when the target function is generic, it swaps all 4 methods for a hardcoded panic instead of generating real code. Might only be worth fixing for the simple case (return/param type is the plain type parameter itself, not something like `[]T` or `map[string]T`) since that part looks a lot trickier.

items.title: fix(runtime): restore default OS signal disposition in handleShutdownSignal
items.body:
### Problem
In `pkg/runtime/setup.go`, `setupSignalHandler()` registers a signal channel via `signal.Notify(sigCh, shutdownSignals()...)`.

When a signal arrives (`SIGINT` or `SIGTERM`), `handleShutdownSignal()` calls `signal.Stop(sigCh)` and flushes the OpenTelemetry SDK. However, `signal.Stop` only stops relaying incoming signals to `sigCh`; it does **not** restore the default OS signal disposition (`SIG_DFL`).

Because neither `signal.Reset(...)` nor process exit is called, standard Go applications that rely on default signal handling swallow the first `Ctrl+C` or `SIGTERM` signal, keeping the application process alive until a second signal is sent.

### Proposed Fix
Call `signal.Reset(shutdownSignals()...)` in `handleShutdownSignal()` immediately after `signal.Stop(sigCh)` to restore default OS signal behavior.

### Target Branch & PR
Branch `fix/signal-handler-reset` pushed to origin:
https://github.com/vedant21-oss/opentelemetry-go-compile-instrumentation/pull/new/fix/signal-handler-reset
items.author: vedant21-oss

items.title: fix(runtime): restore default OS signal disposition in handleShutdownSignal
items.body:
## Description

In `pkg/runtime/setup.go`, `handleShutdownSignal` flushes OpenTelemetry telemetry upon receiving `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM`. However, after calling `signal.Stop(sigCh)`, `signal.Reset(...)` was omitted. This left the signal handler trapped in Go runtime, swallowing the initial `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM` signal in standard Go applications.

- Added `signal.Reset(shutdownSignals()...)` in `handleShutdownSignal` immediately after `signal.Stop(sigCh)` so default OS signal disposition (`SIG_DFL`) takes over if the host application does not manage signal handling.
- Added unit test `TestHandleShutdownSignalResetsSignalHandler` in `pkg/runtime/setup_test.go` to verify signal handler reset behavior.
- Re-packaged `tool/data/otelc-bundle.tgz` to keep the embedded runtime bundle up to date.

## Motivation

Without calling `signal.Reset(shutdownSignals()...)`, standard Go applications that do not register custom signal handlers swallow the initial `Ctrl+C` or `SIGTERM` signal instead of terminating as expected under standard OS process behavior.

Fixes #1282

items.title: fix(tool/internal/instrument): stop GetParam/GetReturnVal panicking for ordinary params on generic functions
items.body:
## Description

Fixes #1280.

`rewriteHookContextMethods` blanket-panicked all four `HookContextImpl` accessor methods (`GetParam`, `SetParam`, `GetReturnVal`, `SetReturnVal`) whenever the target function had a type parameter, even for parameters/return values whose own type has nothing to do with the generic. For example:

```go
func Query[T any](ctx context.Context, query string) (T, error)
```

Calling `ctx.GetReturnVal(1)` to read the `error` panicked with `"GetReturnVal is unsupported for generic functions"`, even though index 1 is an ordinary `error`.

## Fix

Only the slots whose type actually mentions the type parameter (bare `T`, or nested in something like `*GenStruct[T]`) now panic, per-index, with a message naming that index. Every other slot generates the exact same accessor code as a non-generic function.

This is intentionally scoped to the common case: a parameter/return value whose type mentions a type parameter still isn't readable via `GetParam`/`GetReturnVal` (that would need type information that isn't in scope in `HookContextImpl`'s own, non-generic methods), so those indices still panic — just individually instead of taking every other parameter down with them.

## Testing

- Added `TestReferencesTypeParameter` covering the new helper (bare type param, pointer/slice/generic-instantiated composites, unrelated concrete types, nil inputs).
- Updated the `generic-functions` and `generic-before-only` golden fixtures to the new expected output.
- `go test ./tool/...` passes.

items.title: bug(instrumentation/log): messages mentioning trace_id skip correlation injection
items.body:
### Describe the bug

The standard-library `log` instrumentation does not append correlation fields when a log message merely contains the text `trace_id`.

`BeforeLogOutput` currently uses `strings.Contains(string(b), "trace_id")` to determine whether a trace ID is already present. Therefore, a message such as `could not parse trace_id header` is treated as though it already contains a `trace_id=<value>` field. Both the active trace ID and span ID are omitted.

  ### Environment

  - OS: Windows (`windows/amd64`)
  - Go Version: `go1.25.5`
  - Version: commit `3d3d71e1786fb29120a0ce41913ae688fefe266d`

  ### To Reproduce

  1. Add the following temporary test to `instrumentation/log/log_hook_test.go`:

  ```go
  func TestBeforeLogOutput_TraceIDMention(t *testing.T) {
        runtime.RegisterTraceAndSpanIDFunc(func() (string, string) {
                return "abc123", "def456"
        })
        t.Cleanup(func() {
                runtime.RegisterTraceAndSpanIDFunc(func() (string, string) {
                        return "", ""
                })
        })

        ictx := hooktest.NewMockHookContext()
        originalAppend := func(b []byte) []byte {
                return append(b, []byte("could not parse trace_id header\n")...)
        }

        BeforeLogOutput(ictx, nil, 0, 0, originalAppend)

        wrapped := ictx.GetParam(3).(func([]byte) []byte)
        result := string(wrapped(nil))

        assert.Contains(t, result, "trace_id=abc123")
        assert.Contains(t, result, "span_id=def456")
  }
  ```

  2. Run:

  ```console
  cd instrumentation/log
  go test -run '^TestBeforeLogOutput_TraceIDMention$' -count=1 .
  ```

  3. The test fails because the result is only:

  ```text
  could not parse trace_id header
  ```

  ### Expected behavior

  A message that only mentions `trace_id` as ordinary text should still receive the active correlation fields:

  ```text
  could not parse trace_id header trace_id=abc123 span_id=def456
  ```

 Injection should only be skipped when the output already contains an actual trace correlation field, rather than whenever the `trace_id` substring occurs.

  ### Additional context

  The early return occurs in `instrumentation/log/log_hook.go`:

  ```go
  if strings.Contains(string(b), traceIDKey) {
        return b
  }
  ```
The existing `TestBeforeLogOutput_AlreadyContainsTraceID` test covers a real `trace_id=existing` field but does not cover an ordinary message containing the same substring.

 ### Proposed implementation

I have a local prototype that narrows the existing check from the bare `trace_id` substring to the field marker `trace_id=`. This preserves the current behavior for messages that already contain a trace ID while allowing ordinary text such as `could not parse trace_id header` to receive the active `trace_id` and `span_id`.

The prototype also adds a regression test next to `TestBeforeLogOutput_AlreadyContainsTraceID` covering a message that mentions `trace_id` without containing a correlation field.

I noticed that #1215 proposes an allocation-focused refactor of the same hook and states that its behavior should remain unchanged. Could a maintainer confirm whether this behavioral correction should be submitted separately before #1215, or coordinated with that work? I will wait for maintainer confirmation on the preferred direction before opening a PR.

items.title: bug(instrumentation/redis): Client.Conn commands emit duplicate spans
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Commands executed through `redis.Client.Conn()` produce two Redis client spans instead of one.

The parent `redis.Client` receives an OpenTelemetry hook when it is created. go-redis then clones the parent's hooks when `Client.Conn()` creates a dedicated connection. However, the compile instrumentation also injects `afterClientConnV9`, which adds another OpenTelemetry hook to the connection.

As a result, both hooks process the same command. The additional span also has a malformed endpoint because `afterClientConnV9` passes `client.String()` instead of a `host:port` address.

  ### Environment

  - OS: Windows (`windows/amd64`)
  - Go version: `go1.25.5`
  - Repository version: commit `3d3d71e1786fb29120a0ce41913ae688fefe266d`
  - go-redis version: `v9.22.0`

  ### To Reproduce

  Add this temporary test under `instrumentation/github.com/redis/go-redis/v9`:

  ```go
  package v9

  import (
        "context"
        "errors"
        "net"
        "sync"
        "testing"

        "github.com/redis/go-redis/v9"
        "github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
  )

  func TestClientConnEmitsSingleSpan(t *testing.T) {
        initOnce = *new(sync.Once)
        t.Setenv("OTEL_GO_ENABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS", "redis")
        sr := setupTestTracer(t)

        client := redis.NewClient(&redis.Options{
                Addr:       "localhost:6379",
                MaxRetries: -1,
                Dialer: func(context.Context, string, string) (net.Conn, error) {
                        return nil, errors.New("dial failed")
                },
        })
        t.Cleanup(func() { _ = client.Close() })

        afterNewRedisClientV9(nil, client)

        conn := client.Conn()
        afterClientConnV9(nil, conn)
        _ = conn.Get(context.Background(), "key").Err()

        require.Len(t, sr.Ended(), 1)
  }
  ```

  Run:

  ```console
  cd instrumentation/github.com/redis/go-redis/v9
  go test -run '^TestClientConnEmitsSingleSpan$' -count=1 -v .
  ```

  The assertion fails because two spans are recorded:

  ```text
  expected 1 item, got 2
  ```

  The recorded endpoints are:

  ```text
  server.address = "Redis<localhost:6379 db:0>"
  server.address = "localhost"
  server.port = 6379
  ```

  ### Expected behavior

  One Redis client command executed through `Client.Conn()` should produce one client span with:

  ```text
  server.address = "localhost"
  server.port = 6379
  ```

  ### Additional context

`afterNewRedisClientV9` installs the hook on the parent client. In go-redis, `Client.Conn()` passes the parent's hook mixin to `newConn`, which clones those hooks. The separate `redis_client_hook` rule then injects `afterClientConnV9` and adds a second hook.

A post-merge review comment on #292 already noted that `Conn.String()` is not a valid endpoint, but I could not find an issue or pull request tracking the duplicate spans.

Would limiting the explicit `Client.Conn()` hook rule to versions before go-redis v9.9.0 be the appropriate compatibility boundary?

 ### Proposed implementation

  I have a local implementation ready that limits the explicit `Client.Conn()` hook rule to go-redis versions before v9.9.0.

Starting with go-redis v9.9.0, `Client.Conn()` clones the parent client's hooks, so injecting another hook after `Conn()` creates the duplicate span. Versions through v9.8.x do not inherit those hooks and still require the explicit rule.

The implementation adds the `v9.0.0,v9.9.0` version boundary, exercises `Client.Conn()` in the Redis integration application, and asserts that one `GET` command produces exactly one span with the correct `server.address` and `server.port`.

  I will wait for maintainer confirmation on this version-gated approach before opening a PR.

items.title: refactor(instrumentation/k8s.io/client-go): cache GVK lookup per object type
items.body:
## Description

`getObjectInfo` calls `scheme.Scheme.ObjectKinds` on every `OnAdd`/`OnUpdate`/`OnDelete` event to resolve the object's GroupVersionKind. That's a reflection-based registry scan, running in the informer's hottest path, even though a given informer only ever watches a single Go type for its lifetime, so the result never changes between events for that informer.

This caches the GVK lookup per `reflect.Type`, computed once and reused for every subsequent event of that type.

Suggested by @amazingakai on #1183, independent of the open question in that thread about moving span creation to hook `AddEventHandler` instead of the internal `processDeltas`/`processDeltasInBatch` functions. This is scoped to only the caching improvement so it doesn't need to wait on that decision.

## Changes

- `lookupGVK` caches the result of `scheme.Scheme.ObjectKinds` in a `sync.Map`, keyed by `reflect.Type`.
- Both hits and misses are cached. An unregistered type resolves the same way on every call, so caching the miss avoids re-scanning, and re-logging, for a type that will never resolve.
- `objectKindsFunc` indirects the real `scheme.Scheme.ObjectKinds` so tests can substitute a counting stub, proving the cache actually avoids repeat lookups rather than only asserting the returned values are correct.

## Testing

- `TestLookupGVK_CachesPerType`: two different instances of the same type only trigger one real lookup.
- `TestLookupGVK_CachesDifferentTypesSeparately`: two distinct types each trigger their own lookup, and don't share cached results.
- `TestLookupGVK_CachesMisses`: an unregistered type's failed lookup is also cached, not retried every call.
- Full existing package test suite passes unchanged, `getObjectInfo`'s returned values are identical to before, this only changes how often the underlying scan runs.

items.title: feat(pkg): add stripe-go compile-time instrumentation
items.body:
## Description


Adds compile-time OpenTelemetry instrumentation for `stripe/stripe-go`, covering the last two major versions (`v81` and `v82`) in accordance with ADR-0004.
### Design & Implementation Details
- **Single Hook Point**: Every `stripe-go` API call across all ~200 per-resource clients reaches the network through one unexported backend function: `(*BackendImplementation).requestWithRetriesAndTelemetry`. We hook this single function instead of generating hundreds of individual hooks for public client methods, eliminating maintenance overhead as Stripe adds new resources.
- **Span Structure & URL Templating**: Produces one `CLIENT` span per logical request covering the backend's internal retry loop. Spans are named `{METHOD} {url.template}` (e.g. `POST /v1/customers/{id}`). Resource IDs are templated out of the path to keep span names and metric labels bounded, while the raw path is retained on the span as `url.path`.
- **Package Layout & Semconv**:
  - `hook.go` is the only file in each module that imports `stripe-go`.
  - Span naming and attribute mapping logic resides in `semconv/`, which depends strictly on the standard library and OpenTelemetry. It is byte-identical between `v81` and `v82` (following the `openai-go` v1/v2/v3 precedent).
- **Docs & Schema Manifests**:
  - Added semantic convention definitions in `schemas/otelc/groups/stripe.yaml`.
  - Updated coverage tables in `docs/getting-started.md` and `schemas/otelc/README.md`.
  - Regenerated `tool/data/instrumentation-manifest.json`.
- **Testing**: Added unit tests in `hook_test.go` and `semconv/stripe_test.go` for both majors, along with integration test apps (`test/apps/stripeclient` and `test/apps/stripeclientv81`) and end-to-end integration tests.
- 
## Motivation

Provides automatic, compile-time OpenTelemetry instrumentation for Stripe API clients in Go applications without requiring manual tracer configuration or SDK wrapper boilerplate.
